WHY THE MEN DON'T PROPOSE. "Why don't the men propose?" you. ask , In a sighing sort of way; My reasons I would like to give, If you'll list to what I say. The fault is not your mother's, dear, That without saying goes, The fault is nearer home, my dear, Why men will not propose. You may have done your best, my dear, To make your " matches!' flame— They only strike upon that heart That Love his own may claim. You keep a watch for moneyed men, Or handsome dashing beaux; You care not for a loving heart— That's why men won't propose. You try the game of "languishing," Of seeming "quite too-too " A sorry mask! a veil of gauze! One glance will pierce it through. Your cleverness (aSsumed) is like Your gay and gaudy clothes; It cannot bide the crippled mind— That's why men won't propose. And next you try tha "simple" plan, Put on the " shy " and " coy " iri And though we prize simplicity, As gold without alloy, When 'neath her blushes truth is seen, Not so your artful "pose," Nor simple face with scheming soul— That's why we won't propose. "Now, what is to be done?" you ask (For Time goes rolling on),— Just take a gentle hint from me, Ere chances all are gone: Let truthful, unaffected grace A loving heart disclose; Then, should you take the hint, my dear, Why ! I'll at once propose. —Yorkshire Post.
Carittits.

Carve your name on hearts, and not on marble. Well arranged time is the sure mark of a welearrenged - mind: - "Ma," said little Johnny Snooper, "why do they always put in a scythe when they make' a picture of Time?" "To represent the shortness of Time, Johnny. Time cuts people down, you know.' "But whed Time shall be no mower, he'll drop his scythe, won't he?" It's time for you to go to bed, Johnny." "A man came in here one day," said the apothecary, "and asked for a 'raw shell' powder. He metiht a Rochelle powder. On another occasion a customer demanded a ' powder. He got it. A lady came in once, and, holding tins pint bottle. said, "What will you charge to fill this with pneumonia?" Collet, in his" Relics of leteratnreSr relateis that in a French translation of Robertson's "History of Scotland" the following passage occurs :—" Scon heating himself by the fire of his passions and his hatred, he bestirred himself like a madman; he broke his pulpit, and leaped into the midst of les auditors." This is intended for a rendering of that well-known passage respecting John Knox, which tells us that he was so active aild eigorous a preacher that he was like to ding the pulpit into blads and fly out of it. To Collet we are also indebted for the following instance of that species of mistake known as a Milson in one of his sermons says—" it is one amone many proofs of the wisdom and benevolence of Providence that the world was not created in the midst orw inter, when Adam and Eve could have found no- thing to eat; but in harvest time, when there was fruit on every tree and shrub to tempt the willing hand." TOPERS' BLUNDERS.—It goes without saying that those gentlemen who indulge too freely in the flowing bowl are often the perpetrators and victims of the most egre- gious blunders. Quite recently a jovial follower of Simon Peter treated us to a story anent an inebriated citizen 'who meandered down from somewhere at one in the morning, and coolly took a seat on the top of a coffee stall, which is said to stand at the corner of Boar- lane. There he mooned and soliloquised in his boozy way for many an hour, being all the while under the im- pression that he VMS on the Headingley tram. An in- stance of similar misapprehension is given in the pages of Punch i—A middle-aged individual, endeavouring to reach home after a "night" at the club, stumbled at length on one of those railed enclosures which are some- times to be foimd in the squares of large towns. Out friend being somewhat shaky on his legs welcomed the; railing as a friend in'need,' thinking by its aid to travel vet a little further in safety. The result was that he did 20 or 30 laps round a monument, and when it dawned upon him that he was playine the, gin-horse, he sank down in utter despair and remarked, "I'sh no go—l'll be hanged if therhaTnt gor or locked me in."—lderk- shire Post. wrivomEN.-=iirroiirclitia, and not long ago, he regarded as a gentleman who kept a gig,. He is a gen- tleman in one house who does not eat peas with his knife; in another, who es not to be discountenanoedeby any created form of butler. In my own case I have learned to move among pompous menials without much terror, never without much respect. In the narrow sense, and so long as they publicly tread the bo4rdsoL their profession, it would be difficult to find ebnre finished gentlemen; and it would often be a matter Of grave thought with me, sitting in my club, to compare: the hearing of the servants with that of those on vehlni they waited. There could be no question which were the better gentlemen. And yet I was hurried into no democratic theories; for I saw the members' part was the more difficult to play. I saw that to serve was a more graceful attitude than to be served, I knew besides that much of the servants' gentility was ad hoc and would be laid aside with their livery jackets; and to put the mat- ter in a nutshell, that some of the members would have made very civil tootmen and many of the servants in- tolerable mehabers. For all that, one of the prettiest gentlemen Fever knew was a servant. —Retie Louis Stevenson, in Scribner's Magazine for May. Two MILITIA STORIFS.—It seems to have been a very common fashion in Devonshire (says "Door Life of the Rev. John R,ussell"), in years gone by, for gentlemen of standing in the country to adopt the native dialect, especially when conversing with the country folk- habit arising either from carelessness, or perhaps becaesis the speech in that provincial form was best upderstemel by and most natural to the generatity of their neighbours. For instance, a colonel in the North s'Devon Militia was reviewing his regiment, and seeing 1 hare 'jtren up in the midst of his men, he shouted wildly, "There he go'th, boys, a lashing great shaver !'' Then, forgetting the exact point at which he had ceased to give the word of command, he turned round and said," Where wor I, drummer boy "Present arms, sir," responded the youth; and the inspection went on. Again, a Yeomanry regiment were enacting a sham fight among themselves, , when a Captain Pretty john was ordered to retreat before ' the, charge of the enemy. " Retrait! What doth • that Mane ?l' inquired the captain. " Retmit mean'th tinning &way, I aim. Then it shall never be told up to Dod- lirook Market that Captain Prid'gen and his bravo trool mined away." Accordingly. as the enemy came on, bearing down upon him at a rapid trot, he shouted to his troop, "Charge, my brave b'ys, charge Us bain't vexes, and they bain't hounds, us'll face 'em like men." The collision was awful—men, horses, and accoutre- ments strewing the ground on every' side, several troopers being more or less injured, while one positively refused to mount again, saying, "I've abrok'd my breeches already, cap'n, and I won't mount no more !" EtitILISTI SCHOOL ix PERIL : A REPLY.—The dangers we are warned against may be roughly classed as—first, the influence on English art of the works of foreign artists; and, secondly, the preseno.e of the English student abroad. I would like to submit. as a humble contribution to the discussion of a burning question, that the first "danger" is inevitable, and that, on the whole, this influence has been for good; and, in the second place, that the presence of the English student abroad, in yearly increasing numbers, points to but one conclu- sion: that our system of art education at home Is still ioadequate. It is but the symptom, and indicates its own remedy; and, until our doctors desist from de- nouncing the symptom, and set themselves to remedy . the disease, things will go on—for good or evil—much as they do now. The old English school, which is now held in such well-deserved honour, undoubtedly inherited the traditions of the many Dutchmen and , Fletnings who came over here, following the examples of' Vandyck, Lely, Van der Velde, &c. It grew in isolation,: concerning itself mainly with the facts of its time, and reached its greatest excellence about the time of Rey- molds and Ciainsborough, era little later, with Constable; its decline coincides with the rise of the Romantic or Heecrical" school, and the appearance of those old and esteemed favourites—the Cavalier, the knight in armour, the monk, the Roundhead, the distressed lady, and many another dear old puppet. . We spend money enough on our systems of art-eduction, but such per- sonal sacrifices as are made gladly and as a simple duty by the best French artists are absolutely unknown among us. Many of the best men give readily to their pupils, not a few days, but a considerable portion of their time, from year to year, absolutely gratis; and at the Beaux-Arts the profe-sors (such men as Cabanel and Gerocre, giving each two mornings weekly) receive, I am told, something like £l5O per annune—e'he Magazine of Art. . J. Round-, A.P.S., Dispensing Chemist, of Market ?lace, Susan's-road, Eaetbourne, says: "Up to five months ago I have been subject to the most sericus form of neuralgic attacks in the head and temples, whichl catrie'on always once a week, and sometimes as often as I once in four days. At such times you may imagine my sufferings were beyond description, and my business was thereby seriously interfered with. I had heard of St. Jacobs Oil, and immediately borrowed a bottle of a neighbour- ing chemist, and most remarkable to say. in less than WO hours from the time my wife rul be I' be Oil on my temple, I was free from pain, and able to attend to my business. But the most remarkable thing about it is, I have never had an attack of the neuralgia since ; there- fore I have no hesitation in saying that I believe St. Jacobs Oil to be the best known local remedy for neur- algia." •

div.head: ANOTHER CRACK WITH BOSW ELL.
div.p: ANOTHER CRACK WITH BOSW ELL.

Br SIGIL. It is now a few months since I published a series of sketches under the general title of "Cracks with Boswell." Since then business has debarred me the pleasure of spending much time with him. This, ram willing to admit, has been more my loss than his. [though I honestly believe that, such are his powers of 'adaptability, he can derive instruction', or amusement ftom a mule; therefore he will sometimes, when not otherwise engaged, waste a few idle moments on me. I was hurrying past his store the other afternoon, with my eyes bent pavementwards, my mind absorbed in the problems of abstruse ways and means, when I was sud- denly cut short in my wicked career by his sharp, decisive, and cheery, "so, ho !" Stopping with a jerk, as if my mainspring had snapped, I looked in his direc- tion, and, seeing his happy-looking dial in his doorway, I responded with a weak attempt at his style with, , "What, ho! my noble porridge basin cleaner! How wags the world ?" "Oh, gaily, gaily," he replied. Passing into his shop, I said, Well, and how are you getting on by this time ?'' "Well, aw corn'd say as aw all owt. So long akt aw con heyt four shives o tooast un a hofe-a-yard o' bacon, un sup a bowl full o' coffee to mi brekfast, aw dorn'd think as aw's tek much hort i' health; on if aw con keep middlin' clear o' t' paysons un tax collectors, aw con manage ml pockut, aw think." "You're makin' a queer mixture, aren't you, Boswell ?" " Wod paysons un collectors? Yo' may think saoa, but, by gum! they booath meean brass, when .;they torn up. One geils yo'r brass wi' cheek, on t' tether geds id hi law, un law runs queer, yo' kncrya*.: "Does it ? ' I asked. "Does Id! Aw should think id does. By gum! Bob Hindle, as use to live i' Eaeam, thowt sooa.' "Did he? What made him think so ?" "Aw dorred know wod med him think soon, but he sed id dud." "What caused him to say so ?" "Well, aw'll tell yo'. Dun yo' see, his brother, Fatt, Pratoes, as they co'd him, hed hanged hisseP, un were co'd on as a witness at t' crooner's inquest. MIL t' crooner axt him wod he knew abeawt t' case, he sed, 'Well, aw went up eawr stairs yesterday foornoon, u 4; aw see eawr Fatty Pratoes hangin' bi a rooap reawod his neck fro' t' bedpooast.' "

'Was he dead ? V crooner axt. 'Aw dorn'd know; he were frigglin'.' 'Did you cut him down?' ' Nowe.' 'You didn't ! Why, what did you do ?' r Aw went to t' teawn ho' for a policemon.' ' Andieft him hanging?' ' Aw never touched him.' 'Why didn't you cut him down?' t' crooner axt, varra aerply. Bob sed, 'Well, yo' know. t' law runs varra pare, sooa aw thowt wed better nod touch him tell aw geet a policemon.' Why, man; sed t' crooner, you deserve to be hanget yourself for leaving your poor brother in that Nedica- ment. How did you find him when you came back with the officer ?' I 'He'd done friggling.' 'Done friggling r sed t' crooner. 'You ought to be made to friggle yourself. Stand_down r ! Hezeyer bed a bit o' pleasure after thad, hedn'd Bob. 1 If he axt t' simplest queshton i' t' world off onybady, they were sure to ax him heaw t' law run afoor they'd 'answer hirn. , But talkin'abeawt hanginjust reminds me as aw were once welly dreawned." " Indeed ! How was that, Boswell? Were you bathing ?' " Well, aw were bathin' whel aw were i' V watther, but aw dudn'd intend to bathe afoor aw went in. But aw'll tell yo heaw id happened. _ Yo'll remember mo tellin' yoabeawt werkin' at Foryate factry?" • i " Yes." I "Well, id were theer wheer aw welly geet dreawned "At this Foryate factry t' winclin'-room is aboon t' mechanics' shop. T' mechanics' shop, yo' know, is wheer V mechanic, un t' joiner, no t' blacksmith werks. i "Neaw, there's nod so mony windin'-rooms as there isn'd one or two winders as is hot 'tins. Well, at ony. rate, there worn'd i' my day, un aw fancy as id'll be ,summat same yet. But at this Foryate windin'-room !there were three or four as dudn'd keer a rap for owt ,as coma, un wi' urn bein' wi' t' tother winders mi 'warpers ot' day through, they dudn't improve tint A gret deeal. They were them sooart o' lasses as would' iPlay a trick on onybody if they geet a chance. Wl' me beM' like at a lease end, aw often went i' V' windin'- room, un aw use to see ther bits o' tricks. I , Well, deawn below, it' tnechanies' shop, there were, I' 1 one corner, a place where o sooarts o' base tackle were kept, such as nuts; un bdwts, un screws, un nails, for t' joiner un t' mechanic. They were kept Ll drawers, un xes, un bags. Well, just aboon this corner there were 1 hoyle i' one o't' floorm' boards. Whether there were I knot eawt o't' booard aw dornd remember. Well, hen onybody went to this corner for a screw, or owt ~ttrad sooart, if ony o't' winders see urn, they'd drop 10, nae oil ,wt of a oilcan, or some watther, or tay, eawt m, of 'a kit, •on to uif they hed ony handy. Aw'd occasion txignoa or a nut one day, un, whel aw were lookin' ,for one t' size as aw wanted, some o't, winders tfropt a hofe a kitful o' tay deawn t' back o' mi neck. pn they dudn'd pick V tay- leeays eawt, aw con tell yo; bt' lot coom dashin' deawn mi neck, un on to rni heyd. Aw darted up into thad windin'-room un aw axt whoa'd done id, but aw nobbut geet laughed at. Nooan on urn would tell whoa'd done id. "Aw hed to find t' nut as aw wanted,but,by gum! put a lump c' sheet-iron on rot back whel aw we. Wain' for id. They'd a wet me through wi' oil un stufl if aw hedn'd Neaw, bear in mind. aw dudn'd feel satisfied at bein' dosed iike thad un nod payin' aornebry back for id. Aw'm nod exactly one o' thad lamb-like sooart as, when, onybody strikes mo on mi reight cheek aw torn unto um mi left. Nowe; if onybody strikes me on mi reight Cheek aw mon be do to thee left afoor they con wink. Well, aw felt thad way wi' these winders after they'd Put thad tay deawn mi neck. Aw couldn'd tell which on urn id wor as bed done id, un as nooan on urn would tell aw thowt 'Aw moo pay yo' backone or two at a time just as aw con catch yo'. But like as luck were i' mi favvour, for aw dorn'd think as id were aboon a fortnet or sooa at after when sumrnat torned up as- offered mo a chance o' geddin' a bit nearer streight wi' o t' lot. Neaw, at factries wheer there's spinnin' as weel as weyving id sometimes happens as t' winders lies to wait an heawr or two for twist. At these times t' maniger doesn'd allus aileaw t' winders to gooa hooatn, but keeps urn on t' premises sorts as they'll be i eady to start Ili soon as there's some twist for um. Well, at a time e' this sooart V winders 'II often gooa -in for enjoyin' thersels, either wi' rompin' abeavrt or playin' tricks wi' one another, or else wi' sotnbry else,. By gum! aw wodn'd a liked to a gone i' t' corner o' t'' mechanics' shop at Foryate whel t' winders were waitin' for twist. There's no tellin' wed they'd a put deawn thad hoyle. "Well, heawever, id happened one afternoon as V winders at Foryatn were waitin' for twist. After mar- lockin' awhile wi' one another they rued up the Mirada as they'd rnek a collection among thersels un hey a sit' of a sis. Aw just happened to pop in whel they were collectin' thee fourpences, un they med mepay- tupponce tort t' fund. .fter they'd collected aw stopped i' t' room to sea wed they were beawn to hey for thee brass. They decided to hey eighteen pennoth o' cooked herrin', some taycakes, un a pint o' rum. "Neaw, i' lots o' factries they'd a hed some difficulty i' geddin' this tackle inside, un id wodn'd a bin good to do at Foryate factry if them as fotched id hed had to gooa eawt t' gradely way, for they wodn'd a letten um gooa through t' watchheawse. They'd a better tip off than thad. They could manage id beawt gooin'• eawt o' t' wiudin' room. Done yo' see, one side o' this windin' room faced th' Hoyleheawse-loyn, un there were a row o' windows on this side. Well, they'd nowt to do nobbut °ppm one o' these windows un ax ony little lad or lass 'o gooa up to Mrs. Hadfield's, t' little toffy shop, or ony-

where else, un tell um to bring sooa no soca, no they'd bring id, un then they'd hoist id through t' windo' we a string. Well, o' this day as aw'm tellin' yo' on, they sheawted through t' windo' to a little lad, no ordered wod they wanted. "As soon as ever they'd gin ther order, un aw'd getten eawt o' t' room, id struck mo as there were a bit of a opportunity to ged streight wi' um for V tag trick, if aw could only ged at id reight. Aw just studied id *awt for a t,ooathry minnuts, un then id coom to mo like a flash. Aw bowted deawnstairs un into t' mechanics' shop. Aw geet t' joiner, un V mechanic, un t' blacksmith, no his striker together, on B,w sad, Neaw, chaps, are yo' oppen for a bit of a spree ?" . "They o sad, 'Aye. Wod is id, Boswell? "Aw sad, "T winders is waiting for twist, un ther , beawn to hey a bit of a sis. They'n sent up Foryate for some cooked herring, un some buttered taycakes, un a 'pint o' rum: _ _ _

' bi thad?' t' blacksmith sed. "Wed bi thad ?aw sed. Are yo' willin' to heyt, un sup id ?' "Aye!' they o sed in a chorus. But heaw hey we to ged "Aw sed, Fotch a. kit full o' watther to mix wi' th' ,rum, no aw'll tell yo'. But be sherp.' "After they'd getten t' watther aw sed, Neaw then, ther beawn to hoist this tommy un rum up eawt o' t' ,rooad, un into t' windin' room wi' a piece o' string. Neaw, they"l hoist this stuff °together in a basket, un as it's gooin' up kill hey to pass one o' these windo's CV mechanic's shop hed a row o' windo's at t' same side). Well, just as it's passin', somebry mon ged howd on id in drag id in.' "'By gad! we'll do id, certain,' sed t' blacksmith; id'll be a grand spree.' "0 t' tethers chimed in willin', sooa aw sed, Fasten thad dooar, sooa as they cornd ged in when we'n getten id.' - "They lastened t' door, un to mek t' thing eeasier they took part o' two windo's eawt—thad part as swings, yo know, Then t' blacksmith un t' striker stood on t' bench waitin' for t' tomnay un rum comin'. "We hedn'd mony minute to wait afoor a woman coom potterin' deawn t' loyn wi' a basket. They wer waitin' for id. But they hed to throw t' brass deawn to th' owd woman afoor hoo'd send t' basket up. They paid, un then they dropped ther string, un th' owd woman fastened id to t' basket handle, un then id begun gradually tetrise. We were oas quate as meauses when ' t' basket coom sect. Just as th' handle geet aboon th' oppen windo', t' striker seazed howd on id, un he whipped id inside beawt onybody sein' whori'd done id. In a crack t' string were cut, un afoet. yo' could a sett howd onlWe'd o a dobbin o' rum un wattber, i' kits Of kit-lids. "Eh, ther wor a pantomime, aw con tell yo'! ot' winders coom brustlin' deawn them stairs,- un int 6 _ .

factry yard, like a swarm o' hummerbees. When they fun as t' mechanic's shop door. were fast, they welly went mad ; un when they loolitthrough t' windo's un see us stannin' reawnd t' basket; un pitchin' into t' tay- cakes un th' herrin', un t' rum, they fair danced,un they skriked fost ut one windo' un i then t' tother, like stuck pigs. They co'd us everything as they could think on, whether id wer' fit or nod. Every time as we supped we med mooations to urn as if we were drinkin' ther healths, un thad dud wos then oat um. But id unfortunately hap- pened for me as they blamed me for o t' job. If id hedn'd a bin as they'd sent for some rum aw believe they'd a towd t' gaffer, but they dosn't, because bringin' spirits into t' factory were ageean t' rules. Well, we dosn't at- tempt to oppen Clad dooar whel they were theer, un we hed to keep id locked for aboon a hafe an heawr, tell some twist coom deawn eawt o' t' apinnin' room,un then they bed to gooa to ther werk. By gum! but 'aw kept eawt o' ther gait for three or four days ; after thad aw geet friendly wi' urn ageean. Neaw, whenevpryo'rplayin'practical jooaks it's allus 'dangerous to operate on a lot, because there's sure to be some among a lot as con play at thad game thersels Aw've played mony a trick on fooak, un aw've nod allus getten off scot free. Aw dudn'd ged altogether clear i' thad job. Them winders put ther heyds together, un they arranged a little simple trick as landed mo fairly. Aw II tell yo' heaw they dud 020. c "In a spinnin'-room they use two sooarts o' cans for tiler anis, little uns for weft, un big uns for twist. "Soma, o'. these twist cans bed hoyles punched t' botto4l, un odd uns hedn'd. Well, these winders one day geet oteth' these, twist cans un they tried id if id would howd %smaller. They fun eawt wheer id lecked ,un they med th' hoyles up wi' sooap. Then they filled id ageean welly wi' watther, un they mixt some sooart o' black stuff among t' watther, vaira likely soot. They then put some thin bits o' booards on t' top o' t' watther, un two layers o' twist cops at' top o' t' bits o' booards, un they med it look like as nice a can o' twist as ever yo' see i' yo'r life. Then they put id at side o' t' door un lookt eawt for me, "Id wornd so varra long after they'd !fled ready for mo when they see mo comin' deawn t' yard. Bi t' time as aw geet upstairs there were some on um stannin' reawnd this can, un one or two were stannin' dooar- hoyle, wi' t' dooar oppen. Just as aw appeared one at side o' t' dooar sed, 'Here, Boswell 'll do id for us.' "Aw sect Aye, wocl is id? Aw 11 do owt for yo' as 'll pleeaseyo'. Aw like to do owt for women.'

_ . "They sed, There's a can o' twist here as we want dividin' among us; just divide id for us, Boswell,' un the o' howded ther brats eawt. "Certainly,' aw sed. • Heaw mony on yo' is there? "'Seven,' they sed. 0' reet, howd yo'r brats,' un aw bent deawn o'er this can un put mi hands eawt to ged howd of a toothry cops. "They dudn'd gi'e mo time to ged howd o' ony cops, for just as mi fingers touched urn two on um gra mu a shove. Aw tried to stop misel puttin' mi hands on t' cops, bud, them givin. way, aw lost misel °together un splashed o'er heyd un shoothers inter t' nasty watther. To mek t' thing wos aw lost mi feet, un upset t' can, un rolled o'er wi' id. Wi' id cumin' so suddenly mirth aw should think aw swallowed aboon a pint o' t' swatther. • -tv I_ll I- "Yc7fl wertidWed aw dud at um. Aw dud nowt. Wod c• uld air do at a lot o' lasses un women? and mental considerations affecting the progeny. But in many royal families, more especially those of Gertnan origin, the practice is co.nmon enough; which possibly accounts for the personal deteriora- tion manifested in some branches. There was a report that something in the shape of a birthday present to Queen Victoria was to be made to-day by the announcement of the engagement of Prince Alexander of Battenberg and the Princess Victoria, a match upon which the Queen has set her heart. But Prince Bismarck is immovable on this point, and is supported by the unmistakeable sentiment of , the German nation. The Germans think it is all very well for a daughter of the English Royal Family to marry a Battenberg. We have no Bis- mark to veto such a Misalliance. But it is not good enough for Germany and the Germans. London, as far; as Clubland and the haunts of society in the park are concerned, has distinctly emptied during the.Whitsun holichys. But there are still alew millions of people here, and London to-day is at its very best. The parks are a delight. trees and grass benefiting by the sudden incursion of spring weather. It is years since there was such ' holiday time ,as was kept here on Monday and Tuesday. All the vast pcpulation of London was out and about, and the railways and omnibuses and river steamboat service. fortuitously just re-estab- lished. had one of the best days in their record. Railways generally have profited, by the bursting forth of spring. The traffic returns, published to- , day, show enormous increases all round. The Lan- , cashire and Yorkshire, and the London and South- Western each nett over .£O,OOO increase in the week's takings as compared with last year, whilst the Midland took over .£19,000 more, the Great Wes- tern over .£20,000, and the North-Western at the top of the tree with an increase of .£26,369. This is before Whitsun week, and it is likely the traffic returns for the• current week will be even more magnificent In the Cromwell-road there is a national museum which cost some money, and is very little known to the multitude, but does much good in quiet ways. It is the Natural History Museum, of which Professor Flower is director. with a staff which, together with other expenses, including pur- chases, p costs over E 43,000 'a year. ' Mr. Ruskin knows the/ Museum, and has just given tangible proof of liii appreciation of its work. Amongst his posscssions,were a mighty Cape diamond and a fine ruby. He has presented these gems to the Museum. with the stipulation that they shall bear for all time certain labels 'which he has written. That at- tached to the diamond runs thus: "The Colenso Diamond, presented by John Ruskin, in honour of his friend, the loyally and patiently admantine first Bishop of Natal." The ruby carries the legend, "The Edwardes Ruby, presented by John Ruskin, in honour of the invincible soldiership and loving equity of Sir Herbert Edwardes' rule by the shores of Indus." • ' The negotiation', with the managers of the. Paris Exhibition which Buffalo Bill recently carried on having fallen through, that eminent citizen has re- turned to the United States, taking his cowboys and the Deadwood Coach with him. He will setup his eStablisliment in the vicinity of New York, and hopes to do a good business. In the meantirtie, bereft of Buffalo Bill, and with John L. Sullivan gone "on the drink," we are promised a new sensa- tion from Ameri,mt in the shape of the arrival of two base ball clubs. Base ball, it will be remembered, is the national game that Little Lord Fauntleroy pro- posed to teach his grandfather. The enterprfse is pot without its risks, seeing that fourteen! years ago two base ball teams visited England, and:proved a lamentable failure. English people thought Vase ball slowand the teams in despair took to cricket. But they mean to try egain. , , •i•

ANNUAL MEETING. The annual meeting of the Liberal "300" Council ot the Newton Division *Ai held at the Co-opera- tive Hall, Earle-street, Earlestown, on Fridayy etening.' There Was a Very good attendance of representatives from .41 Parts of the division, and Mr. Charles Pilkington, J.P., chairman of the association, presided: Among those present' in addition were ,Messrs. George W. Rawlins (Rain- bill), G. E. Parker (Warrington), F. A. R. Neill (13old), Rawlinson (Newton), J. Mitchell (Ash- -ton), 11 Douglas (Goiborne), P. M. Campbell (regis- ttation' oxen ),

- , • !The Chairman said that before they proceedpd with alikbdiiness he would like to make a personal statement: Having lately 'terminated his business , engagements in that part of the country he had removed -to near. Man- chester, and he felt it his duty to resign the chairman- ship of that Council. He had thought -of resigning when he fir removed, but he had stnek to his gu3ta, bblievingit would be better to resign later On. He then traced the history of the association . m the time when they broke away fretn the old [ uth-West Lancashire Association, and refettitirtOthe ' first election they had, when Colonel McCorquodale or.- tr posed Sir Richard-Cross, he said the Colonelfoug right well. He Wei Well" Supported by all, and altb hhe did not win, Sir Richard's majority iv a very small one indeed. He referred to the two following ,elections, the ,nd of which, he said, was their great difficulty. r eof the leading men had gone overoto,t4o. Unionist - arty, and they had, left the Liberal side, Which, of ,cburse, Meant that'they had Nvithdraivn Mehl 'support. ,Ile believed they had now seen the worst in that resoct, and althotigh they had been defeated in the'eleetiony Of The past, perhaps tictory might be nearer than some of them Supposed. He referred to the fact that Mr. Cabp- hell •is-as about to leave them; and said that gentleman had worked very hard, and had now got the registration into an efficient state. He was sure ' they all felt very _sorry Mr. Campbell was about to leave them, and he would go away with their very best wishes for his future success. (Applause.' They must not suppose that the work of the Liberal party in the past had , been lost, for the measures that were now being passed were Liberal measures, so Liberal indeed that four years ago none of them would have thought they would become law. He would resign the chairmanship that night—but he could not say he would be leaving them altogether. IN TERRORNM., - Madame de Coulon, for the IWort time she is in London has taken-a suite Of rooms atClaridge's and there, accompanied only by a confidential maid and a: old Russian man-servant, who seems devoted to hei ,she appears to be thoroughly enjoying London fashionable life. Like Prince Sergius, she speaks English fluently, to the intense surprise of all those whom she informs that she has ne•Ter been in England before. That she will repeat the visit there seems to be litth. . doubt, that if admiration and adulation are pleasing to Berthe de Coulon as they are to most women. Not but what she is thoroughly accustomed to them, only London is a novel-hunting ground, and she delights in "fresh fields and pastures new." She glories, ,morenver, in the fact that she has made a thorough conquest of Ferdinand Stanhope. Prince Sergius, when he invited her over "to play hostess for . him at his fete, had bidden her for his sake to make as good an impression as possible on the Stanhopes. The mode, however, in which that impression should be made, and the member of the family selected for it, are not exactly what Sergius Lenskeff intended. While she sits in a pretty morning neglige tipping, chocolate,about twelve o'clock, on the day after the 'CM she is reading a letter that has been brought in on the tray with others. "It is from Princ,e Sergius himself • must have been written before he went to bed," she observed to, herself as She opened it.. Aye, Written in the flush of some annoyance with Berthe, whom he was almost sorry he had not left in Paris, sb different a part was he 'playing to that which he had intend e(k for her

" Irene jealous! Lady Fedora inclined to regard her as an intrtgante, who would lure her troublesome younger son into an even greater amount of mischief than that 'in 'which he was already involved! Fer- dinand himself madly in love !" This was scarcely the mode in . which Prince Sergius intended Rutile to make herself ' agreeable to the Stanhopea, and so he told her in absolutely fierce language—so fierce that she -tossed the letter from' her with irritation and exelainied— " I will not be tutored by Prince Sergius; were it not for ,this young Englishman, who pleases me, I. would return to Paris to day. Tiensf if I could per- suade the young savage to go with me! I cannot see either what Sergius wants me to do. Why should I have a magic influenbe' Over these 'Stanhopes, so as to enable him to marry that white-faced Irene? I suppose, I ought to have devoted myself to the two elders and bewitched them as I know I can " (with a glance at a mirror) "then I should have been . sent, as ainbassadress to demand Mademoiselle Irene's 'hand for the Prince. Pah ! Well, I preferred ce beau -*Ferdinand ; and the, mother thinks me an intrigante ; I wonder what the father thinks. Sergius does net mention liim—he only looked at me -I- will give, him a chance of saying a few words when next we meet." She took up the next missive. "To-day, at five, Lady Fedora Stanhope at !Mine." "Generous-minded woman, who can open herdoor to an intrigante I Only intrigantes,lsimpose,who come in the train of a prince. Madame, have no doubt Oil the subject; I will make you nay for that observa ton. I wonder why Sergius told me; it was with a- intention ; he never acts without. Intrigante, Indeed next perliaps she will say that I, the daughter of a 'Russian noble, am also an adventuress. I will teach .:her to beware. Intrigante !an intrigante can work Much misery, my lady Fedora." . At last . the chocolate was drunk, and the subject having been mentally discussed with more -persist- ence than feather-„braseed Berthe de Coulon usually bestowed on any one thing, she rang the bell for the confidential abigail, who was French. "I we.nt the most becoming toilette I possess ; I am going to an up/Iv-midi vu the—as they call it in this country—at the house of some great English people.' "The blue satin embroidered in pearls is charming, Madame." "Absurd, Denise; you are mad. Simpli English taste best. L.-my pink Cotton with straw bonnet, trimmed with rose-buds." "Mais, Madams c'est mac toilette de eampagne." ," Then they can't say it is use toilette d'intri- lante," she answered, laughing; "go quickly and get it ready."!' Denise understood nothing about the " Intel- gantc•"-joke, but went off With notes' an ah ! and oh! to do her mistress's bidding. And very sweet and captivating Berthe de Coulon looked in her simple, Isat exquisitely made, little cotton dress, and most :gracefully. did she accept the homage she received, ' she appeared in the Eaton-spate diawing. - !It was not very full of guests, the party lacing in impromptu one, and composed chiefly of people ,whom Lady Fedora had invited verbally at. Prince Sergius' Ote, to which 'she intended it to be a 'serli ~y of The prince had already arrived, when Madame de Coulon entered: and he was bending over the now radiant Irene in tender and earnest conversation. Irene rose, however, when she saw Madame de Coulon, and came towards her with extended haralsr: " Beni ! The Prince and mademoiselle tinders" stand each other," decided the widow," or, she would not be so civil to me, for I see she does not like we. And she was right. Irene's reception was almost toe cordial to be genuine, anti the expression of her face almost told the fearful eflbrt she was making. . "Pttuvre petite, this is by no means the last time you will be compelled to appear what you are not 0'44 a dire, if you marry our Russian bear," thought ,he to herself, as she talked gay platitudes to oe and looked searchingly rousd the room for .:rdintind, who was not there. !" Ordered to stay away," she, decided, "lest I iould throw the mantle of my charms more nnpletely over him? • No use, papa and mamma tailbone ; these thingsSnever are. If I 4nean'to Ave Ferdinand for a. 'slave, I'll have hhttl nevet ear, whatever yon"tiiity do to prevenf,' it.; Ah, here is M., Stanhope' glaring at me; `ifte if thought my beauty eclipsed his daughter's.. Geed' nfree de fennille these English, to I have always wird: Ile is coming across the room to see snore closely whether tam really as dreadful TOI lani lainted. An intrigante t perhaps he never saw fag :fore." • . !When Henry Stanhope came up, Irene introduced. him to the wicloiv, and then moved away to con: 'verse with some guests who had just arrived. 'Henry Stanhope's manner when lie addressed Madame dc Coulon was almosttender ; it would havesurprised her had she known how stern he usually was, but I she was too much accustomed to empressement and ,tenderness from men,to regard it as anthhig unusual. ; Ferdinand was not there, why not captivate the rather? "I am so gla to have an 'opportunity of talkirax to you," she said '4 Prince Sergius tells me you have Sbeen in Ritmo& .A.,link between Me and any country, oiew that I az vriteng strangers, is most precious." 1" You sureektvior feel that you are in a strange 'laid," said at Dtuthope, gallantly. "It is long ago since I was in Russia; yoneould not have been born." " Oh,l am older than you think—a widew, you know:" He bowed, as he- said casually, French." "My poor husband was French. div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.

THE SITUATION ABROAD.—GATHERING SHADOWS. lbausssis, SUNDAY Nrelac.—The St. Petersburg corre- -BOondent of the Nord, says: "Every Power is uncertain of the morrow, and consequently is bound to extreme reserve. Germany is only half reassured by the im- proved health of the Emperor; France is struggling with the Boulangist crisis, which paralyses her political activity; Italy is waiting to see what her neighbours will ; and England is preparing for every event. Austro-ilungary alone, or rather Hungary, seems agitated by warlike convulsions, which happily no one considers serious, as they are caused by the necessity of keeping up the zeal of her clients—the Balkaric rulers, Who, without foreign support could net stem the national currents against which they have undertakento Btnlggle." VIENNA, MONDAY Me:KT.—The news reteeived by the Austrian Intelligence Department from the Russian 'Provinces bordering on Galicia continues to wear a 3'rious aspect Three high officers, headed by Major- 'General von der Puaitz, chief of the general stiff of the 12th German Army Corps, which is the army of the Icingdom of Saxony, have come for the purpose of making themselves acquainted with certain details of the military arrangements of Austria. The military Preparations these officers are to inspect in Galicia have a special interest for them., as in case of war it would be the Saxon Army Corps that would of all the German forces 'most require to know Galieia in the almost cer- tain event of Germany assisting Austria. PARIS, Mormay Ilions.—Fourteen of the large ocean steam vessels belonging to the Messageries Maritimes and'the Transatlantic Company ore to receive the neces- sary additions to ,enable them to be at the shortest notice transformed into vessels of war capable of serv- ing as auxiliary cruisers. A commission, composed of naval officers and engineers, has been sent from Cher- bourg to Havre to determine the armament of the steamers of the Yrartsatlantic Company. A similar ' commission will be sent from Toulon to Marseilles to ' decide on the armament of the vessels of the Messageries Maritime.

THE VATICAN AND THE 'IRISH NATIONALISTS. Romp, Mr.IDAT Nionr.—The defiant Attitude of the ' Irish Nationalists towards the Papal Rescript has made ' absolutely no impression on the Vatican, •which indeed ~, regards the manifestoes and speeches cf the Parnellite Party with ,00mplete indifference, It is quite taken for . granted at the Vatican that the Pope will not allow him- ' selfito be intimidated, his Holiness being moreover fully • Persuaded after the collective adhesion of the Irish epis- copacy to the terms of the Rescript that the clergy and the real Catholic population will submitv to his injunc.- ,; tong withont hesitation. It is by no means improbable 'i that the document containing the adhesion of the bishops will 'be publishedthnrtly in order .., to allow it to be seen that the 'higher clergy of I, Ireland are not with the Parnellitee. 'The statement of Mr. Fitzgerald, the president of the *National League in the United States, that the Catli, lil papers of America do not approve of the Papal Rego p is,a, good deal won- , 0.. dered at here, as it is impossible to 'see on what it is I' . based unless it he the imagination .Of Mr. Fitzgerald. TERRIBLE FLOODS IN "(THE UNITED STATES. Naw 'YOUIC, MONDAY NIGHT.—This year's flood of the Mississippi has been the most destructive within recol- lection. For 100 miles south of Keokuk the river aver- 'Tea seven miles wide. Every levee or dyke between Reokuk and Alton has been destroyed. In Alexandria (Missouri) the only spot above water is not large enough to hold 50 people. The churches are entered through the upper halves of the windows from boats in the main streets- People reside on the ,second floors of such houses as have not fallen down. Eight thousand acres Of fine farming 'lands in Missouri are inundated. One levee, which cost $750,000, has been washed away, ex- Posing 125,000 acres to a flood of water. The damage by the flood to' the crops is esttinated,at $3,000,000, and to buildings $1,000,000 more.

• THE GERMAN ROYAL MARRIAGE. -"'"-'141s, CaantorrEmazrao, THURSDAY.—The marriage of Prince Henry of Prussia and the Princess Irene of Hesse was • solemnised here to-day. At the stroke of twelve o'clock all the bells in Oharlottenburg began ringing to announce that the ceremony in the chapel had commenced, and at half-past twelve o'clock a salute of thirty-six guns an- nounced that the bride and bridegroom had exchanged rings. The Emperor Frederick and the Empress Augusta 'were both present. Prince /teary, the own Prince, who wore a naval uniform, and Field-Marshal Count Moltke were received on their arrival with enthusiastic cheers by the thousands of people who ware assembled ' outside the castle.' „ •CHARLOTI'ENIIIIII.O, THURSDAY, 4 P.M. Their ,„ ye Highnesses received a most enthusiastic ovation .itom the dense crowds assembled on the road from the •castle and at the-station. " ANOTHER PRISON" TRAGEDY. div.head: KYURRENT POLITICS
div.p: KYURRENT POLITICS

At a Meeting of the Aberdeen Town Cooneft,on Mon- day, it was unanimously resolved to confer the freedom of the city on the Marquis of Lorne on the occasion of pending visit. A proposal to confer &similar honour on the Marquis of Mindy was lost, the minority declaring that the refusal was an insult to the Gordon clan. _ _

Speaking at a Friendly Society's gathering at Wilton on Monday, Sir Thomas Grove, M.P., stated that Mr. lter Lang, M.P., had called him an unmitigated hum- bug. He wrote to Mr. Long asking him to retract, and Mr. Long insinuated that he (Sir Thomas) had impugned his veracity. Sir Thomas denied having done so, and said when a man had insulted him as he was insulted by. Mr. Long, who was a mere windbag in reality, it was his duty to reply. Mr. Gladstone has written the following letter to Mr. Theodore Fry, M.P., in acknowledging the receipt of a protest against coercion by the Home Rule members el the Society of Friends:—" My dear sir,—l have to acknowledge with much pleasure the declaration which ycu have sent me. Quite apart from any such definite evidence, it would, I assure you, have been difficult t. persuade me that any large number of the Society of Friends were so little in harmony with the noble society traditions of their body as to approve of the coercive policy now being pursued in Ireland.—l remain, dear Mr. Fry, faithfully yours, W. E. GLADS ram" •

Mr. Gladstone has written an important letter en .the practice in Ireland of enlarging. criminal sentences on appeal. It is a practice, he says, that he shall continue to censure. When it was challenged in the House of Commons, the Government gave no intimation that there were precedents for this shameful procedure; but he had been tardily informed that the same thing had been done when he and his friends were in power. It WAS without his knowledge; and it was with knowledge in matters not directly of executive action that re- sponsibility began. He was glad the discovery hadA been made, for it was a new proof how deeply the spirit! ot evil had entered into Irish administration. Practices seemed to survive which disgracedthe name of justice, and would not be tolerated for a moment on this side of the Channel; and he hoped Mr. BaTfour would drag into daylight other evil usages which had disgraced Irish judicature and administration, for he woAd thus supply new proofs of the necessity and advantage of investing the Irish people with power over affairs properly their, own, and of providing that they Should be governed in a rational spirit.

div.head: HOW COERCION PS -JUSTIFIED.
div.p: HOW COERCION PS -JUSTIFIED.

Not much importance is attached to the so-called evelations as to the Clan-na-Gael It was always known, writes a Liverpool journal, London Corre- spondent, that there was a band of men ripe for mis- chief, and as opportunity makes the thief, so occasion brings forth the conspirator. As a.matter of fact there is no reason for publishing the story at present, except that the Scotland-yard authorities think that by a timely warning they may be saved trouble in futures The story is consequently so vague that it may apply to anybody and to nobody in particular. It is scarcely a secret that the police are at the back of the warning which has been issued. But if they 1-- n much as they profess to do, it would surely be arrest the parties suspected if ever they attempted to land in England, and the announcement is so issued that it koks very much like a political move. If there are no outrages to justify coercion, and you cannot create them, then suggest them and take credit for having swevented that which was 'never intended.

div.p: • 'THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.
'INTERVIEW WITH LORD CRANBORNE,

On Saturday. the representatives of several local authorities interested in the Local Government Bill had an interview with Lord Cranborne at the offices of the Blackburn Board of Guardians. Amongst those present at the interview were Mr. R. Reddish. Chairman of the Board of Guardians; Mr. Adam Dugdale, J.P., Mr. R. H. Wraith, .I:P., Mr. R. C. Radcliffe, Clerk to the Guardians; Mr. S. Longworth, Mr. A. Clayton, Mr. R. Chippendale, • Clerk to the Harwood Local Board; Mr. Smith. Clerk to • the Clayton-le-Moors Local Board;' Mr. Helm. Clerk to the Rishton Local Board, and others.—Mr. RADCLIFFE and Mr. Cnrrerxnate explained at, some length the grievances which they were likely to suffer if the Local Government Bill was carried in its present form, and they urged his lordship to use his influence to obtain certain modifications in the measure, particularly in rela- `tion to the question of repairine main roads. 'Lord CRANDORNE expressed himself as being highly •pleased that he had had an opportunity of meeting the deputation, from whom valuable information had been obtained. He promised that the matters mentioned ehould have his closest attention, but said he must re- frain from pledging himself to any particular course, as further information might modify his opinion. • The deputation thanked his lordship, and then with-- drew. A special session >f the Grand Lodge of England was held on Saturday, at the Raffles Memorial Schools, Liver- pool. On the motion of the Mayor of Tynemouth (Mr. George Dodds), seconded by Mr. J. Edwards, District Chief of East and Mid-Cheshire, a resolution was unani- mously passed condemnatory of the licensing and com- pensation clauses of the Local,Government Bill. Copies of the ,resolution were ordered to be sent to several M.:P.'s. THE LICENSING CLAUSES. Mr. Caine, M.P., has put cloven three further amend- ments to the Local Government Bill to raise the other side of the compensation question. They provide (1) that whenever oh any licensed premises any person is furnished with drink to excess, and afterwards such person while in a state of intoxication from such drinking , has cometo his death by suicide or drowning or othei Accidents caused by such intoxication, the keeper of such ;dace shall be liable to prosecution by the representatives of the deceased; (2) that any person injured in person or Property by one intoxicated, mar enter an action of com- pensation against either or both the inebriate and the per. win or persons who furnished the liquor; (3) that the relatives, guardians, or employers of any inebriate, may eive notice Jo any licensed person not to serve such in- ebriate with int,oxicants. and may recover from five to one hundred pounds as compensation front such licensed Person if lie furnishes the inebriate with intoxicants during one year after such notice. Laws similar to , these proposals are in force in Canada, and also in the ctates of Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island, New York, Penrovlvania, Kansas, Nebraska, Vermont, ()hie, Michigan, Wisconsin, Arkansas, Missotwi, and West Virginia. In some States license-holders give bonds on which they may be sued, and in Vermont must pay one dollar a day to wives whose husbands tire imprisoned; for intoxication. The Good Templars have proposed the introduction of a Civil Damage Bill into Parliament,. and this has been approved by Messrs. Caine. Cossham, Mc..Lagan, Clark. Burt, and other members of Perlin- inent Mr. Caine's amendments, however; will raise the question.

VIOLENT THUNDERSTORM. - FOUR

PERSONS KILLER—AN ASYLUM SET ON FIRE. Glasgow was late on Saturday afternoon visited by he severest storm of thunder, accompanied by lightning .nd rain, which has been experienced for many vear. Alwmt five o'clock in the afternoon three sehoolboyS were "Tossing Glasgow Green, when two of them were -truck down by lightning. A regiment happened to be 44- drill close by, and two of the regimental ambulance rps ran forward, and found both boys dead. Their ,ames are Charles Mandougal, aged nine, rind William M.Fedents. Macdougall has a black mark round his ;leek, and his companion's hair and chest were badly 4,•orcheri. The ground near by was torn up by • lightning. The third boy had a miraculous --cape, as he was close beside his companions at \the- • imp. About the same time two boys reported at, (loran Police Station that two men were lying at the it elf-way louse on the road to Pinsley. A 1). ainbu la nce waggon was speedily despatched. One of the men was quite dead, while the other was lying insensible. when the latter recovered consciousness he gave his name as W. Sharp, a joiner, of 13roomielaw-road. Govan. Though ,mffering, from the shock caused by the lightning he is ^xnected to survive. The man who was killed is atrout 5'5 year of age, but his name and address are not yet' A perfect deluge of rain came down between wo and five in the afternoon all over Glisgow, and the thunderstorm prevailed with great severity, the rain 4.l(inm ceasing, while at intervals heavy shovers of hail came down. When the storm ceased, the air felt much the purer.

_ A violent thunderstorm broke over Dumfriesshire in he aftarrnoon. • At Cloaeburu, about 1.2 miles from DIIIII- - a man who as driving a pair of horses in a field wts struck by. delitning and instantly killed. The tiorses were also killed. Many large trees have been rri up by the roots, and much damage is reported from various parts of the district,

Whik, the storm was raging in Fifeshire, the County Lunatic Asylum, near Cupar, was struck by lightning and set on ire. The patients, numbering 300, were placed in safety. The femaJes were very much alarmed. hut the nialesibelped much with tho fire engines. One man, however, ,got on the top of the ridge and played antics. and refoced to come down till showered on with the water hose. The damage to the buildings is esti- mated at over £2,000. A violent thuneerstorm broke over the village of Allonby, Cumberland, on Saturday afternoon. Three houses od the seashore were struck by lightning and the fluid passed down the chimneys of each of the three houses. The furniture was smashed to pieces. An almanack hanging in a kitchen was torn into shreds, and the paper was stripped from, the walls. The glass of a picture was shatterecninto fragments, leaving the picture itself uninjured. The gilding of a picture-frame hang- ing in another of the houses was taken off as though it had been scraped away. Urs. Carruthers, who was in one of the porches, had a very narrow escape; the lightning knocking her cle.wn and rendering her insensible. She soon recovered, however, and is not seriously injured.

The war balloon Rookwood made.an ascent from the Swansea racecourse on Monday, in charge of aeronaut Simmons. After crosalngtha Bristol Channel, the balloou boded safely it Sialoaft.,, Bornerietabire.

div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

• THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 26, 1888. 1 RELAND. The Land Sub-Commissioners gave judgment, on Satur- day, at Limetick in 65 cases, in which tenants had applied to have judicial rents fixed. Reductions were made, ranging from 15 to 50 per cent, and averaging 33 per cent The magistrates at Dungannon, on Saturday, rejected a claim of £6O for the burning of a barn, declaring it accidental, though reported as an outrage.—Police- Sergeant Hutchinson explained that he reported all such matters as outrages, having no other official forms. Moonlighters, on Sunday night, attacked the house of tanner, named Riordan, at Doolaig, near Castleisland. Riordan's sons returned the marauder's fire, and kept them at bay until a police patrol, attracted by the firing. arrived. Five young men who were running away from the spot were arrested and lodged it Castleisland police barracks. A daring robbery took place, on Saturday afternoon, at the Royal Bank, Dublin. Mr. John Douglas, linen draper, Wexford - street, Dublin, entered the head office of the bank in Foster-place to make a deposit of £ll5, all the money being in notes. While he was standing at the counter one of two men suddenly asked him, "Is this the Hibernian Bank." Mr. Douglas turned round obligingly, explained to his inter- rogator that he had made a mistake, and explained the situation of the Hibernian Bank. The man expressed his thanks, and left the building, and immediately after- wards Mr. Douglas missed the notes, which had doubt- less been stolen by the second man while the brief con- versation was going on. RELEASE OF MR. CONDON, M.P.—ANOTHER SENTENCE. Mr. Condon, M.P., was released from Cork Gaol on Sunday morning, on the completion of his sentence of 14 days' imprisonment, passed on him under the Crimes Act for taking part in an unlawful assembly. Be was met outside the gaol by the Mayor and the High Sheriff, and was accompanied by a number of people to the Mayor's office. Addressing the people, Mr. Condon said as long as the Castle rule and British law existed in Ireland, so long would he be found its fee. He afterwards left for Mitchelstown. Mr. Condon, M.P., was sentenced to a month's im- prisonment at Mitchelstown, on Monday, for inciting cer- tain persons not to fulfil their legal obligations. The counsel for the defence, Mr. Deasy, M.P., asked that the sentence should be increased in order to admit an appeal, but this was refused. and Mr. Condon was removed to gaol.

THE PAPAL RESCRIPT.—MEETING OF J' NATIONALISTS. A meeting in support of the action of the Roman Catholic members in the Irish Parliamentary party in reference to the Papal Rescript was held on Sunday in Pheessix Park. There was a large attendance. Among those present were Messrs. T. Sexton (Lord Mayor of Dublin), T. Harrington, John Dillon, William O'Brien J. P. Clancy, J. E. Redmond, David Sheehy, Crilly, Cox, M. J. 'Kenny, M.P.'s, and others. The Lord Mayor in opening the proceedings said he felt it his duty to remind them that, while they were entitled -to speak clearly and act firmly in the assertion of their political rights, it was their duty also not to forget for a single moment the profound veneration which, as Catholics, they owed to the Holy See. The Irish Catholics were connected for different purposes and in different ways witlk two powers. By their free con- sent they were linked in their spiritual affairs with the Holy See, and against their will for the purpose of secu- tar laws to the Parliament of England. Their religion /VW independent of England, and their politics were independent of, Rome: and they would as soon think of taking their politics from the palace by the Tiber as their religion from the Parliament of England. A resolution was moved to the effect that " This meeting of the citizens of Dublin cordially endorses and adopts, in their integrity, the resolutions of the Irish Catholic members of Parliament with reference to the late circnlar of the Holy Office of the In- quisition, and respectfully declines to recognise any right in the Holy See to interfere with the Irish people in the management of Irish political affairs."— Mr. John Dillon, in supporting the motion, contended that the rescript had been conceived in ignorance and without the full knowledge of the circumstances, and the sooner it was withdrawn the better.—Mr. William O'Brien said they had enemies 'enough without receiving blows from hands from which they least deserved it. It was cruel, unnatural, and heart break- ing to Irish Catholics to think that the name of Rome could be Bung into their teeth by Mr. Balfour when- ever he struck down an Irish representative. While all the censures of Rome were reserved for the unhappy Irish people, fighting for their lives, there was not one word of censure for the deeds and crimes of landlordism. In all the ages of the suffering of the people they never had been called upon to give a higher proof of their faith or do a nobler service to Catholicity than they did that day, in declaring that the sacred name of Rome must bo no longer dragged through the mire of Dublin Castle. The effect of the circular was purely political, and it had encouraged Mr. Balfour and his hireling magistrates to hound downtnen like Mr. Dillon. Mr. J. E. Redmond said if -they had to ac- quiesce in this Roman interference the English people would be absolute fools to give them 'Home Rule, for it would be a mockery, a delusion, and a danger. The re- solution was passed. THE NATIONAL LEAGUE AND TEE ;PAPAL RESCRI PT. Speaking at tne fortnightly meeting of the Irish National League, bold in Du t Bryon Toe day,Mr. Timothy Healy, M.P., said they could not help feeling regret that the Government had not "suppressed" more branches of the League, because, as the eaceipts showed, the •ffect of Mr. Balfour's action had been to make the soenehes which he 'endeavoured to aenibilate more moire then ever. Referring to the Papal Rescript, Mr. Healy said they should be guided by the manner in which Belgium and Gaimany treated such emendates. The Pope would never have been appealed to by the British Government if the people in Ireland had not sea& themselves formidable, demonstrating their power of opposition and resistance to existing tyranny. The rulers of any country never asked aid or counsel from the i:ope until they found themselves extremely embar- rassed with the National parry. If the Pope .would let them alone they would settle their contest with the ,government in double quick time. (Applause.) instead of the tenants paYiing any more rent to their landlords the landlords 'should pay restitution to them ror the robbery they committed in the past. (Cheers.) In his opinion the Irish people would act exactle the some as they did in 1683, When Mr. Parnell and Isis "gamut," as they were described, were condemned by the Pope. If any usjust boycotting was oirried on it should be condemed every honest man. But every honest, man should at the ';;ILLkil time pass by with scorn, not alone the land erabber, hat his children, and his children's children. (('beers.) As far as he (the speaker) was concerned. he was an nnrepenting sinner. With reference to his advo- racy of boycotting and the Plan of Campaign, he would he willing to regard the Papal cit cider as an error of the Vatican. Mr. DATIL, SLIEF:Hr, M.P., said the J>ranches of the National lea,etie tlmt were suppressed were now the strongest. ((heers.) So far from thespapal circular being an injury to them It would in higeopinion be a 4essefit. There were at. the present Protestant patriots ;n Ireland, and they did not want to give them, any :store than themselves, over to Home Rule. He dial- egi'd the Government to say that he did not always ,anti the people against using boycotting in an unjust immoral manner.. (Hear, hear) Tbe Rev. J. GALBRAITH, who was reeibirvecl with pro. need doers, said that t he prnspects of this country were en,-xl. The question was whether they would achieve suecees sooner or later. He was of opinion that the Na- -mat League hod done a great deal of good. (Cheers.) Ce believed that Ivo cot ting was as old as the Garden of Men. MT. HARRIS, M.P.. also spoke.

The inquest on the five men killed in the explosion at Aber Colliery. Tynewydd, was concluded on Wednesday. The jury returned a verdict of " Manslaughter " againo Mr. Dril7.ol, manager, an Mr. David Ivans, under manager,

in) TO THE CROFTEI29.—An additional Civil Service Estimate was Issued on Wednesday, for a sum of £10,560 to enable certain advances to be made in aid of emigra- tion and colonisation of crofters and cotters of the West Highlands and islands of Scotland, including expenses of administration, which amount to £5OO. This sum is to be advanced on condition that £2.000 is provided by pri- vate subscription.

ODDFELLOWS' CONFERENCII.—At tlit Conference of the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows, which was resumed at Gloucester on Wednesday, the report of the committee on distressed lodges was discussed. The Secretary said the directors would enforce the general rule requiring all valuation lists to be sent in within a month under pen- alty of a fine. Welsh delegates presented the Grand Master with an emblematic picture representing the United Kingdom as a tree and the colonies as branches. The report expressed satisfaction at the increase of 10,000 members and regret at the number of seceding lodges. The annual banquet was held in the evening, Lord Sandhurst presiding.

represent the Queen at the forthcoming Pruseisn mar- Tam SETEISOLILS SAVINOS Bs—The trustees of the Sevenoaks Savings Bank, on Monday, gave notice to their depositors that they have determined to close the bank, and that depositors may receive the amounts due to them on application at the bank. The Duke of Westminster, on Monday, threw open his grounds at Eaton Hall in the interests of a fête promoted by the committtee of the Chester Museum, the object being to ,or-ir off a debt of £l,OOO on the institution. Upwards 20,000 persons were present. Bridget Henshaw, the wife of a foreman bricklayer, re- siding at Northampton was remanded, on Monday, on a charge of shooting at her husband. It is alleged that the Accused discharged both barrels of a gun at her husband AS he was entering the room, the door being riddled with shot.

A letter was received, on Saturday, from the Horne Secretary, stating that the sentence of death passed on Mary Holiday, for the murder of her daughter, has been commuted to penal servitude for life, in answer to an influential memorial, signed by upwards of 1,000 persons in the neighbourhood of Driffield. DESTRUCTION Or • FRENCH FISHINO FLEIST.—The Danish steamer Laura, from Iceland, arrived at Granton on Sunday with 58 French fishermen, who report that the fishing fleet from Dunkirk had been wrecked near Iteyk- iavik during a northerly gale and snowstorm last April. The men belonged to eight boats, and 15 of their crew were drowned. Fifty boats were unaccounted for when they left. Srrocxmc RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—A shocking accident happened on the Chester and Holyhead line on Sunday, resulting in the death of Mr. Edwin Youlton Martin, master carter, residing at St. Domingo Vale, Liverpool. In attempting to leap on to the 7 20 a.m. train at Mostyn „statjortewhile in motion, Mr. Martin fell between the carranti the platform, sustaining such injuries that he died in the afternoon at Chester Infirmary.

SHOCKING OCCURRENCE AT HAWARDEN.-012 Monday, terrible occurrence was reported at Hawarden. John hogers a man with one arm to which a crook was attached, was holding a horse when the animal suddenly bolted. The crook became entangled in the reins, and the poor fellow was dragged along at a terrific pace by he horse, whose terrors were increased by the man's 'ielpless condition. Rogers sustained such severe injuries that he died almost immediately on being released. 'NARROW ESCAPH ,OF Fiaxtitaw iw MANCHESTER:— An alarming and destructive warehouse fire occurred in Mandhester, on Saturday. The outbreak took place in the premises of Messrs. J. and S. Gaskell, cotton waste dealers, Mayes-street, and is supposed to be due to spon- taneouscombustion. The flames raged with such fierce- ness thst the four-storey building was speedily gutted. Ity-the fall of a wall, the lives of a number of firemen were 'jeopardised. A terror-stricken woman was gal- tatty rescued by a policeman. A floanumx STORY.—A remarkable illustration of the cruelties by which Chinese trade societies enforce their laws is given in a report from the American Minister at Peking. From this it appears that a member of a gold- beaters' society at Soochow recently took more appren- tices than one. This is forbidden; so the local trade union took up the matter, and condemned the man to be bitten to death, and the sentence was literally carried out. •" One hundred and twenty-three men had a bite t him before he expired." 'Lovx ROMANCE OF PRINCE GEORGE OF WALES.—The London correspondent of the Irish Times writes :—lt MIS hinted some time ago that one of the Royal Princes had fallen in love with a lady not only of less exalted degree, but of British birth, and that the misplaced ten- derness had caused much anxiety in circles very near the Throne. From the pecuniary point it is almost a case of Cinderella, the pretty aristocrat, being %bsolutely ,sans dot. Prince George, like a true British sailor, does not mind the monetary matter the shiver of a timber or 'he splicing of a mainbrace ; but his 'Royal relatives re- gard the business with more worldly eyes, and have adopted such measures to part the pair that the lady has lost her health, a consequence which aggravates the bit- terness with which her father, one of the proudest if also ene of the poorest of our nobility, has resented what he has declared in a letter on the subject to be the insult inflicted upon •him and his. It is further averred that he young Prince steadfastly refuses to tear the image ,rorn his heart. .

'rue WELSH GOLD MINE.—Mr. Pritchard Morgan. ,wner ot the Mount Morgan Mine, arrived at Do!golly on Saturday evening, and in an address to the workmen lelivered from the hotel, announced as the result of his •nterview with the Crown authoritiea, that work would he resumed on Monday morning at Gwynfyndd Gold- laid. He did not hesitate to say there was untold wealth in that district. —Work was resumed on Monday, the Government having withdrawn the injunction against the further removal of gold. No definite arrangement has yet been effected with the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer, but in an interview with Mr. Pritchard Morgan Mr. Gosehen said the Government did not wish •to sus- pend operations at the mine, but were prepared tomeet him in a fair and 'liberal spirit. They would, therefore, permit Mr. Morgan to remove gold and develop the works while an agreement was being drawn. i7pwarrls of 23,000 worth of geld is stored at the mine for removal to London.

EXECUTION OF A SOLDlER.—Michael Schmidt was hanged on Saturday morning in the Alser barracks of Vienna for the crime of wiliul murder. Executions of this kind heing.of very rare occurrence in Austria, Soinnidt we; ' hanged amid a somewhat 'fanciful military ceremonial. The infantry company to Which he belonged was drawn up in e square around the gallows, two adjutants went through the comedy of applying to the general in Com- mand ,of the army corps for a pardon, which the latter had no power to grant, and after the man had been hanged a general salute to the corpse was ordered, after which followed a prayer. The convict was a ruffian of ,he worst description, who tried to throw upon a corn- ado thc.blanie for the crime which he had committed. 'lis death struggles lasted three minutes, which is a omparatioely short time under the system of hanging hy strangulation which is practised in Austria. A man who was hanged at Trieste the .other day struggled for . i ne minutet.

A CORIOLIS LOTTERY CAS& th:IESSING ROW UN° ‘NDLR WILL BURN.—At the Bury County Police Court. a Monday, Byrom Howarth, grocer, &c., Bridge-street. Henderson stated lrat the defendant offered £5 in six prizes to those pur- thasers of tea who made the nearest guess as to lioa nany hours a large candle would burn. Any person right make any number of guesses, but each estimate vas to be sent on a separate half-pound tea paper. An :dditional prize of 15s. was announced to be given to ,he person who sent in most half-pound tea papers he latter prize alone.
