div.head: ANNUAL CO-OPERATIVE CONGRESS.
div.p: ANNUAL CO-OPERATIVE CONGRESS.

The annual meeting of the Central Co-operative Board, for the consideration of their report to Congress, was held at Dewsbury on Saturday afternoon Mr. Joseph Greenwood in the chair. The report, after noting Hu continued improvement in the completeness of the re- turns made to the chief registrar, proceeds to give an analysis of the returns of the year 1886, the last yet published, and a comparative view of these with the re- turns for 1885. The number of societies making returns in England and Wales is 968. of which 871 are described as retail general. 27 retail special, one whole- sale, 58 productive, and 27 various. The number of members ~elnneing to these societies at the end of 1888 %et- 702,974, with a share capital of £8,400,1713- and a loan capital of £1,401,000. The sales for the year amounted to £25,531,974; trade charges to £1,450,490; net profits to £2,409,889; granted for education, £18,368. The total number of societies in Scotland making returns is 320, of which 271 are described as retail general, 28 retail special, one wholesale, four productive, and 16 various. The membership of these societies numbers 131,269. and their share capital is £888,535, and loan capital £598,430. The sales for the year amount to £5,690,011; trade charges to £261,244; net profits, £554,254; and allowed for education, £1,438. The total number of societies making returns in Great Britain is 1,281, with 833,811 members, a share capital of £9,427,435, and a loan capital of £1.980,944. Their sales for the year amount to £31,222,232; the trade charges to £1,711,994; net profits to £2,961,611; and Applied for education, £19,806. Compared with the previous year, these figures show an increase of 15 in the total number of societies making returns, an increase of 32,334 in membership, an increase of £505,385 in the share capital, an increase of £155,515 in the loan capital, an increase of £1,393,390 in the sales, a decrease of £272,273 in the trade charges, an increase of £84,538 in the net profits, and a decrease of £789 in the amount granted for education. The report states that the registrar's return contains this year, for the first time, a heading for a ques- tion, the answers to which—assuming them to be cor- rect will be an unpleasant surprise to co-opera- tors. The question is, whether credit is given to members or not, and if so, to what limit? The answers show that of 1,255 societies in Great Britain 721 give credit in some form, and only 534 do not. This state- ment in the report gave rise to a long discussion, in the ' course of which doubt was thrown on the reliability of the returns under this head. The report states that at the instance of the Board, Mr. H. D. Acland has intro- duced into the House of Commons a bill, which is backed by Sir W. H. Houldsworth, Sir F. Mappin, and Mr. R. Reid, the object of which is to enable co-operative societies to vote by proxy at the meetings of railway and other companies in which they have investments. The report was adopted, and in the afternoon an exhibi- tion of co-operative productions was opened by the Mayor of Dewsbury. On Monday, the annual congress was opened at Dews- bury. There were 550 delegates present. The President (Mr. E. Vansittart Neale), general secretary of the Co- operative Union, was supported by the Marquis of Ripon, Mr. T. Hughes, Q.C., Mr. A. Acland, M.P., Messrs. FL J. Vansittart Neale, G. J. Holyoake, Hodgson, Pratt, W. Maxwell, M. Deboyve, B. Jones, &c. • w&N VANSITTABT NEALE, in delivering the Ina. ral address, said he desired to supplement the striking expo- sition of Mr. G. J. Holyoake last year at Carlisle by con- siderations specially addressed to that side of the co- operative principle on which he dwelt least, viz., more to the benefits which it had yet to realise through the appli- cation of equity to nroduction. Many who had addressed- the congresses had dwelt more or less fully on the anticipated benefits of a system where the workers should be in this sense their own employers. None. so far as he remembered, ever imagined that co-operative production could mean a system where the profits of manufacturing should be distributed among those who supplied the capital for carrying them on according to their wealth, shown by the amount of their pur- chases, while the worker should permanently remain the servant of those who employed, him, without any share as worker in the management or participation in the proceeds of his work beyond the wages fixed by competition, except the right to buy what he had made on the same terms on which it might be bought. by any one. Yet must we not admit that this was the form which co-operative production had actually taken so far? All wealth was derived from work, but not present work. Wealth was what remained as the result of work, and it was by this inher:tance of the past the change in the original posi- tion of the worker to the results of his work had been brought about. The association of " progress w;th poverty" had a cause more profound than that con- ceived by Mr. Henry George, and the disease, so to speak, lay far deeper than could be touched by any law but the i.iw of reason, which should substitute for the impertect liberty of self-assertion the perfect liberty of self- eovernment. The distributive stare had done some- thing towards removing the disease, and as a further ameliorative he suggested to them whether it would not be possible to follow the example of the late Mons. Godin and establish associated dwellings, where the privacy of a home could be combined with the advantages of a (dub, a store, and a school at their own doors, and where they could have the varied enjoyments of the rich and end the divorce of manufacturing and agricultural industry. The learned gentleman concluded by calling upon those before him to take a front place among the emancipators of labour, the saviours of society.—The first paper read was by Mr. G. E. Quirk, St. Helens, Liverpool, on " What should be the true relations between a wholesale distributive society and the pro- I uctive societies whom work it may sell " If he were asked to answer the question as concisely as possible, he would without hesitation answer " perfect inde- pendence." They were bound to regard distributive and productive societies for commercial and trading purposes as separate and independent eMities. The pri- mary purpose of all trade, commerce, or manufacture Was to make a profit; to benefit and enrich in the first 'nstance those immediately concerned; and the men who professed to be actuated by any other motives—to be d sinterested, and to sell their.merchandise or manufac- ture their wares from nure philanthropy and from a de- sire to benefit their fellow men, were guilty of the most transparent hypocrisy and cant, and would have to tell their story to other than hard-headed Britishers to be believed. He contended that the relations between dis- tributive and productive societies are co-equal and co- ordinate so far as the power to make a bargain, and if hey attempted to interfere with this arrangement by artificial restrictions they must inevitably handicap either one or the other of these agents Neither the wholesale distributive society nor the productive sncieties could control the fluctuations of the market. %rid prices were beyond their power to regulate. In .onclusion, he contended that there was not anything .ontrary to the true spirit of co-operation in the method oe had outlined to "Let well alone:" The second paper on the same subject. was by Mr. C. siievrtesorrom, Coventry. In summing up the rela 'ions between the wholesale and the productive societies. the writer said they should he those of perfect friend- ship and candour, the wholesale giving the productive societies all the information possible, so that they may know what goods are likely to sell, to place their own productive works in harmony with the highest aims of on-operation, and seek to limit rather than encourage he rage for cheapness. They would thereby not only place themselves in harmony with all the productive societies whose work they may sell, but also gain the respect of those manufacturers who already admit the claim of the worker to a share in the profits of trade, and by their own example increase the number of them.- long discussion followed the reading of the papers, he first one being strongly condemned by nearly every telegate who spoke. Mr. W. CAMPBELL (Leeds), who opened the discussion, it appeared to him to be a paper of a most extra- Tdinary character to be read at a co-operative congress. iTo hal tried to look at it through co-operative spectacles, ',et he was unable to make it out at all. But when he ,ait on competitive spectacles he saw through it at once. !here ran through the paper a sentiment not at all in .ccordance with co-operative judgment, co-operative 4entiment, and co-operative practice. The oth- r speakees• were Messrs. .7. Thompson (Cam- bridge), T. Shaw (.1-Imlay), A. Miller and D. Thompson 1.-:eottish Wholesale Society), E. a Greening, E. W. reening, B. Jones, and Foxwell (London). Holl- rob (BurnleY), W. Swallow arid J. Pock''' 'lit on Manc,hester) , Cajti.ncer (lieighley), and T. Hughes (Manchester).—The discussion was adjourned. On To ee lay the Co-operative Congress at Dewsbury was alviitzsi over by the Marc/ads of Ripon. His Lordship t'aiti lie was satisfied Co-operators were now carrying out the ideas of the movement in regard to its applica- •ioti to production, and the workers participating in a onire of the profits. He had always looked upon it that the consumer should have a direct interest, not only in tistributive co-operation, but also in productive co- nerat ion,

The e,ottgressi, concluded its sitting on Wednesday at Dewsbury. Mr. John Cave, junior, chairman of the Dewsbury Pioneers' Industrial Society presided, and opened the proceedings with an address on the advan- tages of associated labour. The rest of the day was oc- cupied in discussing resolutions on the division of the profits of productive and distributive societies. A reso- lution was carried recommending the formation of an alliance on equitable conditions for the sharing of profits and risks between the worker, the capitalist, and the consumer, and inviting the co-operation of the wholesale societies to adopt the principle. _aft

A coroner's jury have returned a verdict of " Wilfu murder" against Charles Latham, in custody for caus- ing the death of Mary Newman, with whom he lived at Somers Town. London. A dog show was opened in the St. James's Hall, Man- ches;er, on Wednesday. The regulations under which the show is baing held are those of the Kennel Club. There are about 1,100 entries, among which are a specially good selection of collies and a tire number of terriers. RELIGION ANT) Pouvics.—Replying to a tbrrespondent who wrote to him on the reration of religious faith to political progress, Mr. Gladstone suggests that he should read the Gospels and se 4 whether our Lord was a friend to injustice, class interest, or abuse. • 'He also asks whether it is not our best and safest rule to follow truth in religion and truth in polities in the faith that we shall find the means of reconciling truth with truth.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present—The Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Greening, Jolley, Jones, Voisey, Derbyshire, Clarke, Ratcliffe, W. Houghton, Eckersley, EH- shall, J. Houghton, Harrison, Balharry; J. C. Sutton r rc clerkl;S.-Suttdn-jeSeinent --derlc7,-and cat: -Ira ,(workhouse master). ' - • rniii; HOUSE COMMITTEE.-FILOPOSED APPOINTMENT OF MASTER' ASSISTANT.

The House Committee on the recommendation of Henley, the Board to advertise for an assistant to Mr. 'Ward at the workhouse.—Mr. GREENING, in mov- ing the adoption of the minutes said that Mr. Henl very strongly recommended in that room that an assis- tant should be provided for Mr. Ward the workhouse master. Mr. Henley considered that Mr. Ward's duties were of that magnitude that they were really more than , he could do if he was to have proper supervision ove,r the house generally. Mr. .Ward had to go about the house very much and tills necessarily took up veryinuqh of his time. It was, however, well known that in &ht. I tion to this, there was a very great deal of wri`ing to be I done in various books, and if Mr. Ward was to doi-this I and at the same time to keep up a proper inspection and supervision of the house he would be at it every night until 12 o'clock, which they were told was the case nova occasionally. It might seem to some members Of the Board that that was a new appointment, and certainly ' it would mean an extra charge on the Union, but in reality it was not an extra appointment inasmuch as the late master (Mr. Mackey) of the house used as an assis- tant an inmate named Webster who did a great portion of writing for him. Mr. Mackey was, therefore; much more at liberty than Mr. Ward was, but, as Mr. Henley had pointed out, the Local Government Board considered it objectionable. to have assistance rendered by an in- 'mate of the house, and discountenanced it in every way. —Mr. JOLLEY seconded Mr. Greening's proposal that the I minutes be adopted.—Mr. DAtimrshuut said he had been inquiring into the subject thoroughly, and he thought the master was overworked. He believed also that Mr. Ward would not stop there if he had not some assistance, and as far as he saw Mr. Ward was a very efficient offi- cer. He supported the proposal of the committee.—The CusianiAN had no doubt that the Union would be better I served if Mr. Ward had more time at his disposal for supervision of the house, and he therefore strongly recommended that the minutes be adopted.—The min- utes were then adopted.—At a later stage of the meet- ing Mr. GREENING moved that a master's assistant for the workhouse be advertised for, the salary offered to be £2O for the first year, with rations and lodgings, £25 for the second year, and £3O for the third year.—This re- solution was agreed to it being enderstood that each mem- ber of the Board would have notice tOthe effect that the the appointment would be proceeded •to at the next meeting.

PADGATE SCHOOLS CO3LMITTEM. The Padgate Schools Comittee in their minutes re- commended that Miss Harriet Morris, West Derby, be appointed school mistress at the Padgate Schools. The doctor had reported that the general health of the children at the sahools was very good.—The CHAIRMAN moved the adoption of the minutes and mentioned that Miss Morris was the only candidate, who turned up at the committee meeting, the other candidate who had ;been asked to attend, and who lived near London not having taken any notice of the letter. Miss Morris' testi- .monial were, however, very satisfactory.—Mr. Istma- WOOD seconded the adoption of the minutes which was agreed to.—Miss Morris appeared before the Board and was informed that she had been appointed to the vacant office. THAT ENDS ve._ Mr. Imre:moon referred to the case of two men named Denis Quinn and McGuiness, who had been injured, the first by a thrashing machine and the latter in a street accident, and who, he said, had been first sent to the In- firmary and then from the Infirmary to the workhouse. He thought the Board ought to set their faces against that practise of sending patients from the Infirmary to the workhouse.—Mr. JOLLEY said the infirmary was a place for serious cases and they could not keep patients there beyond a certain time. He might also tell them that the Infirmary was at present full, there being 24 or 25 serious cases, some of them from the Ship Canal. Mr. Isherwood was under a wrong impression if he thought permanent residents could be kept at the infir- mary.—The CrikIRMAN said they had nothing to•do with the management of the infirmary, which was supported by voluntary contributions and into which people were I admitted in emergencies. When the directors of the in- firmary thought proper, according to their regulations, they discharged patients who if they had a home went home, but if they had no home they necessarily came to the Workhouse.—Mr. ISHERWOOD said if the Infirmary did not deal with such cases as had been referred to it was scarcely worth the while of working-men to contribute to it.—Mr. Vomey thought the remarks of the Chairman very proper, as it was not for the Board to dictate to the managers of the Infirmary, who, he had no doubt, were doing their ut- most with the funds at their disposal.—Mr. HARRISON said the managers of the Infirmary were anxious to ac- commodate the public to the fullest extent, but they could not keep patients in for protracted periods of time. —The Chairman suggested that Mr. Isherwood had bet- ter complain to the managers of the Infirmary as a pri- vate individual.—Mr. DARRYSHIRE did not think it fair that Mr. Isherwood should be asked to write to the Infir- mary managers, as he had brought the matter forward as a member of a publie Board. If the Board did not take it up then it could be let drop.—Mr. ISHERWOOD said he had not brought the matter forward as a private individual nor as an employer, but as a member of the House Committee who went round the hoese.—Mr. GREENING said it was a fact that some patients were in the Infirmary a long time.—Mr. JOLLEY: They are cases that cannot be removed.—Mr. GREENING thought that a man that had had his ribs staved in was not fit to be removed. A man was brought there and made into a pauper, and, what was more, they had no right to bring him there, as he ought to have gone to the Runcorn Union or to his home. Instead of that they pushed him off to that Workhouse.—Mr. HARRISON : Not against his own wish.—Mr. GREENING Said they did bring him there whether or not.—Mr. VOISEY said that the matter had been brought forward in a very ungracious way. If Mr. Isherwood had got any specific case let him give the facts. He was obliged to ask Mr. Isherwood to formu- late a case in the precisest terms, for it was really a, charge against the Infirmary.—Mr. HARRISON : Was the man ever taken to the lafirmary P—Mr. GREENING : think he was never taken there.—Mr. JOLLEY: Then you accuse us of making a pauper of a man who was never taken to the Infirmary. —Mr. VOISEY said he would move that Mr. Isherwood be called upon to make a definite statement in a particular case.—Mr. Iseeawoon did not think he should be put in the position of a relieving officer for Mr. Vokey or anybody else. They had better call in Mr. Garnett.—Mr. GARNETT, relieving officer, was then called in, and in answer to questions said that Quinn was injured on his way from the Croft direction, and as he was very ill Dr. Peacocke was at once sent for. On the report of Dr. Peacocke he (Mr. Garnett) gave an I order for Quinn's removal to the Workhouse hospital. He was never sent to the Infirmary as he (Mr. Garnett) , had no authority to send him there. IleGuiness fell from a cart and hurt his ribs, and he came to him (Mr. 1 Garnett) in the ordinary way and got an order for the I doctor, who recommended that MeGuiness go to the 'Union Hospital, which he agreed to do. McGuiness walked both to him , (Mr. Garnett) and to the Work- house.—Mr. VOISEY: I think that is enough, Mr. Chair- man. (Laughter.)—Mr. HARRISON : I think thfe it about the most glorious fiasco I have ever heard of. qLaughter.)—Mr. JOLLEY thought that after the state- ment that had been made everything that had been said in favour of the infirmary was justified.—Mr. ISMEB- wooD said these were street accidents and when going through the hospital the men did not tell them they had not been to the Infirmary. He could stand being laughed at, as he thought fie had done hie duty. It would be better if those who laughed would make more inquiries themselves.—Mr. W. Flocorrrox understood Mr. Isherwood to say that the patients ofund to bad been sent by the Infirmary people to the Workhouse.- -Mr. Isrinnwoon ; That is what we understood on Fri- daY,—TholLtlnr nal as Chairman he depreca- ted their discussing the conduct of the management of the Infirmary.—The matter then dropped.

Two SUdden deaths in connection with Bank Holiday were rero-ted by the Liverpool policeon Tuesday. Gro. Pickup, 22, went with a picnic to Netherton, and on his 'turn was taken ill and died before a doctor could he minmoned. Frances Rigby, West Derby, went to South- ”lrt with some relatives, and on the return journey aitinupted to get 9n a tramcar while in motion, but missed her looting and fell. Vl'hen picked up she was unconscious, and died almost immc liatelv.

A shockine accident which terminated fatally occurred at New Brighton on Monday afternoon. A rung man residing in the neighbourhood tried to jump on to the /tont of a heavily-laden tramcar in motion, when he ;lipped and fell under the wheels, one of winch passed over his thigh, fracturing it in a terrible manner and nearly severing the limb from the body. He was taken to the Cottage Hospital, where he died about midnight ifter terrible suffering.

SAD SCICI DE IN SHEFFIELD. SEVEN' W lEEE s avrwn MARRIAGE.—An inquest was held at Sheffield, on Fatur• day, on the body of a young man-nained George Jarvis Watson, a grocer's assistant. who committed suicide by hanging himself. The deceased, 'who was 21 veers of ti!e, was formerly in a situation at Manchester. He came over to Sheffield and got married. Soon afterwards he lost his situation. He came to see his wife, last Wetlnes- lay, and then comolaity-d of a pain in his head. On Friday be committed suicide by hanging himself. A verdict of "temporary insanity' was returned.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, MAY 26, 1888.

" TRAMPS, Medieval and Modern;' is the title of 'an interesting article in the " Westminster Review," which those kindly people would do well tO read who are in the habit of giving something to every beggar they meet. It would seem that there is nothing new under the sun in the tramp hue. The only change is as to the mode of Wheedling, and this is the outcome of our complex civiisation; the motive is the same yesterday, to- day, and, shall we say, for ever? The professional beggar does not like work; but, as he must live- 0r at any rate thinks he must—he lives on the kindness of the credulous people who, unlike him, atick to work, though they may not like work. In the "Vision of Peers Ploughman" there is a graphic description of the fraternity, which might have been recently penned. The author speaks of them as : Pilling their bags and stomacks by lies, sitting at 'night over a hot fire, where they untie their legs, hich have been bound up in the daytime, and, LYing at ease, roasting themselves over the and turning their backs to the heat, drinking Pliantly and deep, after which they then draw to oed and rise when they are in the humour. Then th,eY ream about, and keep a sharp look-out where t'eY may soonest get a breakfast, or a rasher of aeon, or money, or victuals, or sometimes both, a ;,?af or half a boat, or a thick piece of cheese, which v carry to their own cabin, and contrive to live la idleness and ease by the labour of other men. IfigNilt the EIGHTH had a sharp way of dealing With the folk who fell under his displeasure. He had no sympathy with people who lived in " idle- nee and vagabondrye:' His idea was to stamp out begging as a sort of plague; and to this end it is ,atated that he eaused to be hanged as many as "great theeves, pettie theeves, and roges." If we were to take to-day to hanging "great theeves," as well as " pettie theeves," we should pass the figure of 72,000. The House of , Lords would not remain untouched, and what a • vaid there would be on Stock Exchange! Rut we are dealing with tramps more particu- -7,13% There is no one, we suppose, who is not L'apared to admit that beggars are, as a class, "a :0 lot," and ought not to be encouraged. "But it will be urged, "there are exceptional 'kl4ties ; anybody with half an eye can see.when he got to deal with a professional beggar, or the 'leserving case of the man out of work." Unfor- blnately, this is just where even the wary are taken The professional cadger is as a rule a fairly good tor; and, as he has found it pays to pose as "the Inan out of a job," he has practised the part until he can play it to perfection. MT. RIBTON-TURNBR, 110 has written a valuable work on beggars and "egging, lays it down as a ride from which there is 10 exception, that "the deserving poor never beg ;" and he declares that he never met with a beggar Who was driven to beg by sheer want or misfor- &le. It might, of eourae, be said as to this that r. TURNER'S experience is necessarily limited; he goes further and affirms that he has never teat with any other person who has known of such 4 ease. Such a statement, coming from such an authority, ought to "give us pause" in the latumer at least of our alias-giving. For this much is quite certain, that when a penny gets into wrong hands it is worse than wasted—it is mischievously aPent. It is a common saying with those who will give to tramping beggars, that they are well re- Paid if they, now and again, relieve one really de- aerving person. There would be wisdom as well aa kindness in taking up such a position, if it could shown that the "deserving person" was ever "410wri to resort to begging. Mr. RIBTON-TURNBR "118 us that the supposition is a myth; and he PPorts his statement by remarkable evidence. laere is a man of the name of G. A. BRINE who haa been sent to gaol in every county in England, e'reept two. BRINE has given his experience as a Professional cadger. All tramps are not of course beggars; there are men who are tramping in aearch of work; but BRINE says, "out of every ten tramps there are nine imposters, or professional vs." He tells how, with all the care taken to 4 the recipients of Watts' Charity in Rochester, ae was a recipient no less than eight times; and adds—e I once gave my ticket, which I had 'htained there, to a poor blacksmith who had been !efused one. The reason he had been refused was that he was not so consummate a liar as I was." 4, reat is the gullibility of the British public. They don't like to be imposed on "—so this ex- Perienced hand informs us—" but the liar, rogue, and imposter, practised as he is, soon convinces them that he, at least, does not belong to the e,adging fraternity." Further, a young thief, Peaking, some years ago, of the vagrants with *llom he had been in the habit of associating, 1441 :—" They all live well, never ate any broken :letuals, but had meat breakfasts, good dinners, 'let suppers, and frequently ended by going to bed any drunk. Not one spent less than 3s. a day, anY a great deal more. They sometimes make *)s. a day, •and average 3s. (id. a day." Think of tithis) you who labour at the forge, the loom, or in "le mine, and button ilp your pockets. Tncliscri- lail nate alms-giving is simply a godly way of doing ,‘‘le devil's work. But people will go on giving, ti'l ?t Westminster and other Reviewers say what ,eY will ; and the question is—What is to be done ith the beggars that over-rim the country? The _bites t suggestion is that they should be detained reforalatorie. with the object of making good tiaeria of them. If the material is as bad as it is presentented to be, we are afraid not mach re- , fiance could be pliteed upon the quality of the rmanufaetured article. But if the article was ..!ally bad, there would be no need to place it in 1.7 market. If vagabonds were kept with their tloB es to the grindstone, as so many better men are, ahi would at least be prevented from doing mis- , and the Houses of Detention would be

badly managed if they did not at least pay their way. Care would, of course, have to be taken to distinguish between the professional and the casual —between the idle ne'er-do-well, and the unfor- tunate fellow who is really seeking employment. The latter deserves much better treatment than he at present obtains; but as to the former—whose sole object in life is " idlenes and vagabondrye " he should be made to feel the truth of the scrip- tural saying that "if any would not work, neither should he eat."

THE twentieth annual Co-operative Congress has been held at Dewsbury during the past week. Mr. E. VANSITTART NEALE, the secretary of the Co-operative Union, is the president for the year; and he delivered an address, on Monday, which shows how anxious he is for a new departure to be made in the co-operative movement. He be- lieves that the time has now come when the ex— periment should be tried of taking the workers in ,their productive enterprises into some sort of part- nership. There is much to be proud of, but there is still much to achieve. Conflicts between capi- tal and labour are not unknown amongst co-opera- tors. Last year, when the Congress met, there was a strike, at Leicester, amongst the boot and shoe workers employed by the Wholesale Co-opera- tive Society. These people had no interest in the concern beyond the wages they obtained; and they were disposed to think that they were en- titled to higher wages than they were getting. Mr. NEALE thinks workmen should have an interest in the profits of labour as well as receive wages; and that Co-operators cannot be said to have attained the high ideal with which they set out until they have solved the problem as to how this is to be ac- complished. When the capitalist is approached on this point, he is, as a rule, disposed to say that he

_ does not see how it can be regarded as fair for a workman to take a share of profits unless he is in a position to meet, as the case may arise, a share of the losses. It would seem to be Mr. NEALE'S idea that this difficulty can be got over by allowing the workman's interest to accu- mulate. Instead of paying out whatever sum might be due the first year there was any- thing to share, the amount would be put to his credit, and he might next year be credited with interest upon what he had in the business, even if there was nothing actually in the shape of profit. There is no doubt that so far as workmen are con- cerned they will be well pleased to become party to an experiment of this kind; and if it be tried, in the first instance, in connection with a well- established business, we do not see why it should not succeed. The main point is whether those who provide the capital will be willing to risk some- thing to carry out an idea. The President of the Co-operative Congress in effect says :—" It should be done; and Co-operators are the men to do it." It should be added that the delegates showed themselves favourably disposed to bring the new proposal into operation ; and, after con- siderable discussion, it proposition was carried to , the effect that wholesale and distributive societies I be recommended to form an alliaace on equitable conditions for the sharing of profits and risk be- tween the worker, the capitalist, and the con- sumer. Whether the resolution will be put in force remains to be seen; but if not, we shall hear sornothing more of the matter at the next Congress.

THE "Birmingham Post," which is understood to be in the confidence of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, has published four columns of "A sketch of Unionist Policy" as to Ireland. The subject is dealt with under three heads, 1, Public Works, 2 Land Pur- chase, and 3, Local Government. As to Public Works, the Irish are to be encouraged to be good boys by plenty of money being provided from the Imperial Exchequer to improve the arterial drainage of Ireland, to embank the rivers, to im- prove and in many instances to create the fisher- ies, to bring the railway system into reasonable co-ordination, and to extend it so as to connect remote parts of the country with the main lines of communication." Although the British taxpayer objected to find the money for a land purchase scheme, it seems to be thought by Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN that there will be no difficulty about his pro.. viding millions for these purposes; but this may prove to be another case of reckoning without the host. With regard to Land Purchase, that is pro- posed to be ac,comllished by the use of Irish, rather than English credit. Land Banks are to be created, which will be under the control of county authorities. Instead of receiving cash down, vendors would have to be content with payment in Land Debenture Bonds bearing a fixed rate of interest. It will be interest, ing to hear what landowners have to say about parting with their land upon such security as would be in this way offered te them. It is cer- tain that Irish county authorities would not be able, with Irish credit, to carry out a scheme of this kind as economically as Mr. GLADSTONE pro- posed to carry his scheme out by the use of British credit; and that would probably mean that the landowner would get less for his land. As to Local Government, the present Local Government Bill is suggested as a basis for Ireland, with provi- sions for Provincial Councils of a kind which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN has advocated all along. There is nothing now said about a National Council; that would be altogether too suggestive of a Home Rule Parliament. The scheme looks pretty well on paper: but it is like the Constitution drawn up by the French National Convention—it "wont march." The Irish leaders will have none of it, for they have only to "wait a little longer" to be in possession of Home Rule of a more thorough-going kind; and it is almost certain that it will not be accepted by Lord HART- INGTON, who has made up his mind not to give the Irish any powers which can be used as a lever for enforcing Home Rule. The scheme would of course have a chance if there could be established that National Party of which we hear something but see nothing. The sketch will therefore remain a sketch. Mr. GLADSTONE'S plan still holds the field. ~

More gold-finding in Wales; and more tempta- tion in the direction of promotion and speculation. But let the investor beware, or he may find, es Tennyson has it— His poor venture but a fleet of glass Wrecked on a reef of visionary gold.

There was a prairie fire, on a small scale, on Saturday night, in the neighbourhood of Gars- wood. Some twenty acres of brushwood took fire through a spark, it is supposed, from a locomo- tive. The spectacle was magnificent; but it was fire, and, like war, that mean:destruction.

The opening of the Widnes baths has led people at Runcorn to reflect on the fact that they are at a disadvantage as compared with their neigh- bours. But they may console themselves with the further reflection that they do not need a bath quite as often as "the folks across the way."

The Paris artronomer has been reading a paper on the "Men in Mars." He doesn't know any- thing about them, but imagines a great deal. It seems to be taken for granted that certain lines going from sea to sea on the planet are canals. As any one of these eanals must be some thousands of miles long and hundreds of miles wide, these waterways put the Manchester Ship Canal some- what in the shade. And the Ship Canal is not yet made.

Excepting the thunderstorm in the north on Saturday, the weather of Whitsuntide has been glorious. There was a rush to the watering places, especially Blackpool. But why are the Railway Companies permitted to overcrowd their carriages to such a frightful extent? One visitor to Blackpool says he travelled from East Lanca- shire with sixteen others in a compartment con- structed to carry ten. Somebody ought to be "run in," either for overcrowding, or cruelty to animals--or both.

It is satisfactory to learn that Mr. Shaw- Lefevre, M.P., has introduced a bill which has for its object the better protection of footpaths and roadside wastes. At present, if the public are robbed it is difficult to bring the offenders to justice. The landlords of this country have taken from the people of thousands of acres by "nobbling" land after the way in which it is being an- nexed in Grappenhall-lane. If this bill should become law, there will be a chance of dealing with land stealers as well as loaf stealers.

The late managing director of our " neutral " contemporary once told a reporter, who was com- plaining that he had been refused admission to an agricultural show, that he must say nothing about the matter. It must not be supposed that the "neutral " ever had a difficulty of that kind. It would seem that this policy survives. Reporters were given to understand that they were in the way at Walton Hall, on Thursday, but the "neu- tral" reporter turned a deaf ear; and went where he was not wanted. Can it be that he thought it. better to sacrifice his self-respect than risk the sacrifice of his situation P

Speaking at the People's Palace, London, on Saturday, the Duke of Westminster touched a weak spot in our educational system when he said children in this country were, as a rule, taken away from school at too early an age. Parents having spent a good round sum in the education of their children naturally want to get them to work, and thus secure some return. If we had Free Educa- tion, there would be less inducement to take chil- dren away too soon. The State ought to meet the parents half way.

"It was a famous victory l" Such, in the lan- guage of Southey, is the Liberal view of the result of the contest at Southampton. The Tories, at the commencement, seemed to have everything in their favour. They chose their own time for the fight; and that was when the Liberal can- didate, who was in the United States, could not possibly be back in time to take part in the struggle. Ani yet they are terribly beaten. A Tory majority of 668 at the last election is con- verted into a Liberal majority of 885.
—Aoly struggle,

The Tories want to make it out that they have been damaged by the compensation clauses of the Local Government Bill. But what of that ? They deserved to be beaten on that account; they are finding that the sop to the brewers is a blunder as well as a crime. Turning their backs on their own bill, some of their leaders were endeavouring to make it out that there would be no alteration of the law; magistrates would still have the power to re- fuse to renew a license without compensation. That was ingenious; but it wouldn't do; the voters were not to be gulled.

The fact is, the Government are found to be altogether wrong in their view of the law as to licensing. But taking them on their new ground, why should an irresponsible body of men, such as the magistrates, have power to cancel a license without compensation while the same power is denied to a Licensing Committee responsible to the ratepayers? If a number of justices may re- duce licenses without compensation, and without assigning a reason, why should not a committee elected to deal with licenses have as much autho- rity? The Government have been trying to hunt with the hare and run with the hounds. They doubt- less thought their practise very sharp; but, when they are found out, it looks very stupid.

The "Freemar's Journal" sums up the result of the Southampton election in language which there is no mistaking. It says :—" Southampton is sick of Balfourism' and has no faith in Chain- berlainism. The electors declare that Toryism is a swindle and Liberal Unionism a humbug, and tfome Rule the greatest guarantee against separa- tion."

The granite monument to the memory of the late Rev. Joseph Raynor Stephens, which was un- veiled at Stalybrisige, on Saturday, is a credit to the actory operatives of Lancashire as well as to the noble worker whom they have thus honoured. The memorial has cost £2OO, and has been erected by the pence of the people. Raynor Stephens, as he was familiarly called, was always in the thick of the fight on behalf of the poor when the poor had few friends; and he had no small share in the labours which broke down the barbarous system of working factory hands from five o'clock in the morning until eight at night. A great change has taken place in the past 50 years, and it is a change for the better.

Mr. Gladstone hit the nail on the head in con- cluding a short address to some 600 Yorkshire visitors to Hawarden, on Tuesday. He said The Liberal party was never engaged in higher aud nobler pursuits. It has noble objects before it as far as the whole country is concerned; but as respects Ireland, es respects that which I have plainly shown, whatever you may say or think or or wish about it, it is at -this moment, the key to the position of every English question, and the real helm that steers the ship of politics. As regards Ire- land, what are we labouring for? We are labouring to restore peace to a distracted country, to restore unity to a divided empire, and at once promote the highest interests, and, let me add, the repair of the tarnished honour of England. (Prolonged cheer- ing.)

It is estimated that the work will cost £l2O, and the contract has been let to Messrs. Aldridge and Ca., of Liverpool. MORE WOUNDING AT WIDNES —Before Mr. Deacon, at Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, Wm. Kinsella, a youth who lives at 95, Midwood-st., was charged with doing grievous bodily harm to a man named John Muffitt, of Elizabeth-st. It was stated that on Tuesday night a number of youths, including Kinsella, set upon Muffitt. who was struck either with a brick or stone at the top of the head. A wound of a serious nature was inflicted, and he was unable to appear in court. Ile is under the care of Dr. O'Keeffe. Evidence was given that the prisoner threw the missle that caused the wound, and he was remanded until Monday next. WHITSUNTIDE TRAFFIC AT RUNCORN.—WIIitSUTItide is a busy time for railway companies, and the Runcorn officials have found this year no exception to the rule. On Monday 1.454 passengers were booked, of whom 220 went to Liverpool, 150 to Chester,.and 500 to Frodsha.m. OR Tuesday 2,976 tickets were issued, and were divided as follows :—Liverpbol 1,000, Frodsham 700, Chester 250, and North Wales 150. The choir of the Methodist Free Church had their annual ex- cursion, Bettwys Coed being the place chosen, for a day's enjoyment. ROBBERIES AT RUNCORN. William 0"roole, of on settled residence, and Thomas Adams, a navvy, were charged with stealing a pair of boots from the shop of Wm. Croley, shoemaker, High-st. On Saturday night the men were loitering about the shop door and Mr. Cro- ley saw O'Toole snatch the boots from a nail. Both pri- soners ran away. They were remanded until Monday.— A tramp named Michael Connor, was charged with steal- ing a pair of boots, the property of William Croley, and also two shawls, the property of William Marsh, pawnbroker, Church-st., on Saturday night. NEARLY STRANGLED AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Frederick Elton, a labourer, was charged under a warrant with assaulting another labourer named James Moran.—Dr. McDougall deposed that on Saturday night he was on the Fair Ground and saw a scuffle between the two men, and the prisoner struck Moran several times. They separated, and shortly afterwards he saw the prisoner seize Moran by the neck and press both thumbs on the windpipe until he fell insensible. The prisoner then ran away, and wit- ness and his assistant, Dr. Fox, and Constables Royle and Gibsoo, and other persons, went in pursuit. He was captured at Astmoor Bridge and brought to the Police Station. Dr. McDougall then attended to the wants of Moran.—The prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour. Dr. McDougall informed the Bench that the constables deserved a compliment for the alacrity with which they joined in the pursuit and the able manner in which they effected the capture. ROBBERY WITH VIOLENCE AT WIDNES.—Peter Glevy, a young man, of 59, Victoria-road, wasbrought before Mr. Brock and Mr. Gaskell, junr., at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, charged with having, on the 21st inst., stolen from the person of Thomas Lewis, blacksmith, Oakland-st., a silver watch and gold chain, worth 575, and further with using personal violence. The evidence showed that on Monday night the prosecutor was at the bar of the Railway Hotel. He paid for the prisoner a glass of rum, and they stopped in the house until clos- ing time. On leaving the two men went down to the river side. The prosecutor was in the act of stooping when the prisoner seized him by the throat, and snatched his watch from his pocket. In so doing he smashed the gold chain to which the watch was attached. The pri- soner then ran away, but next day lie was captured at St. Helens by P.C. Waitland. He had in the meantime disposed of the watch to Mr. Bardsley-, pawnbroker of that town. The prisoner was committed for trial.

SUSPECTED " SMASHERS " AT RUNCORN.—George Fran- comb and Wm. Bevan, who have been employed on the Ship Canal works, were brought before the Runeorn magistrates on Tuesday, to answer a charge of frequent- ing Bridge-A with intent to commit a felony. On the 25th April the prisoners took up their residence at Duckett's lodging-h-use in Church-st., and next day Francomb handed the landlord nine skeleton keys of a very ingenious design, and asked him to take care of them until he and Bevan required them. Francomb said he did not want the keys to be If knocking about," as they might get into trouble through them. A few days afterwards the prisoners left the town, and nothing was heard of them until Sunday last, avhen they turned up and demanded the keys. Information was given to the police, and on Whit Monday Francomb was seen acting in a suspicious manner in Bridge-st , and was taken into custody lw P.C. Taylor. Afterwards Bevan went to the Police Staiioa in an intoxicated condition, and said lie wanted locking up. His wish was gratified. In order that inquiries might be made, the prisoners were re- manded until Monday. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE AT RUNCORN. Before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Mr. John Brundrit, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, John Buxton, a Ship Canal labourer, was charged with having been drunk and re- fused to quit the Navigation Inn, Canal-st., and further with assaulting P.S. Woolley. The prisoner, a power- fully-built man, six feet one inch in height, went into the inn on Saturday night and demanded a pint of ale. The landlord, Mr. Worrall, oobserving that the prisoner was drunk refused to supply the liquor, and the pri- soner said he would have the drink or theelandlord's life. He became very abusive in his language and threatening in his manlier, and P.S. Woolley was called in. He struck the officer a savage blow on the left cheek with his fist, and the sergeant at once closed with his assail- ant, and succeeded in throwing him to the ground. Con- stables Brew and Barter came to tlie sergeant's aid, and after a terrific struggle they managed to put the hand- cuffs upon the man and get him into Bridge-st. Where he was placed in a cart and driven to the police station. For the drunkenness a fine of 10s and costs was imposed, and for the assault a fine of and costs ; total, £2 5.8 4d., or six weeks hard labour. The money was paid. A BUTCHER AND lIIS SCALES AT WlDNES.—William Boardman, a butcher, of Liverpool, appeared before the Widnes magistrates to answer a summons charging him with being in possession of a pair of scales and a weight, which were unjust.—Superintendent Johnston said the defendant each Saturday kept a stall in Widnes market, and on Saturday he went to his stall and found a pair of counter scales, which were half an ounce out of balance against the purchaser, and also a pound weight which was three drachms light. The superintendent said the scales were a very bad pair.—The defendant said they were American made, and he paid £3 3s for them. TREAT TO SUNDAY SCHOOL CHILDREN AT WESTON.— The children attending the Church Sunday Schools at Weston spent a thoroughly enjoyable day on Wednesday, on the occasion of their annual treat. The weather was delightfully fine, and the arrangements made were of a most complete character. Mr. Ford placed one of his fields at the service of the scholars, and after engaging in several gatnes for an hour or two, the children sat down on the field to a capital tea, which, it is needless to add, they thoroughly appreciated. After attending to them the teachers partook of tea in the pavilion. The brass band connected with the schools was present, and performed an excellent programme of dance and other inspiriting music, and thus enhanced the pleasure of the gathering. ' RUFFIANLY CONDUCT AT RUNCORN.—An unpleasant incident occurred on the railway between Froisham and Runcornon Saturday night last. When the train which is timed to leave Chester at 7-25 p.m. had arrived at Halton Junction, the guard was communicated with by means of the cord, and the train was at once stopped. It then transpired that at Frodsharn a middle-aged lady had entered a compartment where were seated two navvies. One of the men, who appeared to be under the influence of drink, insulted the lady, and his companion interposed on her behalf, with the result that a fight en- sued. Upon the train stopping the ruffian left the car- riage, and got upon the embankment, where he was guilty of most indecent behaviour. The guard refused to allow him to complete the journey in the train, and he had therefore to walk. DIRECTED BY THE MOON TO RUNCORN. An elderly man named Thomas Roberts, of Little Lever, near Bol- ton, was brought before Major Hazlehurst, at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, on a charge of being a wan- dering lunatic. The prisoner informed his Worship that he was a shipwright by trade, and came from Ellesmere Port. Ile was directed to Runcorn by the moon. The medal he wore round his neck was a life protector, and enabled him to go through fire and water. Gazing wildly round at the constables in the court the prisoner said "Now it will not fit; you are putting it on too much. I can fight 500 of you, and I want my liberty. Afterwards the prisoner said he had been "new cleansed from arsenic" and now they wanted sto " stuff " him again and kill him. Dr. McDougall certified that the prisoner was a lunatic and lie was during the day con- veyed to Chester Asylum by Mr. G. Ward, the relieving officer, on the magistrates' warrant. MR. SETON - KARR, NI.P., AND STATE-AIDED COLONISATION.—In the Douse of Commons, OR Fri- day Mr. Seton-Karr gave notice that on Tuesday, the 22nd June. he would call attention to the sub- ject of State-aided colonisation, and move the resolution which stood in his name.

THE HOME InoN TRADE.—The English iron mar- ket has been very quiet during the past week, its former dulness having been increased by the inter- vening holidays. But there are other causes at work, chief among them being thl almost general flatness of the pig-iron market, which is due to the downward course in Scotch warrants, and while over production continues, no improvement can possibly set in. Scotch makers' iron still shows a drooping tendency. North of England iron and Bessemer iron in the north-west are not quite so firmly maintained as a week ago, although quota tions are nominally unchanged. Manufactured iron has also remained quiet, with prices, however, toler- ably steady. In the steel business there is a weaker tone, notwithstanding uninterrupted activity at works at present. There is no material cluing,: in the shipbuilding trade, nor are engineers experien- cing a more active call for work.—lron.

(TREAT FIRE ON THE GARWOOD PARK ESTATE. ! —About eleven o'clock. on Saturday night the resi- dents in the northern part of St. Helens observed a great conflagration in the direction of Garswood Park, the estate of Lord Gerard. On inquiry it was found that a game cover of about twenty-five acres 1, in extent, situated northwards of Carr Mill Dam—a celebrated rendezvous of fishermen—was on tire. During the winter the ground was covered with the dead ferns and bracken of last season, and up to Saturday the new verdure to be seen forcing its way through the dead foliage was very small, On ac- count of the hot weather of the past few days, the , cover was in a very dry condition, and not much astonishment was expressed when a corner of the cover was seen on Saturday afternoon to he smoul- dering. But when an hour later fire was to be seen rapidly making iis way, efforts were made to im- pede its progress, and apparently with some suc- cess. Later on, however, the fire burst forth -and, running rapidly up the bill, soon enveloped it in a glowing fire, which was seen for many miles around, and was remarkable for its fine effect. Nothing could be done to impede its progress, and at day- light on Sunday morning about twenty acres of the cover was seen to be in a charred and burning state. Hundreds of people were attracted to the place. It is supposed that a spark from one of the London and North-Western engines passsing be- tween St. Helens and Wigan was the origin of the fire. The brushwood was smouldering in many places on Sunday evening.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AU THORITY. The fortnightly meeting was held at, Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. The Rev. J. Lockwood presided. and there were present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. J. Stokes, E. Aaron, W. Kirkham, T. Lewis, P. Hall. T. Hadfield, J. Mclntyre, J. Parr, J. Brandreth, J. Hall, J. Davies, J. Weir, 11. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), and J. Far- rington (inspector).
ANALYSIS OF WATER.

The Inspector reportedthat he had received the analysis of the water supply to 10 Ship Canal huts at Moore, and , also 10 Ship Canal huts at Acton Grange. Dr. Carter Bell certified that the water was fit for domestic use, but it would be very much improved if filtered, as the water was very cloudy from suspended matter. Dr. Bell had also made an analysis of two samples of water from the Workhouse. He certified that the sample taken from the deep well in the yard was a first-class water of great purity. The second sample, taken from a tap connected with the service system of the house was certified to be

quite fit for domestic use, but was not quite as pure as the other sample.—lnspector Farrington asked for a cer- tificate of occupation to a new house at Helsby belong- ing to Mr. John A. Arrowsmith. Arrangements had been made to obtain water from another house in the neighbourhood.—The Deputy Clerk said the terms of the arrangement should be known before the certificate was granted.—The Inspector said there was a public pumpin the district.—The Clerk said 12 or 14 years ago about an eighth of an acre of common land was wrongfully en- closed at Helsby, and he thought the pump was also en- closed.—The Inspector said the pump was now used by the public.—The Inspector was instructed to make in- , quiries about the land and the pump and report.

div.head: NUISANCE AT KINGSLEY.
div.p: A NUISANCE AT KINGSLEY.

_ The Inspector reported that a serious nuisance arose from a pit at Kingsley, adjoining the land of Messrs. Mitchell and Harvey. All kinds of rubbish was placed in the pit. Mr. Mitchell wished to fill up the pit and en- close it, but strong objections were raised to this course. —After some discussion, it was resolved that the pit be drained and the land left open for the use of the children as a playground, on the motion of Mr. Aaron, seconded by Mr. J. Hall. There was no other business of public interest.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Colonel Ashton presided over the fortnightly meeting held on Tuesday at Dutton Workheuse. Present—the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, Messrs. .T. Mclntyre, S. Taylor, J. Grine, P. Hall, J. Stokes, W. Kirkham. T. Lewis, E. Aaron, John Weir, J. Hall, J. Davies, D. H. Jones, J. Brandreth,J. Parr, T. Hadfield, T. Warburton, T. Hewitt, T. Forster, W. Clarke, G. Priestner, U. Linaker (clerk), and W. 11. Linaker (deputy clerk). THE WEAVER TRUST AGITATION.

Mr. Aaron proposed the of—sZi-cllY;h:lti given , notice :—" That the attention of the Government be • called to the constitution and mode of election of the trustees for the management of the Weaver Trust in the County of Chester, and that the President of the Board of Trade or some other Government department be re- quested to introduce a clause in the Local Government Bill now before Parliament for handing over the manage- ment of such Trust to the County Council, or a committee directly responsible to such Council." Mr. Aaron said if the Weaver was turned over to the county authority under the Local Government Bill it would be managed in a proper manner. Had the Weaver been managed as well as the Bridgewater Navigation, the County of Ches- ter would not have had a farthing of county rate to pay for the last nine or ten years. It was all very well for Mr. Brunner to talk about the salt trade but he now paid himself a mere nothing for his goods being sent down the Weaver. The salt proprietors paid Is per ton for all salt they sent down the river, whilst they were not making one per cent, out of the manufacture of the salt, and Mr. Brunner, who was paying his shareholders a dividend of 20 per cent., only paid about 8d per ton for the carriage of his manufactures. Mr. Brunner's proposition to take the contribution from the ratepayers was preposterous. He had not walked along the bank of the Weaver for 24 years without learning something, and he had hundreds of times seen men who were paid wages for doing neat to nothing. Mr. Brandreth seconded Mr. Aaron's motion, on the ground that the ratepayers were the proper persons to have the management of the river Weaver. Mr. D. H. Jones said before the members could give an intelligent vote more information with regard to the Trust was Lece.ssary. He asked how and by whom were the Trustees of the river Weaver appointed. Mr. W. H. Linaker : By themselves. Mr. Jones: They must have some rule or method of self election.

Mr. W. H. Linaker : They are instituted by Act of Parliament, and they fill up vacancies by themselves. The qualification is £lOO a year for freehold property. Mr. Jones was proceeding to ask the terms of the obli- gation of the Weaver Trust to contribute towards the county fund, when he was interrupted by Mr. Hadfield who said it was not fair to ask the Clerk to answer these questions at once. The Rev. J. Lockwood: The Clerk should have had notice of such questions. Mr. Jones afterwards moved that discussion on the subject be adjourned until the next meeting to allow the Clerk an opportunity of answering his questions. Mr. P. Hall seconded the amendment, as it was im- portant the Board should have the information. Mr. Jones was proceeding to read his questions, when Mr. W. H. Linaker said it was unnecessary; he could hand them in.

Mr. Hadfield said he objected to Mr. Aaron's motion, because it was mizchievous and would not do the county good in any shape or form. The Weaver Trustees were men of business ability and large property owners, and It was to the interest of these men to manage the Trust properly, so that they could reduce the rates of the county. Had Mr. Aaron got any accusation to make that the Trustees were swindling the public? He be- lieved that the whole income was between £60,000 and £7OOOO a year, and out of that the Trustees paid £15,000 a year to the county rate, and was not that better in- terest than any navigation could pay. Besides that the Trustees paid £3,000 a year in poor rates to the county. The Trust was assessed at £13,000 to the poor rate of the Runcorn Union. (A member: Is that all. Laugh- ter.) In conclusion Mr. Hadfield asked if an old cor- poration like the Weaver Trust would be hoisted out by a few vague statements from Mr. Aaron, and he hoped that the Guardians would let well alone.
For the amendment only five voted: for the original motion eight, and against, eleven. The Chairman declared the amendment and motion lost.

SUGGESTED TRIP TO SOUTHPORT. Mr. Cunnah, the workhouse master, asked if the Guar- dians would allow the children to be taken a trip to Southport duringthe summer if he could raise the neces- sary funds.—The Rev. J. Lockwood suggested that the children had sufficient treats at home and abroad during the summer.—Mr. Cunnah said most of the girls had been in the hospital, and he thought a trip to the seaside would do them more good than going to Runcorn or Frodsham.—Mr. Taylor : What would it cost P.— Mr. Cunnali : About two or three pounds.—Mr.Taylor. : As a member of the Board, 1 am willing to render my assist- ance.—Mr. Hadfield said the outside ratepayers ought to pay and not the Guardians.—Mr. Taylor moved that the children be allowed to go if a fund be raised.—Mr. Hadfield: And that no canvassing be allowed amongst the Guardians.—The motion was carried.

div.head: CROWDED OUT.
div.p: CROWDED OUT.

Mr. Cunnah ri-ported--tliiY-at-th-e.present time the ac- commodation for children was insufficient. There were 51 boys and only 46 beds, and there was only one spare bed for the girls. He. however, thought there were some children in the house that their parents could well sup- port outside.—Mr. Ward. relieving officer for Runcorn. concurred in this view and mentioned a couple of instances.—A committee was formed to inquire and con- sider the matter.
• There was no other busineFks of public interest.

PRIVATE IMPROVEMENTS AT WIDNES. At Widnes Town Hall on Thursday morning, Major General C. Phipps Carey, of the Royal Engi- neers, one of the inspectors to the Local Government Board, held an inquiry in connection with the ap- plication of the Local Board to borrow £8,292 for works of private street improvement in John and Gerard-streets (West Bank), Little John. White, Hurst, Oakland, Viaduct, Violet, Bold, Alex- andra, Gerard (Simm's Cross), Travis, Grenfell, Mid- wood, and George streets; Terrace-road, and the back passage off Ditton-road. The following mem- bers of the Board were present :—Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. J. Midwood, .1. Taylor, S. Sadler, R. Cook. and T. Handley, with J. T. Allen (clerk), T. Higgin- son, (surveyor.) The only ratepayer present was Mr. Thomas Sadler.—The inspector inquired if any objections had been made to the making of these streets. —Mr. Allen said a petition had been received from the property owners against the making of the back passage off Ditton-road, on the ground that the work was unne- cessary. Miss Barker, a property owner, had objected to the making of Alexandra-st., because she alleged it was only required for the convenience of Alex- andra Theatre, and she refused to contribute anything to such a purpose. The property owners had also objected to the making of Violet-st. on the ground that it was a general thorough- fare, and was in fair condition. The Clerk added that the making of the present batch of streets had been sanctioned by the lioard.—The Surveyor explained the manner in which the Board proposed to make and sewer the streets.—Mr. T. Sadler made a speech upholding the objection to making Violet-st., which, he said, led to nowhere in particular, and was in better condition than many of the public roads.—The Inspector said he could not agree with Mr. Sadler, as even some of the streets were macadamised.—Mr. T. Sadler said he further ob- jected to the blue brick footwalk being replaced with flags, while blue bricks were being laid in other streets. That was an unnecessary expense.—The Inspector said he did not think it would be right to charge the rate- payers with the maintenance of blue brick tiles as a permanent material for footwalks. Tiles would not last long.—Mr. T. Sadler: I think they last equally as well as flags.—Mr. Sadler asked what the terms of repayment by the owners would be —The Inspector: The Local Board are asking for 10 vears.—Mr. Sadler I have no objection to that sir.—Mr. Allen said the Board considered that it was to the interests of the ratepayers that the footwalks should be flagged. All the streets that had been made during , the past ten years had been flagged.—ln reply to the Inspector Mr. Allen said the estimated population of the town was 33,000, the rateable value was £137,000, and the existing debt under the Public Health Act was £67,252. The general district rate was 2s 2d in the and the poor rate was 2s 4d in the £.—Alluding tn the sewering, the Inspector said it seemed .to him that the flushing arrangements were very poor. He suggested that an automatic tank should be placed at the head of the main sewer, and other automatic tanks at the head of some of the main branches. They would only need te connect the sewer with the tanks once or twice during the summer and the sewer would be flushed from one end to the other.—The inquiry then concluded.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY "ARIL."

(Now that the ball has been set rolling more will be heard about the Weaver Trust. The motion made by Mr. Aaron, at the Runcorn Board of Guar- dians. this week, was a step in the right direction. That the ratepayers are the proper persons to con- trol the management of a public trust, one would have thought that no person except the most fool- hardy would venture to deny, and yet in their col— lective wisdom the Guardians declined to move in the matter. _ _

Mr. Jones has not allowed much time to elapse before making his maiden speech, and he put some very pertinent questions as to the Trust. Would it not have been better to have adiourned the matter in order to obtain the fullest information, and not have acted so precipitately under the ex- cited rhetoric of Mr. Hadfield?

The dreadful picture hr. Hadfield drew of the cost of a conflict with the Trust apparently alarmed some of the farmers, who are great advocates of whit they term "economy." The benefit that has accrued to the ratepayers from the 'Trust, however, is not so great as would at first appear. The £15,000 is spoken of as though it had always been willingly and punctually paid over to the county, but if an average were struck it would be seen that the yearly payment has been much less than that sura ; and that the share of Runcern Union has not been more, probably less, than a penny in the off the rates. Were a thorough inquiry made into the cir- cumstances under which the Trust was instituted, I think there would be found to be more reason in Mr. Brunner's proposition than some persons at the present time imagine. The hot weather is once more upon us in all its intensity, and yet the poor Runcornian pants in vain for a bath. In taking a stroll the other evening, I heard several of the unwashed sing- ing:—
I shall never be happy again, Till Peter the chemist Builds baths as he "premised," I shall never be happy again.

div.head: WHITSUNTIDE AT WIDNES.
div.p: WHITSUNTIDE AT WIDNES.

The "chemical metropolis," as Widnes is now denominated, was quite deserted on Monday. The whole of the works were stopped at noon on Satur- day until Tuesday morning, and in a number of in- stances work was not resumed until Wednesday morning. Of course, it must be understood that certain necessary operations had to be continued, and although the chimnies of the manufactories were not turning out the customary and large amount of smoke and gas, still a thin wreath of brownish vapour was to be seen ascending in the air, testifying to the fires that almost ceaselessly burned beneath. It may be said, however, that to all intents and purposes the holiday was universal. A more favourable day could not have been imag- ined. An almost clear sky, a brilliant sun, and a pleasant wind, was a charming combination of the atmospheric elements; and there was quite an exodus of people from the town. The railway traffic was exceptionally heavy from both stations. From the London and North-Western Railway Station, early in the morning, a trip organised by the officials of St. Bedo's Roman Catholic Sunday schools departed for Llandudno. Upwards of 700 persons availed themselves of the opportunity to visit the queen of Welsh watering places, and they spent a most enjoyable day. To Blackpool 300 persons were booked, and about a similar number travelled to Southport, whilst a large number want to Man- chester with the intention oi witnessing the County Cricket Match at Old Trafford. Apparently, Liverpool presented most attractions to those in search of amusement, and during the day no less than 1,500 were despatched to the seaport city, the ordinary trains being literally packed. About 2,000 also passed across Runcorn Bridge to witness the festivities there, and also to journey to Overton Hills and the ancient city of Chester. Mr. McCon- nell and his staff proved quite capable of dealing with the traffic. From the Central Station about 800 departed to Southport, unwards of a thousand to Liverpool, and a good number went to Manches- ter. The return journeys home were accomplished without mishap.

div.head: WARRINGTON CORPORATION AND
div.p: THE WARRINGTON CORPORATION AND

MR. GILBERT GREENALL. The following is a copy of the address which was prepared by the Warrington Corporation for presentation to Mr. Gilbert Greenall on his coming of age : To Gilbert Greenall, Esq., son and heir apparent of Sir Gilbert Greenall. Bart., of Walton Hall, the member of Parliament for the borough of Warrington.—We, the Mayor, aldermen, and burgesses of the borough of War- rington, on the occasion of your coming of age avail ourselves with much pleasure of the opportunity to offer you our best wishes and heartiest congratulations on an event so important to yourself and so welcome to Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall. You have now reached the period of age which qualifies you to take that part in the active business aid affairs of life for which you *are so well aided by the many advantages by which you are happily surrounded. We trust that your future career may be gifted with happiness to yourself and advantage to those with whom your daily life may bring you into c_mtact. We add to our congratulations the hope that it may please the Giver of all good who has led you hitherto in safety to grant you health and strength to pursue a career of usefulness and honour, and that your I honoured parents, Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall, may live long to witness it. Given under the corporate ; common seal this third day of April. IBBB.—Thomas H. Sutton, Mayor; Wm. Hy. Brook, town clerk.) It was originally ntended by those who prompted r this needless epistle—for Mr. Gilbert greenall does not even reside in Warrington—that the depu- tation to accompany the precious document should include two Liberal aldermen, and we know not bow many Corporation officials. But the Liberal aldermen showed no appreciation of the doubtful compliment which was being paid them—particu- larly as it was rumoured that somebody at Walton Hall had stated that Warrington people were not wanted at that establishment. It will not sur- prise the public, therefore, that the deputation finally consisted of two only—the Mayor (Alder- man Sutton) and Alderman Webster. An intima- tion was sent from the office of the Town Clerk to the newspaper offices that the address would be presented at Walton Hall, at three o'clock, on Thursday afternoon. As it happened, the Mayor and Alderman Webster reached Walton Hall shortly before the hour. The " Guardian " reporter, who • was in in waiting, was, we learn, given to under- stand, when the deputation presented themselves, that there was no room for him—in other words, that reporters were not wanted; hut, notwithstand- ing this snubbing, he pressed forward to report what was said. At three o'clock, representatives of this journal, and of the "Observer," presented them- selves, and were told by the lackey that they could not be admitted—that is io say they did not want any reporters. The order was evidently intended to be imperative, or, it is a matter of course te say, our Tory contemporary would not have been excluded. Upon hearing how matters stood, our representative remarked that if they could do without the reporters, the reporters could do without them. He had an objection to entering a house when he knew he was not welcome, or to hang around picking up crumbs of informa- tion; and so. having discharged his duty, he came away. This treatment of the presentation of the address as a private matter shows, better than any- thing else could, how little it can be said to repre- sent the " burgesses" on whose behalf it has been prepared. The address, as proceeding from the Corporation, has been a mistake from beginning to end. It had its origin in the snobbery of a few; it was regarded with indifference by the many: and has ended, as it deserved to end, in &fiasco.

At Great Yarmouth Police Court, on Wednesday, Wil- liam Lovick. master of the Yarmouth trawler, Lurline. pleaded guilty to damaging the nets of the Dutch fishing boat Poolster, and was fined £l5. A fire, caused by a spark from a threshing machine. occurred on Thursday afternoon at the Firs Farm, Old Trafford. The rickyard and outbuildings were destroyed. The damage amounts to £4,000 or £5,000. THE QUEEN'S BIRTHDAY.—The sixty-ninth anniver- sary of the birth of the Queen was celebrated in London on Thursday by the firing of salutes at the Tower, and the ringing of bells. Flags were hoisted at prominent public buildings. Similar observances took place at Windsor. The event will be generally celebrated on June 2ad. Four only of the Sovereigns of England have attained an age exceeding that of her Majesty, and they are—Queen Elizabeth, who lived 70 years; George 11., 77 years ; George 111., 82 years; and William NI., 72 years. On the 20th•of June next her Majesty will have reigned over the United Kingdom Si years, a period which ha.' been exceeded by two only of the monarchs of- England—namely, Henry 111., who reigned for 56 years, and George 111., whose reign lasted for nearly 80 years. Her Majesty is also the oldest reigning European Sove- reign with two exceptions, they being William 111., King of the Netherlands, who is over 71 years of ace, and Christian IX., King of Denmark, who is over 70 'Tara old. Her Majesty was proclaimed Empress of India in. 1877.

A few weeks ago Mr. Matthew- Arnold, while apparent- ly in the best ehealth, was suddenly stricken down, and in a few hours the world was in tears over the dis- tinguished man's grave. AAmiral Sir Astley Cooper Key, some weeks ago paid a short visit to London, and upon, returning home, the next day suddenly expired. WARRINGTON BOROUGPI POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess. BEGOING.—dohn Reynolds, labourer, of no settled resi- dence was committed to prison for 7 days with hard labour, for begging in Bridge-st., on the previous after-

noon. MONDAT.—Before Alderman Davies and Alderman Harrison. DRITICICILNNESS. The following were disposed of for this offence :—George Hopkins, labourer, Scotland-road, 5s and costs; James Slater, labourer, Howley Quay, 'fined 5s including costs; John Sandwell, tramp, and Ellen McDonald, factory-hand, discharged with a cau- tion. TIIPSDAY.—Before Messrs R. W. Francomb and E. J.

Guest. DRUNKENNESS. Thomas Garrity, for having been drunk and disorderly, on March Ist, lOs and costs; Margaret Bestnall, drunk and disorderly, at Schoolbrow, on Whit-Monday, 5s and costs. Love AT 110s.—Charles Fudge was charged with having been drunk and disorderly at his residence, and further, with assaulting his wife, Mary Ann Fudge. P.C. Chantler stated that he was called to the house of the defendant and found him very drunk. In the presence of himself and another constable, he knocked his wife down and gave her two black eves.—Prisoeer denied the charge. It was stated that the Woman would not appear to prosecute.—The magistrates said that as the woman would not prosecute, the secdnd charge would -be dis- missed. For the first, however, prisoner would be fined 5s and costs. ANNOYING PEOPLE. James Boardman was charged with baying been drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket- st. on Tuesday afternoon P.C. Singleton said that the defendant was annoying Mr. Gilbert Greenall, who was in his carriage, and Mr. P. Stubs. 'As the defendant re- fused to go away, he took him into custody.—The Bench imposed a fine Of ss, including costs. , THURSDAY.—Before Major Litton and Councillors Platt and Greening. THREATENING A WIFE. Samuel Brookes, a respect- ably dressed man, was charged with having, on the 22nd May, threatened his wife, Mary Ann Brookes, by which she feared he would do her some grievous bodily harm. As the complainant brought no witnesses the case was dismissed, the Bench recommending the defendant to keep away from complainant. A SOLDIER'S CHILDREN. A charge against Patrick Ford, for deserting his 6 children and allowing thenk to become chargeable to the Warrington Union was with- drawn, as he had enlisted in Her Majesty's service, and part of his pay was being handed over to the Union. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison and Dr. Gomel'. • DRUNKENNESS IN BANK PARK.—Tyndall Milne and Ed- ward Pritchard were summoned on a charge of haying been drunk in Bank Park on the 22nd of May. Mr. J. L. Whittle appeared to prosecute. A fine of is and costs was inflicted in each case. THE CONSEQUENCE OF A SPREE—Henry Robinson was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in But- termarket-st. on the 23rd just, and further with having assaulted his wife Jane Robinson, at the same time and place. Defendant pleaded guilty. Complainant stated that her husband only abused her when drunk, and she was then in fear on account of him. For the first charge he was fined 5s including costs, and fpr the second he was ordered to find two sureties of £lO each for his good behaviour for the next six months. Defendant pleaded guilty and was sent to Wal- ton to await a military escort. The man seemed to be in the most destitute condition and said "he wished he was in his arave." DISMISSED.—A charge of assault on Joseph and Eliza- beth Molvneux by John and Eli= Hill was dismissed on the defendants paying the costs. AN UNGRATEFUL HUSBAND.—AbeI Mather was charged with having assaulted his wife, Martha Jane Mather' on the 23rd of May. Complainant stated that she had leiien married to defendant 21 years, and when he had not much work she tried to earn something at. Cockhedge Factory. On the evening oP the 23rd she had been at work, and on coming home defendant 'struck her and gave her a black eye. She gave him no provocation, and he had since said that he was sorry for having done it.
