div.head: SOUTHAMPTON ELECTION.
div.p: THE SOUTHAMPTON ELECTION.

GREAT LIBERAL VICTORY. The polling for the election of a Parliamentary representative for Southampton, to fill the vacancy caused by the retirement of Admiral Commerell (Conservative), commenced at eight o'clock on Wednesday morning, the candidates being Mr. Francis Henry Evans (Gladstoniau Liberal) and Mr. Arthur Edmund Guest (Conservative). The contest attracted considerable interest, and the par- tisans of each candidate were early in the field. Although Mr. Evans was not present (being on his way from America) he had many volunteer repre- sentatives. In splendid weather the polling in the forenoon proceeded briskly. Many vehicles were employed, the drivers wearing suits of party colors, while hor-emen similarly attired patrolled the streets. There were fifteen polling stations, the distance between the extremest of them being six miles. The canvassers on both sides were very ac- tive. Lady Ann Blunt, Mis Amy Mender (of Wol- verhampton), and Mrs. Bateson worked for Mr. Evans. Mr. Guest had also \ plenty of assistance. Mr. Guest drove round the town during the morn- ing. Mrs. Evans, accompanied by her daughter and Mr. Cooksey, one of the unsuccessful Liberal candi- dates at the last election, also visited the polling stations. In addition to mounted messengers, the Liberals had a voluntary corps of cyclists employed in a similar capacity. The streets got livelier every hour. and the polling became b^isker in the out dis- tricts. The Conservatives paraded a donkey in their colours, bearing the inscription on his head, "Guest for ever."
About half-past ten o'clock on Wednesday even- ing the result of the polling was declared as fol- lows: Evans (L) Guest (C)

Liberal majority At the last election, Mr. J. H. C,ooksey and Mr. J. C. M'Coan. standing in the Liberal interest, were op- posed by Mr. Alfred Giles and Admiral Sir J. E. Com- merell, Conservatives. The figures of the poll were as follows : _
Mr. Alfred Giles (C) 5,023 Admiral Sir J. E. Commerell (C) 4,726 Mr. J. H. Cooksey (L) 4,384 Mr. J. C. M'Coan (L)
Aggregate Conservative majority 668 At the 1885 poll the votes recorded were as fol- lows:
Giles (C) 5,595 Commerell (C) Lee (L) Jones (L) 4,533
Aggregate Conservative majority 901' ARRIVAL OF MR EVANS.—ETTHUSIASTIC RECEP- TION.

The North-German Lloici—steamer arrived at South- ampton on Thursday afternoon, and Mr. F. H. Evans, the newly-elected member for the borough, who had crossed in her from New York, landed at the docks about half-past one. He had a most enthusiastic recep- tion from his friends, among those present being Sir William and Lady Harcourt, Mr. Harcourt, and Mr. Her- bert Gardner, M.P. In response td calls for a speech, Sir William Harcourt spoke a few words, declaring that the electors of Southampton had won a glorious victory, and paid a tribute to the energy shown by Mrs. Evans in the contest.

Mr. Evans, M.P., speaking at Southampton On Thurs- day night, said he was so much surprised, after eight days' steaming across the Atlantic, to find the election over, that words failed him to express his feelings of gra- titude. At the time when he learned in Newfoundland that the Southampton election was pending, the entire coast was blocked with ice, and it was only by a fortu- nate chance that the block was raised in time for him to catch a steamer. Every advantage had been taken of his advantage in hurrying forward the election, but, thanks to his wife and his friends, they had achieved the victory.

At Runcorn as at other places the projectors of the great under- taking, at the outset, met with existing rights and interests and arrangements, and before these could be interfered with they had to submit to various conditions, most of which are embodied in their Act of Parliament, and it is to these conditions we propose to refer in the present article.

OPENING OF A .MISSION HALL .AT THELWALL.

On Sunday morning the mission hall, which hasp been erected at the cost of Mr. Walker, the Ship Canal con- tractor, on the Thelwall section, a short distance from Morris Brook farm, was formally opened for "religious services." The building is constructed of wood, is com- fortably furnished, and will accommodate about 400 per- sons. On Sunday it was made to look as attractive as possible by flowers/ which were placed on the window ledges, and texts and mottoes on the walls. At one end of the room is a platform, on the higher part of which is a desk, at which stands the minister when conducting the service, while on the lower part is a table, upon which stood a number of vases containing choice flowers. On each side of this platform is a classroom. At the op- posite end of the building there is another platform for the convenience of the choir, a harmonium being placed in the eel-I%re, and it can also be used for the accommo- dation of the children of the workmen. Between the two platforms benches are placed' in• rows, upon which had been laid a large number of bibles, and copies of the sacred songs and solos (Nos. land 2 combined) composed by Mr. Ira D. Sankey. There was a: small attendance at the opening service on Sunday morning but that, it was presumed, was owing to the Whitsuntide holidays, to the date of the opening not being generally known, and to other causes. Mr. Price, the principal agent for this sec- tion was early in attendance, and to him and to his wife and daughters (who led the musical part of the service), great praise is due for the excellent arrangements which had been made for the opening and subsequent services. His son, Master Harry Price, presided at the harmlnium. The minister appointed to take charge of the services is Mr. Stephen H. Jenkins, who won the res- pect and esteem of the men when engaged in similar work for Mr. Walker at St. Fagan's, Cardiff. The services are of an entirely unseetarian character. In the course of his address, Mr Jenkins said that whilst the hall had been erected by Mr Walker chiefly for his employes, they would be very glad indeed to see any of their neighbours, and would endeavour to give them a hearty welcome. He hoped they would come as fre- quently as they could. Services would be held twice on the Lord's Day, in the morning at eleven o'clock, and in the evening at half-past six, and he hoped that as soon as the huts were occupied a Sunday school would be opened similar to the one which was conducted at Car- diff, and that the friends in the neighbourhood, whose children did not attend any other school, would send them to the Mission Hall. In the evening the service was attended by over a hundred persons.

div.head: RUN'ORN " PROTECTED."
div.p: RUN'ORN " PROTECTED."

First of all, we find that "for the protec- tion of the port and town of Runcorn and the Improvement Commissioners of the said town, and the shipowners and traders carrying on business at Runcorn" a variety of pro- visions are laid down. In the event of the Canal Company acquiring the Bridgewater undertaking— which as we know they have done—they are not to levy or charge any higher tolls or charges for its use than were charged in -1885 by the Bridgewater Company; no canal tolls are to be demanded by the company for any nightsoil, ash-pit refuse, cinders, or street sweepings carried by the Commissioners or any of their contractors or servants; all vessels carrying- salt only and not exceeding 450 tons gross register, and carrying not more than 500 tons, in passing from the docks and basins down and out of the canal are to be exempt from the payment of all ship dues and canal and lockage tolls; all vessels, whether light or in ballast, not exceeding 450 tons gross register, and destined for the docks and basins at Runcorn, for the purpose of loading salt, are to enter and pass along the canal between Eastham and Runcorn without payment of any ship dues or canal and lockage tolls; all ves- sels destined for the docks at Runcorn whose cargo consists only of flints, felspar, china-st6ne, china- clay, or bones for the use in the manufacture of pot- tery and n t exceeding 450 tons gross register, and not carrying more than 500 tens may also enter from the estuary of the Mersey and pass along the canal to Runcorn on the payment of half the ship dues, and such cargo, if destined for the Staffo-dshire potteries, is to be liable only to the payment of half the tolls prescribed by the Ship Canal Act. It is further declared that if the Canal Company make any exemption from any portion of any dues pay- able under their Act in resp-ct of any vessels er cargo, beyond those mentioned above, , they are to make the like exemption in respect of all vessels and cargo destined for the Runcorn docks or basins, falling within the same class or description, and using or carried upon the same section of the canal, and subject to the same dues and in the like ' circumstances.

STREETS AND DRAINS. The Commissioners are protected in respect to the streets and drains under their charge. It is enacted that in the event of any alterations in, interference with, or damage or obstruction to, any street, road, footpath. sewer, or drain, belonging to, or under the control of, the Commissioners, being at any time caused by the works or operations of the Company. the latter shall forthwith make good the same, at their own cost, to the reasonable satisfaction of the Commissioners; and the Company shall also be liable to compensate the Commissioners for any damage or loss occasioned to them. The Company are not, without the consent of the Commissioners, in any way to interfere with the free flow of the sewerage of the district into the Mersey or its es- tuary, unless the Company have beforehand provi- ded at their own expense and vested in the Com- missioners all proper and sufficient outfalls and works for conveying the sewage under the canal and into the Mersey. In case of extra expense being incurred by the Commissioners in working and maintaining the new sewers over what it costs them in connection with their present sewers, the Canal Company are to recompense them to that extent. The Company likewise bind themselves in their Act to at all times afford the Commissioners all reason- able facilities and accommodation for carrying through, or under, their property any sewers, drains, or outfalls, it may be necessary to construct hereafter for the proper drainage of the district, and this work is to be carried out in such manner, and upon such terms as to wayleave and other matters, as the Local Government Board may determine, having regard to the facilities which the Commissioners at present possess for carrying out and executing works for the sewering of their dis- trict. In case any new drain or sewer or other work of the Commissioners affect the Canal or other property of the Company, it is to be carried out, according to plans previously submitted to and approved, and under the superintendence of the Company's engineer, and shall not interfere with or affect the working cf the canal or its future im- provement, and in the event of the canal works or other property of the Company sustaining any damage in consequence of the execution of such Works the Commissioners will be held liable to com- pensate the Company. Should any dispute arise be- tween the Commissioners and the Company respect- ing the necessity for any works proposed by the Commissioners, or shoulA the Company require the Commissioners to execif;.e any works which the lat- ter may consider to be unnecessary or unreasonable, the Local Government Board shalLon the application of either the Company or the Commissioners, deter- mine the question as to whether the requirements of the Company are necessary and reasonable, and to what extent. HOW TO CROSS THE CANAL

The Canal Company are to provide sufficient ac- commodation by a ferry or other means to enable persons to pass across the canal to or from Runcorn from or to the Mersey. WIDNES "PROTECTED." Though the chemical town lies on the side of the Mersey opposite the Ship Canal, there are some of its interests which it has been thought might be prejudicially affected by the canal, and it, too, there- fore, has sought "protection" in Parliament. As a result, it is laid down in the Ship Canal Act that if at any time, during or after the construction of the canal works, the entrance channel or approach from the main low water channel in the upper estuary of the Mersey to the Widnes dock and the West Bank dock at Widnes, the Sankey Canal or to Ditton brook, shall be impeded or rendered less deep than before the passing of the Act, the Canal Company— unless they can prove to the satisfaction of an arbi- trator that such impediment or damage is not to be assigned to their works—shall from time to time at the request of the Widnes Local Board, or of any company or person aggrieved, remove or remedy the impediment or damage by dredging or otherwise. Further, the Local Board, or aggrieved company or person, may recover from the Canal Company com- pensation for damages sustained by them or him by reason of any default on their part in meeting the requirements of the Act. If during or after the con- struction of the canal the outfall of any watercourse or sewer within the Widnes Local Board district become prejudicially affected the Canal Company— unless, in this case as in the last, they can prove to an arbitrator that the damage is not to be assigned to their works—shall, at the request of the Local Board, or of the owners for the time being of the watercourse or sewer in ques- tion, restore and make good such outfall to the reasonable satisfaction of the Lucid Board or owners, and these latter may recover from the company compensation for damages sustained by reason of any default on the part of the company. In case that, at any time during or after the con- struction of the canal works.the Mersey from the most easterly boundary of Widnes downwards hpcome so changed as to hinder such vessels as are now able to enter and leave Widnes and West Bank docks, Sankey canal and Ditton brook, and to navigate between Widnes and any place lower down the Mersey from continuing so to do in as free and ample a manner as they have heretofore done, the Canal Company—unless they can prove the change to be not due to their works—shall, at the request of the Local Board or others aggrieved, from time to time during the continuance of the change, keep open, by dredging or otherwise, convenient COM- rounications between the docks named, Sankey canal, and Ditton brook, and the wharves adjoining the entrances to the Sankey canal belonging to Messrs. Gossage and Sons, Messrs. J. Hutchinson and Company, Messrs. William Cooper and Com- pany, and Mr. Thomas Wright, and one or more of the locks and entrances to the Ship Canal, so as to enable vessels to enter or leave the canal at the times they had previously been able to navigate the

div.head: WHITSUNTIDE FESTIVITIES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: WHITSUNTIDE FESTIVITIES AT RUNCORN.

Whitsuntide was celebrated in Runcorn in the customary manner. It is a time of great rejoicing amongst the younger portion of the population, and Whit-Monday may with truth be described as the "children's day." Each year the members of the friendly societies attired in the gay regalia of their respective orders. display their quality and impor- tance to the public gaze, and in the afternoon the children in atttndance at the various Sunday schools in the town parade through the public streets. For ' this outward show. new garments are, deemed especially necessary, and Whitsuntide is the great harvest time of the tailors and drapers of. the town. On the Sunday preceding the festival, the town pre- sents the appearance of a "Vanity Fair." By both young and old it is apparently an established cus- tom that the recently acouired apparel shall see the light on that day as though to prepare for the com- ing show on the morrow. The scene is indeed a gay one, as the gentler sex attired in all the colours of the rainbow pass to and fro along the streets, those of older growth being attended by swains, who, although not shedding the same brightness, are nevertheless resplendent in new raiment. Of course, fine weather, is highly essential for the proper and pleasurable observance of the festival; a wet Whitsuntide is a period of urea misery. For- tunately, on the present occasion, the atmospheric elements were exceeding favourable for the holidays, which commenced on Saturday at noon and extended to Wednesday morn- ing, and in many instances to a day later. There was a clear sky, a brilliant sun, and a pleasant breeze. It should be stated that every third year a special effort is made, and it is in consequence styled the "big day." Monday last was not the "big day," but the processians formed a pleasant sight, and attracted large numbers of people from the surrounding towns. About 2,000 crossed Runcorn Bridge from Widness, and some hundreds came from North wich and Winsford by boat down the river Weaver, whilst others came from places more distant, and the town presented a most lively and busy appearance.

THE CLUBS. The demonstration of clubs this year was confined to three only, and they commenced their peregrinations through the principal thoroughfares about ten o'clock in' the morning. 'The Duke Club, which was established in 1790, occupied the position of honour. Headed by Wid- nes Soap Works band and their beautiful banner, they lead the procession. Dr. Robinson and Dr. Mangan, and Messrs. J. Meadowcroft (agent to the Bridgewater Undertaking), J. K. Digges, T. Simister, and T. Done, occupied prominent positions in the procession. Then followed the members of the Ebenezer Lodge of the In- dependent Order of Oddfellows, M.U., which was estab- lished in 1828, and is the oldest registered lodge in the district. This lodge meets at the New mu. They marched to the music of the Weston Church Brass Band. The rear was brought up by the members of the Duke of Edinburgh Lodge of the Grand United Order of Odd- fellows, whose headquarters are at the Bull's Head, Halton-road. Altogether there would be about 250 mem- bers in the procession, which wended its way through the principal streets to Fountain-square, where a stop- page was made, and the combined bands played a selec- tion of music. Bridge-st. and Halton road, as far as the Crow, was traversed. The Duke of Edinburgh Lodge went forward to the village of Flatten, whilst the Duke's Club returned to the Parish Church. A short service was held, and the vicar, the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, ' preached an appropriate sermon. 'Ale Ebenezer Lodge journeyed to Higher Runcorn, to the residence of Mr. S. B. Chadwick, who is a member of the Order. The members were hospitably entertained, and the bandhav- ing rendered several pieces of music, the procession re- trned to the Lodge-room and dispersed. THE NONCONFORMIST SCHOOLS. In the afternoon the procession of scholars took place, and excited great interest. The streets were lined with thousands of spectators, of which parents of the children taking part in the demonstration formed a large propor- tion. The scene was a very pretty one. Flags fluttered i in the breeze from numerous buildings, and n.the ranks of the processionists were carried aloft banners of every device and hue, whilst the children were attired in colours of every shade and style. Conforming to their usual practice, the schools of the Church of England demonstrated on their own account, but the Noncon- formist schools held a united display, and a feature that was received with much favour was the presence of the Catholic scholars in the procession. The position of each school in the ranks was determined byothe date of its establishment, and Brunswick Wesleyan school, com- menced in 1800, led the way. As they passed along the- choir sang a hymn and their voices had a very pleasing effect. At the head of the 650 scholars marched the Rev. G. Wood (the superintendent minister), Messrs. J. Simp- son, T. Simister, R. Norman, S. Ravenscroft, W. Corns, E. Taylor, B. Kniveton, Sic. Next in order came the 220 children from St. John's Presbyterian School, estab- lished in 1818. The two superintendents, Messrs. James Pritchard and J. Kirkham, with Messrs. John Pritchard, R. Baxter, and F. Hewitt, walked in front. Following was St. Luke's Congregational School, established 1833, number of scholars 160. Messrs. J. J. Speakman, J. Slade, and W. Lacey lead the way. Bethesda Congrega- tional Sunday School, established in 1835, consisting of 250 scholars, then followed, and prominent in the ranks were the Rev: J. D, Thomas, Messrs. W. Handley (super- intendent), T., Riley, James Aikenhead, J. Ornsson (Garston), T. Machin, H. Chadwick, and S. Watson. Established in 1837, St. Edward's Roman Catholic School was next in order. The scholars' numbering 300, were headed by the Band of the Widnes Irish National Foresters. In front was carried a handsome new banner with the inscription, "Prosperity to Runcorn," and immediately behind were the Revd. Dr. Gastilda, Messrs. M. Nickson, J. Byrne, James Lea, and T. Wil- liamson.—The Primitive Methodist scholars numbering 300 followed, and were headed by the fife and drum band connected with the school. The date of the estab- lishment of this school was 1839. In the front ranks were the Rev. J. Causland, the Rev. G. Rennison, and Messrs. R. Midge, J. Bate, Fleet, Upton, and J. Stubbs. Following were the scholars of the Mill Brow Wesleyan

div.head: THE_ CHURCH SCHOOLS.
div.p: THE_ CHURCH SCHOOLS.

The children attending the National Schools, number- ing about 500, started out at one o'clock, accompanied by the Rev. A. Maitland Wood (xicat), the Rev. G. A. Tindall, Messrs. E. Marwood and W. Whittaker (churchwardens), Messrs. A. Jordan (supt.), &c. The School Band headed the procession. Following were 102 scholars and 17 teachers from St. Michael's and All An- gels. Walking in front were Mr. Charles Pownall (superintendent), G. Summerfield, J. H. Cropper, T. Blundell, and E. Ridge. The procession wended its way through the principal streets to the Vicarage, where it was joined by the scholars from the schools at Weston, and together they spent the afternoon on the common. Upon separating. they retired to their respective schools and were regaled with tea, &c., and entertainments were held. The children from Holy Trinity Schools, number- ing about 370, walked in.. procession to a field. They were accompanied by the Rev. W. Preston (7icar), Rev. G. Fisher (curate), Messrs. Buckley, Goodall, Cannington Leithwood, Broughton, Hulse, Haplehurst, and West. Tea was afterwards provided in the school, and an en- tertainment followed. MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN.'

An independent procession was also held in conncetion with this mission. Including a number of sailors, Bat- men, and boatmen, about 450 scholars took part in the procession, which was led by the Mission Fife knd Drum Band. Mr. W. Shaw, the missionary, walked in front. About 100 children of tender years were conveyed through the route in floats, lent by the Manchester Ship Canal Company. On returning to the school, tea was provided and an entertainment given.

div.p: AFTEE THE PROCESSIONS

many of the inhabitants went in of pleasure. Liverpool, Chester, and Frodsham were the chief places of resort, and 1,454 passengers were booked from the railway stations. Hundreds, however, travelled to Fred- sham by road. The Ship Canal works at Norton were besieged with visitors, who viewed with wonder the execution done by the steam navvies ,and the other mechanical appliances on the spot. Nor were the pretty spots in the neighbourhood left unpatronised, and par- ties who had evidently been on botanising intent were I to be seen returning home laden with their spoil. In the I town the fair ground was the scene of noisy merriment from morning until late at night. With the exception of a few fights amongst those who, having "drink in," had "wit out," the order of the town was well preserved by Superintendent Hollingworth and his constables.

div.head: 'HALTON TRINITY WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.
div.p: 'HALTON TRINITY WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.

In connection with the above school, the Whit-Monday treat was observed as usual. This arrangement was re- solved upon about ten years ago to facilitate means of enjoyment for the purpose of shielding the young people from the existing evils which so abundantly prevail on festive days. The object has been accompanied with de- served success. The teachers and scholars met at the school at half-past one, when a procession, numbering about 250, was formed, and paraded round the village. A stoppage was made ell royte when all united in singing the well-known beautiful hymn "There is sweet rest in heaven." Proceeding to a field placed at their disposal by the kindness of Mr. William Nixon, out-door sports were engaged in until half-past four. A procession was again formed to the school to do justice to the good things provided. Over 200 children sat down to tea at a charge of 2d each, the adults numbering 120, having refreshed themselves at the small charge of ad each. The Rev. R. F. Hornabrook expressed his pleasure in seeing so many friends and strangers present, and said he hoped that throughout the day they would enjoy themselves as had been evidenced during tea. Presiding at tables were :—Misses Gamon, Rowe, Hornabrook, :Lea, Saun- ders, F. Rowe, Astbury, Howard, and Mason. Games were again resumed until a quarter to nine, when the , scholars finally wended their way to the front of the chapel andjoined in singing the Doxology, after which lusty cheers were given for Mr. and Mrs William Nixon for the use of the field, bringing the day's proceedings to a pleasant termination. FRODSHAM.

This year Whit-Monday was, as usual, duly observed as a day of public demonstration by the friendly socie- , ties, and the main street from an early hour was all alive with swings, round-abouts, itinerant vendors of holiday luxuries, and all the other a.ccessories to the "fun of the fair." The clubs formed in procession and walked up to the Parish Church,and were headed by banners and brass bands. The following was the order :—Ancient Order of Foresters, number 410, Court Independence, number of members 250, in the procession 44, beaded by the Elles- mere Port Brass- Band, conducted by Mr. J. Garner; Modern Druids' Society, Maiden Queen Lodge, number of members 87, in the procession 44, headed by the Prod- sham Parish Church Brass Band, conducted by Mr. John Attains; Grand United Order of Oddfellows Society, "Emblem of Hope Lodge," number 516, number of members 128, number of widows 4, in the procession 45, headed by the Frodsham Volunteer Band, conducted by Sergeant Bugler William Jones. On arriving at the venerable fane the bands rendered the National Anthem. In the absence of the Vicar of Frodsham, the Rev. E. 0. Rawson, vicar of Ice, con- ducted the service, and delivered a practical sermon from the:text, "Quit ye like men; be strong." After the service the clubs paraded the district, calling at the Vicarage and other private residences on the route to the Castle Park, the residence of Mr. Wright, who had again generously thrown open his grounds to the public,' and large number of pleasure seekers availed themselves of the opportunity to view the grounds, which were well , worthy of a visit. The following is a report of the position financially of the above men- tioned elubs, gathered from the reports of the income and expenditure during the year 1887 : Ancient Foresters, total worth of funds, including all moneys, invested and interest due 31st December, 1886, £2,584 35.; total income for 1887, £435 ss. 6,id.; total, £3,019 8s sp. Payments: Sick pay to members, £245 lOs ; funeral allowances, £lO9 103 •, management fund, £B6 17s 8d ; total worth of funds December 31st, 1887, £2,577 los bid; total, £3,019 8s 61d. Modern Druids : Balance in hand, January Bth, 1887, £223 3s 7d ; contributions, &c., £lO9 18s ; total, £333 Is 7d. Ex- penditure: Sick pay, £47 19s 6d ; funeral allowances, £4l; other expenses, £29 3s lid; balance in hand on January 14th. 1888, £214 18s 2d; total, £333 is 7d. Oddfellows : Amount of funds at commencement of the year, £1,258 1.9 s Bd ; contributions, &c., £236 17s 9d ; total, £1,495 17s sd. Expenditure : Sick pay, funeral allowances, £242 Is 8d; other expenses. £4l 4s 9d; amount of funds at end of year, £1,212 lie ; total, £1495 17s Sd.

At the Mansion House, London, on Wednesday, Dr. George Frederick Philpott and Arthur William Plulpott, his son, were remanded, charged on a summons with obtaining an accident assurance policy and certain sums as compensation for accidents which never oc- curred.

•-••• BRITISH AND FOREIGN UNITARIAN ASSOCIATION.—The meetings of this association were resumed in London on Thursday morning under the presidency of Mr. Barry Rawson, of Manchester. The Rev. J. Page-Hopps read a paper on some of the special difficulties besetting Uni- tarians, and how to overcome them. If, he said, the Unitarian minister could see what he is to-day and not hanker after being a priest, he might become the most trusted and most really powerful teacher in the land. Mr. Hopps went on to speak of the importance of a rational religion at. the present day. Mr. Ellis, of Guild- ford, read avaper on the same subject.

ITHE.:ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER AT WARRINGTON. INQUEST AND COMMITTAL. On Saturday, Mr. Yates, coroner, opened an in- quest at the Cheshire Cheese Inn, Latchford, as to the death of Antony Gibbons, 43 years of age, a labourer. The particulars of this case were given at length last week. Briefly Btated, it appears that Gibbons and _another but younger Irish labourer' named Michael Garner, were in company with each 'other on the nikht of Saturday, the 12th inst. On the Sunday, Gibbons complained that in the course of a quarrel he had been both struck and kicked by Garner, and as he died on the Wednesday night, Garner, svho had for some time back contemplated going to America, was arrested on the following day at Liverpiol, on the steamship Bothnia, bound for Boston, and charged with having caused the death of Gibbons. - Garner was present at the inquest in custody. The first witness called was Martin Gibbons, a labourer, living at Grappenhall, who said that deceased was his father but he did not know how old he was. He last saw him on the previols Satur- day when he was all. right. Deceased left Ireland when he (witness) VAM only-five months old, an-I it was only because he had been told by other people that he knew him to be his father. James William Marsh, landlord of the Railway Inn, Latchford, said that prisoner and deceased came into his house about half-past 10 o'clock on the Saturday night previous. Neither of them were sober nor were they drunk, though the deceased was the worst of the two.' Prisoner had a pint of beer but deceased had nothing, and he had to eject deceased on account of his lois-con- duct. Prisoner stayed from ten minutes to' it quarter of an hour later. There had been some words between the two, and Garner told witness that Gibbons had been taking some money—about 4s— from him. Gibbons said it was not so and as he took to swearing,witness had to eject him.—Cross examined, Mr. Marsh said hefted noticed that Garner always treated deceased well when they had been in his house as deceased never had any money. He did not serve deceased with anything on the i night n question, but his servant girl might have done. Thomas Hewitt, farmer, said he lived at the farmhouse , Lower Wash-lane. Garner had been in his employ about two years, but Gibbons had not been employed by him [except for about two days during the last six months., Gibbons had, however, lived on his farm for about five weeks, but Garner did not live there. •About five o'clock on Sunday morning Gibbons came to him and said he , alid Garner had had a row on Saturday night in his yard and that Garner both hit and kicked him. There were no marks or bruises on Gibbons that could be Seen, and ,he appeared to be drunk. About 10 o'clock Garner was present when Gibbans again complained about be- ing kicked but Garner denied having kicked deceased. On: Monday, Gibbons lay in what was known as the " Paddy " house on witness's farm, but on Tuesday he I said he had been out. About Wednesday at noon deceased said he was worse and he (witness) told him he would have to see somebody about shifting him. Later in the same day witness gave information to a police- man, and about half-past 7 at night Dr. Spinks saw deceased and said that he was too weak to be removed. A man named Spruce was, therefore, got to sit during the night beside Gibbons.—Cross examined, Mr. Hewitt said it was nothing fresh for deceased to lie about two or three days. He had been aware kir some months that prisoner was going to America, and he knew that his passage had been actually taken. Gibbons complained ,that prisoner had hit him on the nose and kicked him on the stomach. He (witness) heard Garner say that Gib- 'bons had tried to pick his pocket. Mrs. Lowndes, who lives at 41, Redden Cottages, opposite Mr. Hewitt's yard gate, stated that between 12 and 1 o'clock on the Sunday morning previous she heard te noise outside her house. She heard some onegroaning, and after a while she got up and heard some one say • "Oh, Lord.help the, lam murdered • Mike Garner has I murdered me." She did not know wissit was that made use of the words; and as she thought she saw a police- man and the noise stopped, she did not go out. The sound' proceeded from the direction of Mr. Hewitt's gate. Thomas Spruce spoke to having sat beside deceased on the night of his death, having been engaged by the reliev- ing officer. Deceased never said anything except ask for a drink, though he made a rattling noise in his throat. Witness was present when a statement was taken from 'deceased about aouarter of an hour before he died. He heard the statement read by Inspector Spinks and saw it signed by deceased. At this point the inquiry was adjourned. THE ADJOURNED INQUEST. The adjourned inquest was held at the Cheshire Cheese Inn, on Tuesday morning, before Mr. Yates, when more evidence was taken. Mary Ellen Turton, Railway Inn, Latchford, deposed that she was a domestic servant in the employ of Mr. ' Marsh, the landlord. She remembered Gibbons and Garner corning into the house shortly after half-past ten on the 12th May. They did not appear to be drunk. She did not hear any high words between the men. She served Garner with a pint of beer, and he asked ,her not to let the deceased see her give him any change. - Dr. C. N. Spinks said he was called in to see the de- ceased on Wednesda,x.evening, the 16th inst. He got these about half-past eight, and found him lying in what was called the "paddy braise," mt some straw. He spoke to him, and asked him what was the matter with him,, and the deceased spoke in a husky voice. He could find no pulse in the man's wrist, and his hand and arm were perfectly cold. The relieving officer • yes with him and a policeman, and he told the,former that he could not certify to .the deceased's retneval, tis'he was in a dying state. He asked him what was the matter with him, and he said he had been kicked in the ,belly 4 and that he was "bad all over." He sent him some medi- , eine, and he took some of it. The man died at twelve o'clock. He had since made a post mortem examination of the body. There were no marks of violence oiosida the body. On opening the head he found the brain was healthy. The membranes of the brain were adhering to the skull cap. On opening the chest he found the heart healthy. The hinge were diseosed—of long standing— strongly adherent to each side of the chest. The bowels were in a state of disease from peritonitis. The liver was enlarged. The stomach was healthy, and contained a little fluid and gas. The kidneys were enlarged and congested. He found the bladder empty and ruptured: The rupture had caused the water to flow into the bowels, and produced peritonitis, which was the cause of 4:l6th on the fourth day. The rupture must have been caused by a blow or a fall from a high place on a hard substance. If done by a kick it must have been done by a 'Severe kick. The bursting of the bladder would cause Intense pain. The rupture might have been caused by running against a rail or falling on something that pro- jected above the ground. PC. Baxendale said that at 12-15 on Sunday morning, the 13th inst., ,he was passing the Cheshire Cheese Inn, when someone palled out Oh dear, dear; lam des- troyed, I am destroYed. Will no man come to my help ?" 'Witness went to Mr. Hewitt's farmyard, but could hear nothing. He then went to the next farm (Ford's) and made a earch, but could see no one. At ten minutes to one o'clock he went into Hewitt's farm again, when he heard men speaking in an out-building on the right. He was unable to open the door, and he asked "What is to do with von in there'? You are dis- turbing the whole neighbourhood," but there was no answer, and then he left, thinking the matter was an ordinary Saturday night's brawl. Inspector Spinks said that on Wednesday night, the 16th inst, he wept to Mr. Hewitt's farm at half-past ten, and saw the deaeased lying in one of the out-buildings He was very ill and cold, but he was quite Sensible. After informing him what the doctor had said about him, he asked him if he was aware he was in a danger- ous state, and likely to die at any moment. The de- ceased replied" Yes." He then told him he was about to take down in writing any statement he might chooae to make. The prisoner was not present, as he had left for Liverpool on his way to America. Ile made a state- ment which he signed in the presence of Thomas Spruce.' Inspector Cox, and Mr. Garnett, the relieving officer. The statement was to the effect that the deceased was 48 years of age, a native of Castlebar, County Mayo, Ireland, and that both he and prisoner were under the influence of drink when they arrived 'at Mr. Hewitt's farm on the night in question. The prisoner struck de- ceased with his hand and knocked him down and whilst he was lying on the ground he kicked him two or three times in the stomach and chest. On Thursday, the following day, witness went to Liverpool, where he ob- tained the Services of Detective Inspector Thornthwaite, of the Liverpool city police, who accompanied him on , board the Cunard liner Bothnia, which was bound for ' Boston. He arrested the prisoner, and, having cautioned him, told him he woe going to take him to Warrington' for having caused the death of Anthony Gibbons. The prisoner replied "I never did anything to him; he has ,been bad for a week; I never kicked him. I gave him a fist in the nose or face somewhere." Witness then brought the prisoner to Warrington, and in reply to the charge he said "I did not kick him. I should not have touched him, but I had a couple of shillings in my pocket, and he (Gibbons) wanted to take them from me. He was going to strike me, and I struck him a fist in the nose. That is all I done to him. I offered to bring him twice to the workhouse, and anywhere as he wanted. He was right enough yesterday aziorning when I left him." In answer to the Coroner, prisoner said he. did not wish to make any statement. The-Coroner having- recapitulated the evidence, the jury paid a visit to Mr. Hewitt's farmyard, where the quarrel was said to have taken place, and afterwards considered their verdict in private. The Coroner having been called int 6 the room, The Foreman said the verdict of the jury was that Gibbons had died from peritonitis, caused by the rup- ture. They believed, also, that the rupture was caused by the violence received from Michael Garner at. the time of the quarrel. The Coroner (to the prisoner) : It is my duty to com- mit you to the ensuing Assizes at Chester to take your trial for the manslaughter of Anthony Gibbons. PRISONER BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. At the Borough Police Court, on Wednesday morning, before , the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), Garner was

" BELLEROPHON" REDIVIPUS. Sir,—" Bellerophon," who is again on the warpath, tells us that from boyhood he has been in the habit of attending various places of worship, Church of England, Nonconformist, Roman Catholic, Unitarian, and even Agnostic. I think we have here an explanation of the amazing contradictoriness and inconsistency of the ideas he expressed in his previous letters. Is it to be expected that a persmi who has gone through such a "mixing-up" process from his boyhood upwards could display any coherence of argument? In his letter of last week we find the same old defects. He says that to deprive a publican of his license without compensation is a theft, but he never tells us how he comes to this extraordinary conclusion. To commit a theft is to take something from somebody that one has no legal right to. It would be extremely interesting to learn from " Bellerophon" in what manner the theft would come in if the State declared that licenses might continue to be withdrawn without compensation.—Yours, Szc.,
CADMUS.

WARRINGTON POLICE. Sir,-1 have been looking in the Court News of your last issue to see if I could find any trace of the distur- bance of the peace in the neighbourhood of Latchford Post Office on Sa.turday,May 12th, but can find none. It was my lot to be near the Railway Inn on that particular night, , a little after eleven o'clock, and while there, was much attracted by a great noise that was being raised by a number of men who had been drinking. The language they were speaking was excessively vile, not fit to pene- trate the ears of any intelligent being. It was, in fact, a case of "drunk and disorderly." I saw one of our policemen steal towards the fray, and was pleased to see how skilfully he fell upon them in the very act. May I ask, through your columns, why the offenders have not been brought to account for thus disturbing the general peace? I can see a case of one fined for being "drunk." but this exceeds that offence, in that it was not simply an act of personal injury, but the infusion of a tenor of evil in the peace lovers of the neighbourhood. Under the existing state of law, it is right and fair that one offender should suffer penalty for transgression as well as another, although I think an imperial enactment is in- consistent with itself, when it legalises a fluid of mad- less, and then punishes them when they do the actions of mad men. The person who made them drunk is an offender, but so common has the breaking of this law be- come, that it is almost, if not altogether, winked at.— Yours,

THE LICENSING CLAUSES--COMPENSATION. Sir,—l have read with interest your local tit-bits column, and note that all the remarks regarding the compensation clauses are very one-sided, and are dead against giving compensation to those who have em- barked in a trade which is as legitimate and honest as that of the grocer, tailor, shoemaker, or any other busi- ness, and is under more severe legal strictures, police surveillance and interference than all other trades put

together. I should like to know, and I take this means of asking your anti-conspensationists how would they act towards the many widows and orphans who, after losing their breadwinners, have invested their all in a public-house, its purchase, alteration, improvement, and decoration to render it as perfect as they could for its business require- ments, and have conducted it quietly and orderly. If the local authorities, or ratepayers' association, or other bodies get the above houses condemned, would these poor widows and orphans be cast on to the cold world without a penny? without any return for all they had expended in what they believed to be, and what actually was, a perfectly lawful business? If the compen.sation clauses are not passed, it will be impossible to dispose of the existing licensed houses so as to recoup what has been expended thereon. Perhaps some of your anti-compensation readers who have raised this "bitter outcry" against the Local Government Bill will pleas* reply, and explain how they would carry out, in above cases, the golden rule, or render simple juatice.—Yours, ONE PERPLEXED.

Sir,—! have just been reading, in your last Saturday's issue, the report of a meeting held at the Liberal Club on Thursday, the 17th inst. How I should have liked to be there! to listen to the clever sophistries of Mr. John Walker, the unctuously grammatical conceptions—(no, he said he couldn't concave, and what a blessing that was!) of Mr. Wm. Roberts, and the "knock em' down" arguments of Mr. E. Plinston, of whom Byron must have known a strong prototype, when he wrote: "Well might triumphant genii bear thee hence, Illustrious murderer of common sense !" Time fails me to point out some of the odd notions, which were, no doubt, intended to enlighten the meet- ing, but which," some considerable " must have fogged them. I will, however, return to the subject, by your permission, later on. Meantime, when a man whom all shades of pglitics—Radicals particularly—have cracked up as eminently endowed with common sense—l mean Lord Derby—says distinctly that publicans are entitled (and shows why) to compensation, it is enough for - me; and I should think, except in the case of those who are blind to all notions of equity, and who are led by the nose by that arch-buffoon, Sir Wilfrid Lawson, is amply sufficient for all lovers of fair-play. Besides, what good can there be in a cause that has , the "brand ef Caine upon it ?—Yours truly, BELLEROPHON. May 24, 1884,

"THE CHRISTIAN WORLD" AND MR. GLAD- STONE. Sir,—ln the issue of the "Christian World" for the 17th instant, the following paragraph appears respect- ing Mr. Gladstone's speech to the Nonconformist minis- 'tors, in the Memorial Hall, on the 9th May :—" Those who had not an opportunity of seeing or hearing Mr. Gladstone for some time must have felt on Wednesday the exceeding pathos of his reference to 'the life of an old man,' because the signs of increasing age were in- deed painfully apparent in the difficulty with which he made himself audible to those at a distance, in his in- ability to read some of his notes. and in his occasional failures of memory." I felt as I read the paragraph that whatever "exceed- ing pathos" there may have been, and doubtless was, in Mr. Gladstone's reference to "the life of an old man," there was exceedingly bad taste, to say the very least of it, in the criticisms upon his speech contained in the paragraph. Having been personally present when the speech was made, I knew its three criticisms to be un- founded, and felt impelled to write to the editor of the "Christian World " a letter of remonstrance awl con- tradiction. This letter, with strange impartiality (?) the editor has suppressed. As your columns are doubt- less read by many in this locality who are readers of the "Christian World," and who have of late been not a little disgusted with its Unionist tendencies, and consequent misrepresentation of the prevailing Non- conformist views, I venture to send you a copy of my first draft of the letter to the" Christian World," which, with some minor alterations in language I cannot recall, I sent to that paper.—Yours faithfully. JOHN YONGE. 13, Wilson Patten-st., May 25, 1885.
(COPY.) MR. GLADSTONE AT Tar MEMORIAL HALL. TO TAB EDITOR OF" THE CHRISTIAN WORLD."

Sir,--:I must ask you to allow me to take very serious exception to a paragraph in your last issue, in which you make some assertions respecting Mr. Gladstone's speech at the Memorial Hall, which I hold to be alto- gether contrary to facts. With what I cannot but describe as very doubtful taste, your paragraph asserts that Mr. Gladstone's speech displayed unmistakeable signs of his advanced age. It says that he had great difficulty in making himself heard. I happened to be at the very back of the hall, under the gallery, opposite the platform, and with the exception of a brief interval in the middle of of 75 Minutes, when, doubtless for relief, Mr. dropped his voice to his House of Commons tone, with perfect distinctness the entire speech from first t, last. Standing next to the Rev. Mark Wilks, I observed to him, "lie is in fine form to-day !" and Mr. Willks rejoined with emphasis, " Excellent !" lam bound to say that neither in the vigour of his delivery, nor in the vivacity of his gesture, did Mr. Gladstone betray any sign of his almost octagenarian age. You say, also, that his speech gave signs of failure ef memory. If so, my own memory is also failing, for I do not recollect noticing any such indications. But the most gratuitous and misleading statement of all is that 'he could not see to read his own notes." The accuracy of this I venture entirely to impugn. What Mr. Glad- stone could not see was a quotation from a speech by Lord Hartingten, presumably a newspaper cutting. The light in the hall was not bright, the print was pro- bably difficult to read from, and the fact that Mr. Glad- stone had to ask Dr. Clifford, the chairman, to read it for him, was one which ought not, in my opinion, to have been remarked upon by a religious Liberal journal. I must be allowed to say that, in my firm belief, this paragraph, reflecting so needlessly upon the great states- man, where the vast majority of Congregationalists and Nonconformists honour and revere, and whose political leadership they trustfully follow, is unworthy of "The Christian World." You, sir, are fully entitled, if you think fit, to express the views contained in your leading article in the same issue, in which you comment upon what you call the Nonconformist idolatry of Mr. Glad- stone, If those views are true, which I certainly do not admit, you are to be commended for their bold enuncia- tion. That, however, is one thing, but it is a very different thing from the entirely needless and inaccurate paragraph upon which I have ventured to remark. Against that paragraph, as one of your constant readers, for upwards of twenty-five years, I respectfully but most earnestly protest.—Yours faithfully, JOHN YONGE, Warrington, May 22, 1888.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continua fron page 6.) EASTHAM, INCE, Sm. The men have enjoyed the Whitsuntide holiday season, work being suspended from Saturday until Wednesday morning. A large mission hall is now in course of erec- tion here, right in the centre of the men's huts, and further preparations are being made to hold additional services in the camp. Up to the present a wooden stracture, which was built for stables, has been, and will be, till the new building is finished, utilised for a mission hall. The men are now busy on the second depth of the cutting, but a few are yet engaged on the first dip up by the wood, where the canal will enter the river, and cut across a small bay, coming into the land again at Pool Hall. The operations in the river will not be commenced for some time. During this week one of Murray's brick-making machines has been set to work, driven by a powerful engine of Ran.somes, Sims, and Jeffries. The machine is turning out a large number of bricks per day, but not so many as it would were the clay more favourable, when 1,500 an hour would be about the average. The bricks will be used principally in making culverts and bridges. A number of men are now busy in making a large culvert, which is to drain the land on that side of Eastham nearest the canal. Hitherto the land has been drained by means of an open ditch. Nearly all the huts that were erected last week are now inhabited, a few more men having been taken on during the week. At Ellesmere Port and Ince the holidays have also been observed by the men, and there ts nothing fresh of any account to report. RUNCORN AND WESTON. During the past week matters have been very quiet on these sections, and there is nothing new to report. The men had a holiday until Wednesday, but large numbers had apparently not got over their 'Whitsuntide junketings, and very few turned up to work on the morning of that day. Yesterday many navvies could be seen sauntering along the streets or lounging about some corner. Pro- bably next week active operations will be commenced on the Weston section. THELWALL AND LYMM. There is little to be added this week with regard to the works at Thelwall. Progress continues to be made at the same rapid rate, and now an additional steam navvy has been put in operation a little to the west of the river bend near Thelwall village. This navvy is known amongst the workers as the " Jubilee " navvy, and is of a different type to both the German and the American sorts. As in the case of the latter it works with a single bucket, but the bucket is manipulated in a different fashion. The makers of the new navvy are Whittaker Bros., of near Leeds. At Statham the operations are still lielayed by the negotiations as to the purchase of land to the north of the cutting, and a new roadway is being made so that the existing road may be cut away. WARBURTON. It is considered that the Rixton part of this section has such an elevation that it will be the deepest cutting in the line of the canal, and, therefore, it will be neces- sary for the steam navvies to sink three times before the requisite depth is obtained. On the west side of the Warburton New Bridge-road the cutting has been made to the required width for a distance of several hundred feet, but as yet no attempt has been made to increase the depth beyond 20 feet. The quantity of soil already moved is enormous, covering several acres of ground to the depth of 18 or 20 feet. The number of men now em- ployed on the Warburton section exceeds 500. There are six steam navvies here but at present three are idle, be- cause the ground is not prepared for the second cutting. Two steam pumps are at work night and day to keep the water out of the cutting, where the three steam navvies are to be fixed. There is a temporary hospital erected on the works by Mr. Walker, and at present it has one in- mate, whose foot was crushed by an empty waggon, but he is progressing favourably. Drs. Lovegrove and M. Bannister are in attendance for this section of the canal. EXTRACT FROM "THE TIMES." Referring to the Manchester Ship Canal "The Times" says :—The Ship Canal may be expected soon to have Its popular guide books, like the great trunk railways, pictorial and descriptive, not only of the work itself, but of all the places of interest within its vicinity. A route through some of the most rural and iteresting parts of Cheshire may well have claims upon the tourist, and there are many curious relics of antiquity included in it. Eastham and its woods are so familiar to the excursionists from Liverpool or Chaster that the pains taken in this notice to specify the situation to strangers runs risk of being scorned. Its admirers are already "loud in their wail" at the changes and the havoc that are being wrought. Hawthorne's notice of it as the pret- tiest village he had seen in England has been , widely quoted. Its ancient red stone church spire, and its still more ancient yew tree, are worthy of all veneration, and there is no need to detract from the highest opinion of the beauty of the place before the canal-makers invaded it ; but it is consolatory to note that Hawthorne's record of his visit occurs rather early in his" English Notes," and it is conceivable that the illustrious American afterwards made acquaintance with other English villages which he would himself have thought as delightful in all respects as the one he visited on the Ist of April, 1854„. The canal is being made as a highway of commerce, but there is, perhaps, no good reason why it should not also have its share of pleasure traffic. There are bad rea- sons to the contrary, but they ought to be re- moved. In Sir George Head's entertaining book of home travel, published about 1837, he devoted some cheery pages to the merits of canal journeys at ten miles an hour between Preston and Kendal. He seemed to think the pace killing for the horses, changed though they were about every four miles ; but for passengers the swift packet had charms which made good its com- petition with the stage coach. His experience of simi- lar locomotion between Liverpool and Manchester was less agreeable, the pace being slower, the company on a voyage rougher and ruder, and the water for a dozen miles from Cottonopolis filthy and" pestiferous?' These two evil qualities can hardly have mended in the the later years of the system yet there must be many persons left in middle life to remem- ber travelling, much nearer the half-century than Sir George did, by "the Duke's packets" along the Bridgewater Canal to pleasure sports like Dunkam, and to remember also the sensation of those in the swift boat as it haughtily gave the go-by to the cheaper and slower barges. The railways at length extinguished this diver- son. But if the Ship Canal Company succeed in their pressure of the provisions of Rivers Pollution Acts upon laggard local authorities, and get the Irwell and Mersey water purified for the ships of commerce, there inity be at least portions of its route that would continue to attract excursionists long after the fading of that interest of mere novelty which will at first draw crowds to visit the canal from end to end. Already the mere work of making it is enough to do so, and a weekly paper, the "Manchester Mer- chant," finds it worth while to make Ship Canal news and engravings and descriptions of the route its leading feature. The general curiosity cannot be gratified by complete surveys, but glimpses can be had at an increas- ing multitude of points, and since spring weather lightened the effort of holiday explorers they have thronged the county lanes, the ferry steamers, and other approaches to the canal works, which are seldom acces- sible without a walk or drive of considerable distance from the nearest town or village. To think of the Ship Canal as even partially a pleasure resort may conflict with some calculations of its entire banks blocked up with masts and warehouses ; but before that consumma- tion is reached a year or two of grace may perhaps be left to uncommercial sightseers.

A fire broke out on Wednesday in Dr. Walsh's house, Stonyhurst College, and was not extinguished until it had seriously damaged the roof and two bedrooms, with the contents. HORRIBLE MURDER IN OXFORDSHIRE.—A horrible murder was committed on Wednesday evening at Mil- ten-under-Wychwood, a village in the northern division of Oxfordshire. It appears that a labouring man named Hobert Upton, in the employ of Mr. Groves, builder, had been working at Shipton Court, the seat of Mr. Saniunda, a county magistrate, and returning home about six o'clock a quarrel ensued between himself and his wife. Subsequently Upton is alleged to have dealt his wife a fearful blow across the temple, instantly kill- ing her. Several neighbours state that they witnessed the deed, and Upton was arrested and conveyed to Chipping Norton Police Station. He was teken before the magi- strates on Thursday morning, and remanded on the charge of murder. MB HOSPITAL MATRON AND HER ALLEGED " CON- TEMPT."—A gentleman having called the attention of Sir Wilfrid Lawson to the fact that Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, had fined the matron of the St. Helens Cottage Hospital 40s. for refusing to attend an irnpaest, as re. ported in our last issue. Sir Wilfrid has replied as fol- lows:—" Thanks for yours. This holding of inquests at public-houses seems to be a very objectionable practice. I hardly know how the evil can be dealt with at present, but it is well to have public attention called to it as much as possible." Since the Coroner imposed the fine in question, Miss Stocks, the matron of the hospital, has explained that, while she had a strong objection to attending inquiries at public-houses, she, would have gone if she had understood her evidence was necessary. The nurse who went was the person present at the death of the man, and she was the only person who could give evidence. Mr. Brighouse has caused further in- quiry to be made in the matter, and having come to the conclusion that there was some misunderstanding, he has intimated to the matron that the fine will not be enforced.

CAIRO-STREET CHAPEL, WARRINGTON. HISTORICAL SKETCH. In a quiet street leading off one of the busiest thoroughfares in this town is a plain brick building, half-covered with tangled ivy. It stands in a pretty grave-yard, down the centre of which a path leads to a rather newer building, which, at the first glance, one recognises as a school-room. A board at the entrance to the grave-yard—one might almost say grave-garden—informs the visitor that the building is "Cairo-st. Chapel, for the worship of God." Secluded, yet in the centre of the town, it looks like a building with a history, and so it has. At a period when Warrington was known as the "Athens of Lancashire." this plain, unpretending edifice was as well-known as was the Warrington Academy itself. Drs. Priestley, Aikin, Enfield, and many other eminent divines, have occupied its pulpit, and men such as Howard, the philanthropist, Roscoe, the botanist, Pennant, the naturalist. a-41 Currie. the biographer of Burns. have listened in their oaken pews to the lofty discourses. The quiet grave-yard is full of monuments testifying • to the piety and worth of men once well-known on "Academy?" committees, and in other Presbyterian ! circles, of "Academy " students, " Academy " tutors, and townsmen of acconnt in the history of Warrington. , This, however. was not the first chapel built by the old Presbyterian congregation. The history of that congregation is a history common enough to , many old dissenting bodies. A history of change, • removal, division—yes, and sometimes of persecu- tion; but still, through all, the spirit of progress L remained with them and seems to abide there now. _ .

In 1662, Robert Yates, Rector of Warrington, was ejected from his living, under the " Bartholemew's Let," and, gaining a license from Charles 11, (the original of which is in the possession of Mr. F. Monks), he assembled a congregation at his house and ministered to them in the Presbyterian faith After a while, however, their meetings were held in the Court House, which stood in the Market Place, but as the congregation continued to grow, they at last built a chapel on the site of the present one. In 1678 Mr. Yates died. He had had a stormy life, and must sadly have wanted rest. At one time he lay under sentence of death, in Lancaster gaol, on suspicion of haying been concerned in the "York- shire Plot." By the aid of influential friends, how- ever, he was pardoned; but both he and his congre- gation were subjected for a long time to the greatest annoyance. His son Samuel succeeded him in ministering to the congregation. .After him fol- lowed in turn the Revs Peter Aspinwall, and Chas. Owen. Very little is known concerning the minis- try of these two gentlemen. The congregation seems to kayos steadily increased under their leader- ship, for in 1745, the last year of the ministry of Mr. lOwen. the old chapel was pulled down and the pre- sent one, which is very much larger, waft erected on its site. Another period of quiet followed as to which little is known. The Rev. Charles Owen was suc- ceeded by the Rev. John Owen, who, however, only ministered for a year. The Rev. John Seddon then succeeded to the vacant pulpit. Of him much more is known, for he became famous as the originator, and afterwards secretary, of the Warrington Academy, which, for nearly 30 years, made Warring- ton of some account in the literary world. He seems to have been a man who had one absorbing idea. He lived to see his great sch eme (the Academy)realised, but just as it was in the zenith of its glory he was seized with apoplexy when riding, and only sur- vived a few hours. His place both in the pulpit and in the Academy was filled by Dr. Wm. Enfield, who had been the mathematical tutor at that insti- tution. During Dr. Enfield's ministry many gradual changes were made in the doctrines preached in the chapel, which began to assume a Unitarian charac- ter. This became obnoxious to some of the old Presbyterians, andin 1779 they withdrew, and after a time built Stepney Chapel, in King-st., which was the foundation of Golborne-at. Baptist Chapel and Wycliffe Congregational Church. After the death of Dr. Enfield, the Rev. Joseph Beasley was called to the pulpit. During his mini- try, at a meeting of the members of the congrega- ' tion, it was unanimously decided to form a Sunday school. This school was at first held in the vestry, bet in later years. as its numbers increased, it was helcl in the chapel, and there are still members of the congregation who remember its being held there. Years passed on; the Academy had been closed long ago, and many ministers had in turn filled the chapel pulpit. Among them may be mentioned the Revs. William Broadbent and Francis Bishop. In 1846 the Rev. Philip Pearsall Carpenter, 8.A., was appointed pastor, and for 16 years ministered to the congregation. Under his active care new life seemed to spring up in the quiet chapel. A print- ing press was erected by him, and from it came books, pamphlets, hymns, and music of many kinds. Open-air services and temperance meetings were ' held by *he indefatigable pastor that attracted half the town; but his health failed him, and he went for a short time to America, where he received the degree of Dr. of Philosophy. On his return he found the chapel in such an unsanitary condi- tion that he obtained an Order in Council to close it. Great alterations were then made, and after some time it was re-oponed. He ministered there tor a while, but he wished to return to America, and so he resigned. He went back to Montreal where he died a few years later. A writer soon after said orhini= "He was a student of nature, a servant of God, and a lover of mankind. As a r her he was simple, faithful, and he' I as a teacher lov- ing and belovet in the service of men with a called foolish- ness." ted to th, .uemoi The Rev. J. N. .. Carpenter, and was in his turn Rev. 11. Vv. Perris. In 1877, however, Mr. Perris resigned, and shortly afterwards accepted a call to the Octagon Chapel. Norwich, and the Rey. R. Filcher, 8.A., was ap- pointed his successor. The memory of this gentle- man's services is still fresh in the mind of many Warrington people besides the members of his con- gregation. Besides his pastoral work, Mr. Pilcher took great interest in all the political questions of the day. He was a strong Liberal, and at the War- rington Liberal Debating Society his quiet wit and telling speeches were highly appreciated. As MI organizer and Sunday school worker, he had few equals; and his work amongst the young was par- ticularly successful. He gathered about him a band of young men with whom his influence was most plawerful for good. He established many evenipg classes, in which he was always the mainstay, and at which he sometimes gave elocutionary lessons in a manner which was the delight of those who heard him. He was genial, earnest, and indefatigable. His hand and purse were ever ready to help in any work of usefulness. Few men have gained such esteem during a nine years' ministry, and left bc- hind them such a record. A large stained window, representing the parable of the Good Samaritan, has been put in the south end of the chapel in memory of him: and in the Unitarian Church, Bradford, where he laboured 14 years ago, a similar tribute has been placed, showing that the work of a good man is not forgotten. The present minister, the Rev. Priestley Prime, was appointed in December, 1887. Mr. Pnme early entered the ministry, and studied at Manchester New College, London. For some time before his appointment to this chapel, he officiated as assist- ant to the Rev. Dr. Sadler, at Hampstead. Although he has been in Warrington for so short a time. he has already given valuable proofs of his ability both in and out of the pulpit. Both chapel and Sunday school, with the nume- rous institutions connected with them, are in the most flourishing state. The Sunday school contains nearly 300 scholars, and the difficulty will soon be to find room for its increasing numbers. On Sunday next the centenary of the chapel will be celebrated by special services; on Monday a public meeting will be held in the school, at which some of the most eminent men in the Unitarian body, as well as several of the older members of the congregation, will speak; and on Thursday the teachers and their friends s.re to celebrate the event by a social gathering in the same place.

The centenary of the School in connection with Cairo-st. Chapel will be celebrated to-morrow and Monday. To-morrow, sermons will be preached morning and evening by the Rev. James Drummond 8.A., L.L.D., of London, and in the afternoon by the pastor. the Rev. Priestley Prime. On Monday even- ing a public meetirg will be held in the schoolroom. The chair will be taken by Mr. Prime, and amongst the speakers will be the Rev. R. A. Armstrong, of Liverpool, Rev. C. C. Coe,--F.R.G.S., Bolton, Rev. H. E. Dowson, Dee Cross; Rev Joseph Freeston, Staley- bridge, and Messrs. W. D. Houghton, F. Monks, and T. Birchall!

H (LM) COMPANY. - On Saturday afternoon this company assembled at headquarters, and headed by the band, marched to Tatton Park, where they are camping out.

DRUNKENNESS AND DAMAGE—William Bowne, a man connected with the swing-boats at Lyrnm, was yesterday brought up before Mr. W. Armitage, at Altrincham, charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Lymm; and also with damaging the office door at Lymm police station. He was fined is, and ordered to pay 2s 6d damages. ACCIDENT AT THE BRASS WORKS.—A youth named Samuel Bond, son of Mr Samuel Bond, Statham, met with a somewhat serious accident at Mr Murgatroyd's brass works, near the station, on Tuesday afternoon. While tending a machine he, in some way or other, re- ceived a severe cut in the left hand. He was at once carried to the surgery of Dr Williamson, and his injury was attended to. ATHLETIC SPORTS AT OUGHTRINGTON.-0/1 Monday afternoon sports were held in Oughtrington Park, Mr. 0. G. Smith acting as handicapper and starter, and the Rev. W. G. Knocker as judge. The programme in- cluded 120 yards handicap flat race, quarter mile handi- cap flat race, obstacle race, wheelbarrow race, putting the weight, long and high jumps, climbing greasy pole, and tug of war contest. An entrance fee of one penny was charged for each event. The prizes amounted to £2 10s. WHITSUNTIDE.—On Monday, and indeed during the whole of the present week, Lymm has been visited by very large numbers of people from neighbouring towns. Most of the visitors, of course, came by rail, but num- berless vehicles, of almost all sizes and varieties, have also been put into use. Yesterday there was a consider- able number of school children from Manchester in the village, and these disported themselves in the usual games in fields which had been placed at their dis- posal.

div.head: FOOTBALL CHAMPIONSHIP. EARLESTOWN V. HAYDOCK.
div.p: THE FOOTBALL CHAMPIONSHIP. EARLESTOWN V. HAYDOCK.
tE ,KKKOLI

The second match for the handsome gold centre medals, and to decide the championship of the dis- trict, was played between the Earlestown and Hay- dock clubs, on the ground of the first-named or.zanisation, the Mesnes, Earlestown, on Saturday afternoon. It win be recollected that tne clubs in question were thrown out of the competition for the Wigan and District trophy on questionable grounds, arising from protests by their opponents, and as each clubs supporters and committee con- sidered theinselve, aggrieved by this seeming in- justice it was arranged that the two clubs should play for the championship of the district, the win- ners to have handsome gold-centre medals and the losers, handsome silver medals. The conditions of the somewhat novel contest were that a match should he played_ on the ground of each club, and that the team scoring the most goals in the aggreg- gate were to be adjudged the "Champions" and the winners of the gold-centre medals. The teams met on the ground of the Haydock club, last Saturday week, when the result of a hard-fought game was a draw— each side scoring two goals. The second meeting of the teams on Saturday after- noon, at Earlestown occasioned a widespread feeling of interest among the football enthusiasts of the two towns. The weather was brilliantly fine about noon, and there was a very large attendance of spectators. The home team was exactly the same as that whieh played in the first match, but the visitors left out Norcross and E. Smith, and substituted R. Whittle (of Preston North End Re- serve) and J. Mackey. The team also under-went some re-arrangement. The play during the first half was very fast and exciting, and was slightly in favour of Haydock, whose chances of scoring were spoiled by wretchedshoot- ing. In the second half after Kilner had left the field owing to an injury, the play was all in favour of Earle*. town. who pressari their opponents most severely. The closing period was a poor display of football and far below the standard of both organisations. As will be seen from the details below, Earlestown were declared the winners by three goals to none, and thus became en- titled to the claim of "Champions of the District," and the accompanying medals. The teams appeared on the field about half-past three, and took up their positions as follows: Earlestown :—T. Champion, goal; J. Green and P. Fazakerley, backs; Johnson, W. Allison, and R Ilowker, half backs; J. W. Sims and E. Morris, right wing; T. Siddeley, centre; J. Shaw and W. Shaw, left Wing. Haydock :—J. Taylor, goal; R. Whittle and T. Hat- ton, backs; .1. Stirrup, J. Kilner, and J. Smith, half I backs; J. Blackey and J. Knowles, right wing; J. Harri- son, centre; P. Twist and R. Stoddart, left wing. The visitors won the toss, and during the first half played with a strong breeze in their favour. Siddeley started the leather for Earlestown, and Kilner returned with a good kick. Fazakerley again sent the ball into the Haydock quarters, but Twist finished the "passage of arms" with a clever long shot, which necessitated Champion to use his hands in saving his goal. The brothers Shaw put in a splendid passing run, and Hat- ton to ease the pressure deliberately kicked the ball out, and gave a corner kick. This was taken by " Jimmy " Shaw, and a free kick by Bowker followed. The ball was nicely dropped in front of the Haydock goal, which was momentarily endangered, but "hands" off W. Shaw made the attack fruitless. The brothers Shaw were again applauded for another brilliant run, and" Jimmy" centred the leather beautifully. Whittle "headed" back, but Allison rushing up met the ball, and with a splendid shot sent it just beneath the crossbar, while Siddeley " took " the goalkeeper; and this scoring of the first goal for Earlestown—only three minutes from the commencement—was greeted with almost deafening en- thusiasm. On the game being re-started the Haydor" forwards played hard and passed fairly well, but fol.- the opposing backs and half backs in fine form. Stod- dart and Harrison made a good run up, and the ball was well centred, but Blackey "headed" it outside. A cor- ner kick for the visitors followed directly afterwards, but Smith sent the leather on the wrong side of the posts. From the goal kick the home team got into their oppo- nents' quarters through the efforts of Sims and Morris, and secured a free kick in front of goal. Allison was entrusted therewith and after an exciting scrimmage Morris pat the ball through the uprights but the point was disallowed on an appeal by the Haydock men. Harrison and Twist took the leather te the opposite end and evaded the backs: The Earlestown goal seemed their mercy and the ball was passed to Knowles, who M. a splendid chance of scoring, but with a wild kick he sent the leather flying over the crossbar. Haydock con- tinued to play well and kept up the pressure for some minutes, Blackey taking two corner kicks. From the second of these Harrison made a splendid overhead shot and almost scored, but Champion proved a veritable champion and saved almost miraculously. Smith took a corner kick at the opposite side of the field but he again sent the leather on the wrong side of the posts. After some play in the centre Stirrup, who had exhibited con- siderable roughness in his play, struck Siddeley and the play was stopped for a few minutes in which the referee (Mr. Lamont, of Liverpool) gave a warning and caution to the players. Kilner robbed Sims and Morris, but he in turn lost the ball at the feet of " Dick " Bowker, who was warmly applauded. The home half backs here- abouts exhibitedsome splendid play. Blackey put in a good corner kick and Kilner " headed " the ball into Champion's hands. Sims made a good "corner" at the opposite end and after some play in front of the Flaydock goal Morris headed outside. From the goal-kick Harrison dashed up the centre and essayed a long shot, but the leather went wide. Directly afterwards the same player shot into Champion's hands, and the latter was just in time to throw away before three of his opponents were upon him. 134ackgy had a chance of scoring from a good pass by Twist, but he put the ball outside the posts. Just on the call of half-time W. Shaw compelled Taylor to use his hands in order to save his charge. Half-time was then called, with the score—Earlestown one goal, Haydock none. Before play was re-started, Kilner, who had sustained an injory by a collision with Sid- deley, left the field, and the Haydoek team, thus weak- ened, seemed to become thoroughly disheartened and disor4anised. Directly after the re-start Morris put in a good shot, and Whittle, in attempting to clear, kicked the ball against Morris, and it rebounded through the goal, making the second score for Earlestown, amidht cheers. A heavy shower of rain fell for the next twenty minutes, during which the ball was continually in the Haydock quarters. The monotony was relieved by Champion being twice called upon to save his charge, directly after which the Earlestown forwards rushed %) the opposite end, where, from a free kick in front of the goal, Allison notched a third goal for Earlestown. The remainder of the play was in the Haydock quarters, but Harrison and Twist made several good combined runs. They were badly suynorted, however, and the leather was invariably retuited without much effort. The play of the Earlestown forwards was ludicrously slow, and their "shooting "wretched, while the Haydock goal- keeper and backs repelled any really dangerous attacks. When time was called Earlestown were declared the win- ners by 3 goals to none.
