A number of Quakers send a joint letter to the London papers protesting against the assumption that the recent document, emanating from 1,200 members of the Society of Friends, is an official declaration of the sentiments of that body on the Government's Irish policy. WRECK OF A YACHT.—A pleasure yacht belonging to Dr. J. H. Lister, of Manchestsr, sank on Tuesday night in Cardigan Bay through striking an old wreck. The boat was put down, and Dr. Lister and the crew escaped. They came ashore on Wednesday morning, having been out all night in the open boat. THE WORKING CON EXPLOSION.—At the Workington colliery explosion inquest, resumed on Thursday, very interesting evidence was given. It was stated that there had been a considerable quantity of gas in Hogg's Brow in the pit, and that in the opinion of more than one miner it was injudicious to fire a shot in the locality. One witness asserted that it would have been possible to bring up the remaining bodies of the dead if the explorers had not been stopped by some one in authority. The in- quiry was adjourned until to-day.

LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, FRIDAY. - Beef moves but indifferently at yesterday's rates. Pork continues to be firmly held. Bacon has met a steady demand, and previous values for all cuts, with the exception of Staffordshire cut middles, are maintained. In hams, long cuts are scarce and dearer ; short cuts steady at unchanged rates. Shoulders re- main without alteration. For cheese there is no appreciable alteration in prices, although the demand Is slow and irregu- lar. Butter is quite nominal. div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Preseot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday afternoon, when there were present :—Mr. J. Kenwright (chairman) Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. W Mid- dlehurst , J. Buckley, J. Whalley, W. G. Ashton, E. Rirchall, W. Tyrer, J. Ranson, J. Birchall, T. Eatock, J. Lowe, J. Fisher, J. W. Wareing, R. A. Graves, J. Leatherbarrow, J. Burchall, W. Twist, W. Swift, H. Hulme, R. Tuson, J. Griffiths, and S. H. Hartley (clerk.)

RELIEF.—The 'Workhouse Maste „r reported that there were 462 inmates of the house this week, 491 last week, and 472 in the corresponding week last year ; 68 vagrants had been relieved against 84 last year. A. QUESTION. FOR RELIETING OFFICERS.—The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board enclosing an extract from the report of Mr. G. Flazlehurst, district auditor, respecting the accounts of Mr. C. M. Stuart, relieving officer for Windle, for the half year ended at Michaelmas last, and asking for the Board's observations and the relieving officer's explanation thereon. The ex- tract in question stated that the school cards presented by the officer were unsatisfactory in many respects. In a great many instances the names of the school, the name of the teacher, and the periods for which the cards pur- ported to be were omitted therefrom. It added that te relieving officers generally complained of the difficulty they experienced in getting teachers of elementary schools to fill up the school attendance cards properly.—Mr. Swift said it was not part of the relieving officer's duty to fill up the cards.—The Clerk said if the Guardians ordered the relieving officers to do that it would be a reasonable order. He then read a letter received from Mr. Stuart, who explained that the unsatisfactoriness complained of arose from the careless- ness, indifference, or neglect of the various school teachers, who seldom filled up that part of the school cards which was left for them to fill up. Since the last audit he had endeavoured to secure a different result, but with what result remained to be seen. The Clerk (continuing) said he had a few of the cards, and explained that according to the statute unless all children of poor persons who were in re- ceipt attended school regularly the whole of the relief should be discontinued. The cards were provided ' to enable the relieving officer to ascertain whether all the children of poor parents were attending school, but there were no obligations upon the school masters or teachers to fill up the cards. That was a question raised in 1877, when the school teachers went in a body to the Local Government Board, and asked to be paid for that extra work, but they were told that the Board was not aware of any fund out of which they could be paid for the extra labour, and the Education Department upheld them in their decision. It seemed to him (the clerk) see- ing that the teachers in the Prescot Union had worked well with the Guardians, that the relieving officers should have orders to fill up the cards.—Mr. Burchall wired if there was any difficuky in filling up the cards, aid the Clerk replied that there was not.—The Rev. Dean Finegan then movedthat the relieving officers be re- quested to fill up the cards as far as they could, and ex- pressed the hope that the teachers would assist them as much as possible.—Mr. Burchall seconded the motion, which was passed. THE MASTER'S REMUNERATION.—A communication was read from the Local Government •Board approving of the payment of £25 to Mr. A. H. Hale, master of the Workhouse, in consideration of the extra services ren- dered by him. SAFES.—The Clerk reported that according to in- structions he and Mr: Leatherbarrow had examined several makes of safes, and had purchased three from Messrs. Milner at £47 10s.—This action was approved by the Board.
intim I

THR LATE MR.SILVESTER Mk-RM.—Mr. LeatherbarrOW drew attention to the recent death of Mr. S. Marsh, a former chairman of the Board, and expressed regret that they had no intimation as to when the funeral was to take place, so that the members of that Board could have attended. He thought they ought to express their thorough sympathy with the family, and he moved that a letter of condolence be sent.—Mr. Buckley seconded the motion, which was adopted.
This concluded the business.
Dr. O'Callaghan, Roman Catholic Bishop of Hex ham and Newcastle. has resigned. His successor is Canon T. W. Wilkinson, Vicar-general of Crook, Dur- ham.
UNJUST SCALES.—At the Prescot Police Court, on Tues- day, John Rowe, Grocer, Whiston, was summoned for having unjust scales in his possession, and was fined lOs and costs. •

"COERCION AND DRINK."—Sir William Harcourt, speaking at Southampton on Thursday, said the Unionist press was trying that morning to explain away the crushing defeat of Wednesday; but he denied that the Southampton election had been fought upon side issues at all. It had been fought upon the old issues of the Liberal cause, and he believed it had inflicted a fatal blow upon the iniquitous compensation clauses, and had also struck a blow at the coercion Government—a Go- vernment which had for its two main principles coercion and drink.
The late Mr. Matthew Arnold's personal estate has been valued at £1,040. In his will he leaves all to his wife.

The decisions of the Ulster Sub-Land Commission, just announced, embrace reductions varying from 20 to 25 per cent. At Gort, county Galway, on Friday, six young men were arrested in connection with the moonlight outrage committed there a fortnight ago. At least twenty thousand people left Bolton on Friday morning by the Whitsuntide trips. Blackpool, Liverpool and Southport were the principal resorts. A Canterbury, telegram states that the severe frost of the last few nights have played sad havoc with the Ken- tish fruit crop, reducing it probably by one half. The meeting to be addressed by Mr. Dillon in Kildare, on Sunday. is the first of a series organised to endorse the resolutions of the Dublin meeting of Irish Catholic members. For the past few nights a nightingale has been heard from eleven until two or half-past two a.m, within the private grounds of Captain Rowley Conway. three miles south of Rhyl. Mr. John Bright, writing to a Belfast Quaker, says the out-and-out attachment of some members of the Society of Friends to Mr. Gladstone is the result of emotion, and not of reasoning or of knowledge. A BRICKFIELD ON FIRE.-A large brickfield at Teyn- ham, Kent, was on Thursday set fire to by a spark from an engine, and was soon a mass of flame. Thousands of bricks were spoilt, and other property destroyed. Two hundred hands were employed, many of whom are de- prived of occupation. FIRE IN A WELSH COLLIERY.-All the men were taken from the pit at the Maritime Colliery by four o'clock on Friday morning. They were almost stifled by sineke, but were otherwise uninjured. Some of the burning timber actually fell into the pit, but the shaft being saturated with water, no harm was done. EXPLOSION ON BOARD A STEAMER. - The steamer Deutscher Kaiser, of Stettin, was proceeding down Shields harbour on Friday morning coal laden, when ac- cumulated gas in the hold exploded, blowing up the hatches and deck, burning the boatswain's face and hands, and throwing the pilot from the bridge. The ves- sel returned to Shields for repairs. ALLEGED FRAUDS BY A TOWN COUNCILLOR.-A war- rant was on Friday issued for the arrest of Mr. Joseph Markham, town councillor of Neath, a mineral water manufacturer and an accountant, who is charged with embezzling £450 belonging to Mr. Naylor. of Svi'ansea. Mr. Markham has left Neath suddenly for Paris, and it is believed he has now set sail for America. DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT GRIMSBY.-A destructive fire occurred at Grimsby on Friday morning, at the creosote and sleeper works of Messrs. Calder and Co., Alex- andra Dock. The fire was discovered about 3-30, and the Dock Company and Corporation steam fire engines were soon on the spot with their respective brigade. The outbreak was eventually subdued, but great damage has been done.

VISITORS TO HAWARDEN.—About 300 Liberal Unionists from Lancashire, Derbyshire, and Cheshire visited Hawarden on Friday, and were welcomed by Mr. Glad- stone, who, however, made no speech. Subsequently, while a trap containing six of the visitors was being driven towards Brough Hall station, the horse bolted, the vehicle overturned, and the party were thrown out, several being severely injured. ODDFELLOWS' Coiirsanwcs.—At the resumption of the Oddfellows' Conference at Gloucester, on Friday, the directors' and auditors' reports were passed. A new rule was adopted providing for the establishment of a Unity Travelling Relief Fund, each district to contribute on such scale per member from the Management Fund as the A.M.C. shall decide. It was also decided that lodgers neglecting to carry out the resolutions of districts shall be fined £5, and that the age scale in sick and funeral benefit be altered from "85 to 70" to 65 and upwards. ALLEGED MURDER IN LONDON. A dastardly outrage is reported to have occurred on Thursday night in York Terrace, Regent's Park, London. Two youths and two young women were walking in the direction of Park Square when they were attacked from behind by four men. The youths defended themselves and a free fight ensued, during which one of the four men produced a knife and stabbed one of the youths in the back. The men then made off. The wounded man died whilst being conveyed to the hospital. The attack is believed to have been the result of a feud existing between the parties. DARING OUTRAGE IN BIRMINGHAIL—This morning a mysterious discovery was made in one of the Birming- ham slums. At the back of New-st. Station a soldier was found in a state of insensibility in an entry, with his pockets rifled. He had come into the town from Plymouth with £65 in his pocket, and had gone out into New-st. to get a drink before going on to Liverpool, when he was accosted by two women, who took him to a brothel, where he was drugged, robbed, and then thrown out into the entry. He was seen by a detective to meet the women, who are of the lowest class, and a vigorous search is being made for the thieves, who can be easily identified. The victim of the outrage did not recover consciousness for several hours. THE MURDER OF A PRISON WARDER.—A man answering the description of Jackson, the Strangeways murderer, was seen on a ferry boat at Sunderland, on Friday. Jackson has not been seen at Durham. The inquest on the body of Webb was held at Strangeways Gaol on Friday, and a verdict of wilful murder was returned. —Seeking the Murderer at Warrington: kis said that a Manchester detective has been in Warrington since Wednesday morning, and has, in company with a local officer, made a round of the lodging-houses and lower public-houses of the town to see if there are any traces of Jackson, the Manchester murderer, in the town. It was rumoured on Thursday that a man, answering in slime respects to the description of Jackson, took a ticket from Warrington to Liverpool, but on inquiries being made, it was found that the man in question was a War- ringtonian, and had taken a return ticket. So far as we can learn nothing has transpired to encourage in any way the suspicion that Jackson has been in this neigh- bourhood.

div.head: MURDER AT NEWPORT.
div.p: MURDER AT NEWPORT.

At Newport Police Court on Friday, Ralph Jones, aged •twenty-two, labourer, was remanded on the charge of causing the death of Elizabeth Channing that morning. The deceased, who was prisoner's neighbour, accused him of breaking her window. Thereupon he ;struck her behind the ear with his fist, and she fell down dead.

EXPLOSION IN FRANCE.— PERSONS KILLED. Shortly before five o'clock on Thursday al. ,errible explosion took place at the well-known i. And cartridge factory kept by M. Morlot at Pantin, Pres A. Gervais. The effects of the ca.tasti..„ terrible, the building being almost entirely demoub._ So far 12 bodies have been discovered, the number of in- jured amounting to 30. The explosion was distinctly heard in the Rue Lafayette, and not long afterwards the news was known at the Prefecture of Police. Several doctors immediately started from Paris for the scene of the explosion. It is feared that a great many more lives have been lost than those reported, as the workpeople had not left the premises.

div.head: VEHICLE COLLISION AT LYMM.
div.p: VEHICLE COLLISION AT LYMM.

At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, Major Ritchie, of the 2nd South Lancashire Regiment, stationed at Orford Barracks, sued Mr. H. Lawley, cab pro- prietor, Lymm, for .£8 3s, the amount of damage alleged to have been received in a collision between Major Ritchie's " Stanhope " and a cab belonging to the defendant. The prosecution sought to prove that the collision was caused by negligence on the part of the defendant's servant, who drove the cab in Booth's-lane, Lymm. Mr. McConkey, barrister, instructed by Messrs. Evans and Lockett, of Liverpotl, prosecuted, and Mr. Byrne, barrister, of Manchester, instructed by Mr. G. L. Welford, of Lymm, appeared for the defence. Mr. McConkey having briefly opened the case, Major Ritchie stated that on the day in question he was driving in his "Stanhope" from Lymm to Warrington. A cab, con- taining a lady, preceded him along Uooth's-lane for about 100 yards. The " Stanhope " was about thirty yards behind, when the cab pulled up at right angles to the road opposite to Mr. Crreenall's gate. The cab- man glanced round, and he (the Major) thought he wished to intimate to him that he might go on. Witness drove on at a slow pace, and when just past the gate the cab backed suddenly into his carriage, damaging the panels, axle, 3rc. There was a space of three feet between the vehicles before the cab began to back. He asked the cabman what he had backed into them for, and the cabman denied having done so. There was a lady in the cab, which had a lot of luggage upon the top of it. Captain Kelly, also of the 2nd South Lancashire Regiment, who was driving with Major Ritchie at the time of the collision, and Thomas Drew, groom, in the employ of Major Ritchie, gave evidence to the same effect.—Edward Connor, coachbuilder, Warrington, gave evidence as to the damage done to the "Stanhope.'— Cross-examined by Mr Byrne, he said the carriage was 7 or 8 years old, and wanted painting, if the collision had not happened. He estimated the damage and painting the damaged parts at £5 3s, and painting the rest of the " Stanhope "to match at £3, making a total of £8 3s.— For the defence it was alleged that there was no negli- gence on the part of the driver of the cab, and that the collision might have been avoided by more care on the part of Major Ritchie.—Henry Booth, the driver of the cab; lsaac Mairs, coachman to Dr. Brabazon, Lymm; and Mr. Lawley, proprietor of the cab, having given evi- dence, his Honour gave judgment for £7 damages for the plaintiff, costs (including counsel's fee) to follow the verdict.

CRUSHED TO DEATIL—Jesse Wright, labourer, 28, em- ployed at Calder Vale Boiler works, was crushed to-death on Thursday morning under a large boiler which sud- denly rebounded whilst being rolled over on to the stocks. Wright leaves a widow and three children.

WORKHOUSE MASTER'S ASSISTANT WANTED.— The Guardians of the Warrington Union propose to appoint an active and intelligent single man to not as a general Assistant to the Master of the Union Workhouse. The per- son appointed must be healthy and strong, of good personal character, a good writer, and have a fair knowledge of book- keeping and accounts. His duties will be, under the super- vision of the Master, to assist in office work and render all such services as the Guardians or the Master may direct, information upon the nature of which may be obtained from Mr. Ward, at the Workhouse; or at the Clerk's Offices, Dew- sey Chambers.' The person appointed will be provided with rations, washing, apartments, 8.c., and (subject, however, to the appointment being determined at anytime by one month's notice on either side) will be paid wages at the rate of £2O for the first year, £25 for the second year, and £3O for the third year. Applications must be in the handwriting of the appli- cants, and must state age and previous occupation, and be sent to me, at my office, on or before Thursday; May 31st. By order, J. C. SUTTON, Union Clerk. Bewsey Chambers, Warrington, May 23rd, 1888.
